title: Software breach affects three Pa. courts and Environmental Hearing Board
description: West Publishing, a division of Thomson Reuters, said it detected unauthorized activity involving its C-Track case management system June 30.
text:
West Publishing, a division of Thomson Reuters, said it detected unauthorized activity involving its C-Track case management system June 30. (Getty photos)Three Pennsylvania courts and the state Environmental Hearing Board were hit by a cybersecurity incident affecting case management software that may have compromised individuals personal information.
West Publishing, a division of Thomson Reuters, said it detected unauthorized activity involving its C-Track case management system June 30. It announced the breach, which had been ongoing since March, on Sept. 2.
It affected more than two dozen courts nationwide including the Allegheny County, Monroe County and Washington County common pleas courts and the state Department of Environmental Protection’s (DEP) Environmental Hearing Board, which handles appeals to environmental permitting decisions.
Court administrators in Allegheny, Monroe and Washington counties did not respond to requests for comment or referred questions to the Pennsylvania Administrative Office of the Courts (AOPC).
A spokesperson for the AOPC said questions about the breach, including the scope and potentially affected information,should be directed to Thomson Reuters. The DEP did not immediately respond to questions.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Thomson Reuters said in a statement that it has notified all affected customers.
“There has been no operational disruption to C-Track as a result of this incident. Our products and services remain fully operational and are safe to continue to use. Independent cybersecurity experts assisted in the investigation and validated the remediation measures implemented,” a company spokesperson said.
In a notice online, West Publishing said the company promptly started an investigation into the incident, engaging law enforcement and third-party experts, and took steps to contain the unauthorized activity and its systems.
Based on the investigation, West said, a subset of court records was affected which could include individuals’ names, Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers, medical information, date of birth and health insurance information.
Confidential, redacted or sealed court information may also have been exposed in certain courts, according to the notice. 
“While these courts’ data was affected, the incident was not caused by the courts’ networks, systems or data security. There is no evidence that systems used to process financial transactions were impacted by the incident,” West said.
The company said it has no evidence the incident led to any fraud or misuse of information and it has undertaken significant mitigation steps to minimize the risk of fraud or misuse. 
West said it has undertaken additional security measures to improve the security of its systems and data. It also advised individuals who may have been affected to remain alert.
It offered support through a phone number, 833-918-5294, and complimentary access to the Experian credit reporting bureau’s identity protection service. More information is available at https://www.ctracknotification.com/

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Higher education in Pa. should challenge itself the same way we challenge our students.
description: Higher education teaches our students to ask hard questions. Colleges and universities should be ready to do the same.
text:
Indiana University of Pennsylvania (IUP) campus on Jan. 21, 2026. (Photo by John Beale for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Higher education teaches our students to ask hard questions. Colleges and universities should be ready to do the same.
That was the thought I shared recently during a summit of higher education leaders from across Pennsylvania. While I am chancellor for the 10 state universities of Pennsylvania, I believe it applies to every institution represented in that room and across the industry.
As the fall semester begins, colleges are urging students to be curious and brave, to push beyond their expectations, understand that taking a thoughtful risk can move them forward, and not to accept something simply because it’s always been that way.
Colleges and universities must do the same because the students we serve, and the world we’re preparing them to lead, are rapidly changing.
People on the University of Pittsburgh’s Oakland campus, with the Cathedral of Learning towering in the background on Feb. 6, 2024. (Photo by Stephanie Strasburg/Pittsburgh’s Public Source)
Pennsylvania is changing. It’s an aging state with fewer young people and a declining population in many regions, which leads to an overall shortage of workers. By 2032, our state is projected to have 218,000 jobs without enough workers with postsecondary credentials. What is our solution?
The universe of students who want a college education is also changing. Most higher education institutions are structured to teach 18-year-olds fresh out of high school. But increasingly, we need to educate working adults, such as mid-career workers who are balancing jobs, children, mortgages and more. What is our solution?
What about those who started college, but life “happened” and they got derailed? They took jobs, gained experience, and now want to strengthen their skills so they can advance their careers. But going back, or starting college for the first time, can be overwhelming. Pennsylvania has 1.2 million people who started college but left without a credential. What is our solution?
These are just some of the hard questions that Pennsylvania’s colleges and universities cannot ignore. We must be willing to push the boundaries of who we serve and how we serve them if we are going to find solutions.
The good news is we have remarkably talented faculty and staff who know how to solve problems. They know that the most critical skills our students graduate with will serve them throughout their lifetimes. The ability to think critically, solve complex problems, communicate clearly, work in teams and adapt to new circumstances are all skills that will allow humans to direct artificial intelligence, not be directed by it.
We should design every course, whether in the sciences, humanities, business or the arts, to strengthen these core skills. Doing it well takes time, something in short supply on busy campuses where people are pulled in many directions. We already do it well, but we can do it even better.
Addressing the workforce shortage means connecting with and supporting those working adults. It means awarding course credit for learning on the job, in the military and in life. That is harder than it sounds, but it’s worth the effort.
It’s also time to ask whether we should build more pathways to a degree. For some students, in a limited number of carefully selected programs, that could mean earning a degree in three years instead of four. Those programs would be built around the competencies that a graduate needs, but with fewer classes. That could give some students new options that better fit their lives while still meeting licensure requirements and demonstrating to employers that they can do the jobs. 
A statue of the Penn State Nittany Lion at Penn State’s New Kensington campus on Jan. 16, 2026. (Photo by John Beale for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Of course, challenging the status quo raises legitimate questions about quality and impact. I welcome that scrutiny because it leads to better solutions. We ask our students to assess difficult problems, challenge assumptions and find new opportunities. Shouldn’t higher education be willing to do the same?
No one can do it alone. It will take trade schools, community colleges, state universities, state-related institutions and independent colleges doing their part. Some are already leading the way. Many have room to improve, including my own system.
Higher education cannot control the future, the impact of artificial intelligence, or shifting cultural and economic forces. But we can control how we respond.
 We can ensure that every course strengthens the thinking and communication skills students need throughout their lives, better serves working adults and others who need more flexibility, and creates new pathways to a degree without sacrificing quality.
None of those solutions will be easy. But asking hard questions, considering new ideas and solving problems is exactly what we expect from our students. We should expect the same from ourselves.
Higher education changes lives. I am confident we can change too.
 
Christopher Fiorentino is chancellor of Pennsylvania’s State System of Higher Education.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Film explores the sack of New College
description: Ron DeSantis and his over-paid, under-qualified, anti-education Visigoths have been on a mission to ruin every college and university in Florida. Things have mostly been going according to plan. Mostly, but not entirely. Kids at Florida International University recently scored a small victory for free speech when a federal judge ordered the administration to[...]
text:
College Hall faces Sarasota Bay on one side on this visible side, faces the campus of New College of Florida. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Ron DeSantis and his over-paid, under-qualified, anti-education Visigoths have been on a mission to ruin every college and university in Florida.
Things have mostly been going according to plan.
Mostly, but not entirely.
Kids at Florida International University recently scored a small victory for free speech when a federal judge ordered the administration to stop punishing them for “expressive activities” indoors.
University President Jeanette Nuñez was hosting a “fireside chat” with Alex Rodriguez, former shortstop with the Seattle Mariners (just the kind of hard-hitting intellectual activity Florida colleges are becoming famous for), when 20 students in “ICE Off FIU” T-shirts stood up in silent protest.
They did not disrupt the event; they did not utter a single word.
That was the “expressive activity.”
And it was, as anyone with the least acquaintance with the First Amendment could see, constitutionally protected speech.
Nevertheless, university cops demanded the students’ names, threatening them with expulsion. University administrators disciplined them, demanding they record two-minute apology videos “reflecting” on their sins.
Wonder why the big brains at FIU didn’t sentence them to wear a scarlet “E” for “Expressive” and spend a night in the stocks?
The students had been trying get a meeting with President Nuñez to register their concerns over the university’s deal with ICE allowing campus police to crack down on supposed undocumented people.
The student body at FIU is 65% Latino: DACA recipients, F-1 visa holders, some asylum-seekers, and many, many children of immigrants.
Jeanette Nuñez, a child of immigrants, refused.
I mean, why should a university president actually speak to the students at her university?
 Contempt
The Board of Governors and the various university boards of trustees are now stocked with DeSantis’ hand-picked vandals.
Former politicians or businesspeople with no higher education experience have been made presidents of FIU, Florida A&M, Florida Atlantic, the University of West Florida, and, most famously (and egregiously) New College of Florida.
They demonstrate contempt for the institutions they run and the students who come to those institutions to learn and grow and the scholars who teach them.
They despise critical thinking; they want to push “patriotic education,” focusing on the fantasy of “American Exceptionalism,” pretending hard that our history of violence, racism, homophobia, and misogyny is either exaggerated or no longer relevant.
They are at war with the 21st century.
The pathological hatred that drives DeSantis and his vandals is on full display in “First They Came For My College,” a scorching documentary about how the state dedicated itself to destroying what once was a top tier liberal arts school, producing scores of Fulbright Scholars, Emmy Award-winners, musicians, politicians (some Republican!), and artists.
New College once prided itself on providing “an Ivy League education for the price of a good stereo.” Its new masters are turning it into a jock-and-Jesus junior college.
In the first scene, a student named Gaby Batista addresses the audience with a series of questions: “Who has been to college? Raise your hand.”
Batista went on: “Who’s been to Florida?” And, “Raise your hand if you’ve ever experienced a Christo-fascist takeover of your college.”
If that sounds a little dramatic, keep watching. It’s an understatement.
 Vandals
On Jan. 6, 2023, exactly two years after a MAGA mob rioted at the U.S. Capitol, hell-bent on overturning the 2020 election, a smaller bunch of MAGAs seized New College.
As Harry Hanbury, producer of “First They Came for My College” and a New College alumnus, says, “There’s no mistaking the point of that date.”
Ron DeSantis had sacked the entire Board of Trustees, replacing them with political allies who stomped into Sarasota, preening and sneering like low-rent Bond villains.
Few had ties to Florida, much less New College. There was a former member of Donald Trump’s “1776 Commission,” an outfit dedicated to pushing lies about American history; a climate change denier; a COVID conspiracy theorist; and Christopher Rufo, a think-tanker dedicated to protecting oppressed white people from DEI.
He’s the guy who ginned up the national moral panic over Critical Race Theory and assured the nation Haitian immigrants were, indeed, eating America’s pets.
Rufo’d seen a video of somebody grilling something at an Ohio backyard barbecue and swore it was a cat, never mind the “cat” had wings.
Rufo gleefully uses the language of violence, proclaiming, “we are over the walls and ready to transform higher education from within.”
It was, as the governor’s wrecking crew said themselves, “a hostile takeover.”
“I wanted to create a historical document,” says Patrick Bresnan, the documentary’s director, to “bear witness” to how Ron DeSantis’ hatred of what he calls “woke” and New College’s former students call “radical acceptance,” led him to target this small, diverse, welcoming institution.
Bresnan, whose work has won top awards at Cannes, Sundance, SXSW, and many other film festivals, wanted “First They Came for My College” to “empower the students to tell the story.”
 ‘They really don’t care’
Instead of spending a lot of money on a professional film crew, Bresnan hired New College students as his camera people, giving them iPhones with big hard drives. Young people like Gaby Batista and colleagues at The Catalyst, the New College student newspaper, chronicled the “hostile takeover,” from the trustees’ smug faces as they fired Patricia Okker, the president (she was insufficiently anti-woke), to refusing tenure for high-performing professors to throwing hundreds of books into a dumpster behind the library — the administration had shut down the Gender Studies Program, so who needs to read about LGBTQ or social justice topics?
Bresnan and his young collaborators play fair, bringing in students favorable to the new regime and trying to get Richard Corcoran, the cigar-chomping DeSantis ally installed as New College president, to talk to them.
Of course, he blew them off.
In one of the most powerful scenes, capped and gowned students surrounded by cops and monitored by surveillance cameras are subjected to one of the most chuckleheaded graduation speeches in history. Megabucks DeSantis campaign donor Joe Ricketts, famous for calling Islam a “cult,” drones on about how he became successful because he never spent money on fun things and his wife never bought a “new dress.”
The students decide they’ve had enough and begin to chant “Free Palestine!”
Ricketts gives up: “I hate it, but they really don’t care what I have to say.”
Corcoran comforts him, saying, “We will win, Joe.”
Maybe.
Maybe not. The young people in this documentary will give you hope for a better day. They are bright, funny, generous, and dedicated to carrying the tolerant, intellectually honest lessons they learned at New College out into a world in sore need of them.
They are Ron DeSantis’ worst nightmare.
 Four months
There are only four months left before Florida is finally rid of him, but don’t think he’s easing up on his mission to turn our colleges and universities into MAGA academies.
He’s the most proudly backward governor since (acting Gov.) Charley Johns, who, you will recall, dedicated himself to rooting out non-existent communist infiltration of the NAACP at Florida A&M and outing gay professors at the University of Florida.
In 2025, the state prohibited in-state tuition for undocumented students. Now we’re going to ban them altogether, even kids who may have been brought to the U.S. as babies, even ones with better test scores than many a Florida native high school valedictorian.
In addition to ridding ourselves of the foreign-born students and professors who may elevate both the academic and cultural qualities of our colleges and universities, why not also stop taking so many out-of-state students?
Who knows what “woke” ideas they’re bringing across the Georgia border?
The boards of trustees, usually weak-kneed in the face of governmental bullying, are not happy with this.
UF trustees chair Mori Hosseini called attempts to limit non-resident enrollees “a travesty.” FSU trustees chair Peter Collins called the move “ham-fisted.”
“I think the question you have to ask yourselves is, how good do you want us to be?” said Collins. “If you don’t want us to be great, yeah, we can start admitting a lot more students that don’t meet the criteria.”
Other than in football, the administration doesn’t much want our state universities and colleges to be “great” — unless their definition of “great” is Bob Jones University.
Meanwhile, New College has become a pitiful shadow of itself, fixated on teaching a retrograde version of American “greatness” and giving scholarships to hordes of baseball players with unimpressive test scores.
Spending is out of control: Educating each New College student costs around $134,000. The average in the rest of the state university system is $11,000.
Graduation and retention rates are plummeting. New College’s rankings are, too, falling almost 60 places since the takeover.
In an almost unbearably apt metaphor, Corcoran has bulldozed the college’s glorious nature preserve, destroying century-old pines and oaks and astroturfing the gardens.
As “First They Came for My College” recounts, they couldn’t even leave New College’s mascot alone, ditching the Null Set — which looks like this { } — and signifies both something and nothing.
Instead of a clever math joke, New College is now stuck with the “Mighty Banyon,” a cartoon tree.
“We were the canary in the coal mine,” says Gaby Batista. “New College was their little political playground.”
DeSantis, Corcoran and the rest of the vandals may think they’ve won: New College is now Bob Jones on the Beach.
But as long as there are smart, determined people like Gaby Batista and the makers of this documentary resisting and testifying, we’re not yet lost.
“First They Came For My College” is showing at venues around the state and at the Tallahassee Film Festival on Oct.11th.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s lakes bring families together
description: CT has an opportunity to create clear, commonsense, consistent wakesurfing rules.
text:
One of my earliest memories is climbing from my dad’s arms onto his back while he waterskied across Lake Lillinonah. I was three years old, and even then, the water felt like home.
Nearly 40 years later, boating remains one of the biggest parts of my life. Today, I’m fortunate to share that same passion with my wife and our daughter on several of Connecticut’s lakes, especially Candlewood Lake.

Christopoher Perry

For our family, boating has always been about more than spending time on the water. It’s an opportunity to share experiences, create lasting memories, and develop valuable life skills. Watching my daughter build confidence, develop perseverance, and learn to respect others on the water reminds me why these places matter so much.
Our experience isn’t unique, though. Connecticut’s public waterways are where grandparents teach grandchildren to fish, teenagers discover a love for sailing, families spend weekends together, and children learn to waterski. These lakes belong to all of us, and they should remain safe, accessible, and welcoming for everyone who enjoys them responsibly.
That is why the conversations taking place across Connecticut this summer about wakesurfing and public water access are so important.
As a lifelong boater and someone who teaches wakesurfing through camps and private lessons, I’ve learned that responsible boating starts long before a boat leaves the dock. It starts with education.
Every season I meet families who genuinely want to do the right thing. They ask where it’s appropriate to wakesurf, how to safely share the water with paddlers and anglers, and how to be courteous to nearby homeowners. When people understand not just the rules, but the reasons behind them, they make better decisions.
Safe wakesurfing means maintaining appropriate distances from shore, docks, swimmers, anglers, paddlers, and other boaters. It means avoiding repetitive passes, minimizing unnecessary noise, and recognizing that we’re all sharing the same public waterways. Those aren’t simply recommendations. They’re part of being a good neighbor on the water.
Education, however, is only part of the solution.
Today, most water sports in Connecticut are governed through a combination of statewide boating laws and locally adopted ordinances, meaning the rules can vary from one lake to the next. While general boating laws apply statewide, municipalities and lake authorities may adopt additional restrictions on boating activities. This patchwork of regulations can be difficult for boaters to understand and equally challenging for law enforcement to enforce consistently.
As communities continue discussing wakesurfing and public water access, I believe we have an opportunity to focus on what unites us by creating clear, commonsense, consistent statewide rules. Pairing those rules with strong boater education will improve safety while making it easier for boaters, lake communities, and law enforcement to understand what’s expected on the water.
Every time my family heads out on Candlewood Lake, I’m reminded of what these waters have given us: unforgettable memories, stronger family bonds, and lessons that extend far beyond boating.
When my daughter was just one year old, I held her in my arms as we slowly rode a wave together. Today she’s a dedicated wakesurfer, and watching her confidence grow has been every bit as rewarding as watching her skills improve. I hope that one day she’ll have the opportunity to share those same experiences with her own family.
Through boater education and clear, commonsense statewide rules, we can keep Connecticut’s public waterways safe, accessible, and welcoming for today’s families and for generations to come.
Christopher Perry of Brookfield is Sales Manager at Candlewood East Marina.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: No new data centers in New England until we write the rules on AI
description: I am calling for no new data centers anywhere on the New England grid until we have strict laws on AI and data centers.
text:
What would you want to know before a building that uses as much electricity as every home in Norwalk moved in down the road?
Who pays for the power? What happens to your electric bill? Who is watching what goes on inside?

Bob Duff

Those are fair questions. They are exactly the kind of questions we spent most of last year asking about housing. For months, the legislature debated how much the state could ask of our 169 towns. We argued over parking spaces. We argued over whether a two-family house could go up in a neighborhood. Towns wanted a say, and the law we passed makes sure they have one, with local plans for how each community will grow. It was a long fight, and it was worth having.
But while we were debating a duplex, something much bigger was getting ready to plug in.
A typical AI data center uses as much electricity as 100,000 homes, according to the International Energy Agency. The largest ones under construction will use 20 times that. Right now, Connecticut has no statewide rules on how much power these facilities can draw or who pays for the grid upgrades they require.
We spent a year arguing about a two-family house. A building that consumes as much power as a small city deserves at least that much attention.
That is why I am calling for no new data centers in Connecticut, or anywhere on the New England grid, until we have strict laws on AI and data centers. 
Our towns are not waiting, with some already passing local moratoriums on new data centers. But here is the problem: a town can say no to a data center. It can’t say no to the electric bill. New England shares one power grid. Imagine your neighbor ran an extension cord into your garage to power his new business, and the bill showed up in your mailbox. That is what happens when a massive new load plugs in anywhere on our grid. The strain does not stop at the town line or the state line.
So ask yourself a simple question. Would any family in Connecticut have agreed to pay more for electricity so a tech company could train a chatbot? Of course not. Nobody asked them.
We have seen what happens when lawmakers wait. Social media grew up with no guardrails, and now we have apps engineered to be addictive, a mental health crisis among our kids, and a small group of billionaire tech bros who got rich while the damage piled up. We are watching it happen again right now with prediction market apps that let anyone bet on a football game from their phone while claiming our state’s gaming laws don’t apply. We cannot let AI follow the same path.
Gov. Ned Lamont said in his State of the State address that Connecticut should slow down new data centers unless they bring new power generation with them. I want to build on that.
Connecticut has already started laying that foundation. This year, led by Sen. James Maroney, we passed Senate Bill 5, one of the most wide-ranging AI laws in the country. It protects kids from dangerous AI companions, makes sure workers are treated fairly when AI is used in hiring, and requires AI-generated images and video to be traceable. It was a strong step, but more work remains. 
We still don’t have rules for the energy these systems consume, who pays for it, and what happens to the workers whose jobs are on the line.
And this cannot be just a Connecticut fight. Last year, Washington tried to slip a 10-year ban on state AI laws into its budget bill. Through the National Conference of State Legislatures, Democrats and Republicans came together and said no: states’ rights should win on this issue. That provision was stripped out in the U.S. Senate by a vote of 99 to 1. The Trump regime has since tried again by executive order to stop states from protecting their own residents.
As president-elect of NCSL, I spend a lot of time with legislators from red states and blue states, and I hear the same concerns everywhere. Parents are worried about their kids. Workers are worried about their jobs. Seniors are worried about scams they can’t see coming. Nobody wants a higher electric bill. Sen. Maroney and I will take that to the national stage and work with lawmakers from both parties to write model legislation that any state can pass.
The order of operations matters. Rules first, then data centers. 
We gave a two-family house a full public debate. The least we owe our children, seniors, workers, and families is the same debate before the biggest power users in history move in next door.
Bob Duff (D-Norwalk) is Majority Leader of the Connecticut State Senate and president-elect of the National Conference of State Legislatures.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland is closing the gap. Here’s how to boost it.
description: Gov. Wes Moore has given mixed signals on the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, but the state has to opt in if it wants to take advantage, and it should, writes Jorge Elorza, who says that doing otherwise is just leaving money on the table that could help schoolkids.
text:
The latest news from Maryland’s classrooms may look promising at first glance, but a closer look paints a far more urgent picture. While academic gains have been real, the pace of change has been far too slow and notably uneven. 
Consider Baltimore, where fewer than one in three students read at grade level and multiple schools don’t have a single child doing math at grade level. Statewide, barely half of all students read at grade level, and for Black, Latino and special needs children, the numbers fall even lower. At less than a point of progress a year, Maryland is failing to close achievement gaps fast enough for thousands of kids.
There is a way to speed things up and reach those kids now at no cost to the state: It takes just one decision from Gov. Wes Moore.
Starting in January 2027, the new Federal Scholarship Tax Credit allows Americans to take up to $1,700 of the federal taxes they already pay and redirect those dollars to nonprofits that support K-12 students. The tax credit dollars can pay for tutoring, technology, transportation and special-education services for public school students.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Under this program, a Baltimore student falling behind in math gets a tutor. A Rockville child with dyslexia reaches a specialist her district can’t staff. A Cumberland teenager earns college credits his school is too small to offer.
Contrary to the messaging from its main opponents, the teachers unions, the tax credit is not a voucher program. It does not take a single cent from public education funding and would be entirely additive to the investments the state is already making. But first, Gov. Moore must choose to opt in. 
In public statements, the governor has given mixed signals. At a June meeting of the Education Writers Association, when asked about the tax credit program, Moore stated encouragingly that he would “never leave money on the table when it comes to supporting our kids.” By contrast, at the American Federation of Teachers’ national convention last month, he struck a decidedly skeptical tone; tying the program to Republicans and calling it a “tax scheme.” 
Moore has stated clearly that he opposes private school vouchers. But that’s not the question this program poses. If Maryland opts out, then $1.8 billion will automatically leave the state and go to the US Treasury. But if the governor opts in, Maryland residents can take advantage of the tax credit and send their money to local organizations that serve K-12 students, including those in public schools. The federal law has already passed and the money will be spent. The only  question is whether it will be used in Maryland or elsewhere.
The tax credit program can provide critical resources to help close academic achievement gaps. Affluent families already buy tutoring, test prep and enrichment out of pocket, thousands of dollars a year that compound into a widening advantage. Meanwhile, working families get left behind. This credit puts academic enrichment support within reach of the students who need it most. 
In a statewide survey last month, voters backed opting into the program 68% to 21% — Republicans (71%) and Democrats (69%) alike. Support ran highest exactly where the need is greatest: 78% among Black voters, the heart of the coalition Democrats represent. 
And here is what every Marylander should know: taxpayers can claim this credit whether or not the state opts in. If Governor Moore opts out, Marylanders can use the tax credit but only by sending their $1700 to organizations supporting students in any of the other 30 states already participating. 
Moore has built a national following by positioning himself as a principled, pragmatic leader who puts results over partisanship. That is why this should be an easy decision. Opting into the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit endorses no one in Washington, it simply keeps Maryland’s money in Maryland. A leader willing to do what’s right for Maryland’s children—whatever the source of the idea, whoever lines up against it—is exactly what this moment calls for.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Texas man canvassing for Tiffany charged with drunken hit and run
description: A Texas man hired to canvas neighborhoods for Republican candidate for governor Tom Tiffany has been charged with hitting a bicyclist with his car while intoxicated in a hit and run incident in Washington County, before fleeing police.  Duane Maiden, 32, was hired by Echo Canyon Consulting, a Phoenix-based political campaign and public affairs firm. […]
text:
Getty ImagesA Texas man hired to canvas neighborhoods for Republican candidate for governor Tom Tiffany has been charged with hitting a bicyclist with his car while intoxicated in a hit and run incident in Washington County, before fleeing police. 
Duane Maiden, 32, was hired by Echo Canyon Consulting, a Phoenix-based political campaign and public affairs firm. The firm confirmed Maiden’s employment, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported. 
The firm had received $2.5 million from the Florida-based Restoration of America PAC to support canvassing operations for Tiffany, according to campaign finance records, according to the Journal Sentinel. The PAC is heavily funded by the billionaire Richard Uihlein, cofounder and CEO of the shipping company Uline, based in Pleasant Prairie, Wisconsin. 
On Sept. 3, a Washington County sheriff deputy responded to a crash involving a car and a bicycle in the town of Jackson. The victim sustained injuries including fractures to his leg, pelvis, and spine. Witnesses said they saw a car “flying eastbound on Western Avenue,” blowing through a stop sign before striking the bicyclist and continuing on without stopping. A coworker of Maiden’s called 911 to say that he was with the driver and identified Maiden.
Deputies went to the Town of Cedarburg where the coworker had been dropped off, the Journal Sentinel reported. The coworker said that he and Maiden had come to Wisconsin to canvas for political campaigns. They planned to be in Wisconsin for the next two months before traveling to New York and Florida. They were working the morning of the crash. The coworker said that Maiden bought and drank from a bottle of Vodka before stopping for pizza and gas. 
After the hit and run, the coworker said, he asked to be let out of the car and then called both 911 and his supervisor
Deputies spotted Maiden’s car while talking to the coworker and chased him into Ozaukee County where they arrested him and took him to jail. Maiden said he started drinking and driving  because he had to wait too long between assignments. Maiden denied knowing that he hit the bicyclist.  
Although Echo Canyon Consulting claimed Maiden was not working for the firm during the hit and run, court records contradict those claims, according to the Journal Sentinel. 
Tiffany’s campaign denied any connection to Maiden. 
Maiden was charged on Sept. 4 in Ozaukee County Circuit Court for felony fleeing an officer and misdemeanor resisting. Then on Sept. 11, he was charged in Washington County Circuit Court for felony hit and run  involving great bodily harm and felony intoxicated use of a vehicle. He faces more than 27 years in prison and up to $95,000 in fines.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico ag officials announce expanded surveillance following new screwworm case
description: New Mexico agriculture officials on Friday confirmed expanded surveillance following the Sept. 17 detection of a second New World screwworm case, afflicting a horse in Grant County.
text:
A closeup of a New World screwworm adult fly. (Photo by USDA)New Mexico agriculture officials on Friday confirmed expanded surveillance following the Sept. 17 detection of a second New World screwworm case, afflicting a horse in Grant County.
“We are working as quickly as possible to increase surveillance, inspect animals and monitor for additional cases in and around the affected area,” State Veterinarian Dr. Samantha Holeck with the New Mexico Livestock Board said in a statement.
The pest, which has advanced rapidly through Mexico after being mainly contained in Central America for several decades, is named for the maggot’s behavior of feeding on live tissue. The fly made its first new incursion to the United States in early June, when it was detected in a south Texas calf. Officials subsequently identified a separate infection in a Lea County dog in New Mexico a few days later. The state has since stood up a stand-alone website, screwwormnm.org with resources and reporting information.
The expanded surveillance and fly-trapping following last week’s new case includes establishing a minimum 12.4-mile radius infested zone around the affected animal’s location, according to a news release from the state agriculture department, within which animals must be inspected and, if necessary, treated.
The agency says that routine animal movement, in which animals are transported to livestock auctions, fairs, vet appointments or other types of trips won’t be restricted unless an inspector identifies higher-risk situations.
In addition, the New Mexico Department of Wildlife (formerly the Game and Fish Department) is coordinating with the New Mexico Livestock Board to address wildlife surveillance and monitor hunting activities. The news release advises hunters, animal owners and others to “remain vigilant” and monitor horses, dogs and other animals for signs of New World screwworm, which include: wounds that don’t heal or worsen over time; wounds with maggots; wounds that smell badly; animals persistently licking or otherwise aggravating a wound; and any unusual behavior/irritation around the site of an injury.
“We appreciate the continued vigilance and cooperation of livestock producers, veterinarians, pet owners and other stakeholders as we respond to this second confirmed case of New World screwworm in New Mexico,” New Mexico Secretary of Agriculture Jeff Witte said in a statement. “Our immediate focus is expanding surveillance around the affected area so we can identify any additional cases as quickly as possible. Early detection and prompt reporting are critical to limiting the spread of this pest, and we encourage everyone to remain vigilant and work closely with animal health officials.”
United States Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins last week visited Santa Teresa last week to announce the opening of the cattle crossing there; which the agency says remains on track to take place on Sept. 24 despite the new case.
Additional information, maps of affected areas, reporting resources and updates are available at ScrewwormNM.org.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota’s top election official, a Republican, endorses a Democrat to succeed her
description: Four years after refusing to acknowledge the legitimacy of a Democratic president’s electoral victory, the Republican who serves as South Dakota’s top election official has endorsed a Democratic candidate to succeed her. “I understand that this decision will disappoint some people in my party and anger others,” Secretary of State Monae Johnson said Saturday[...]
text:
South Dakota Secretary of State Monae Johnson addresses the state Republican convention on June 27, 2026, at The Monument events center in Rapid City. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Four years after refusing to acknowledge the legitimacy of a Democratic president’s electoral victory, the Republican who serves as South Dakota’s top election official has endorsed a Democratic candidate to succeed her.
“I understand that this decision will disappoint some people in my party and anger others,” Secretary of State Monae Johnson said Saturday in a written statement.
The announcement was the culmination of a shift that Johnson had been signaling for several years.
She won her office in 2022 with the support of activists calling for changes such as hand-counting instead of machine-counting votes, due to allegations that vote-counting machines — which are not connected to the internet in South Dakota — could be hacked.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Some of the activists who supported Johnson were motivated by Republican President Donald Trump’s claims of fraud in his 2020 election loss to Democratic President Joe Biden. When South Dakota Searchlight interviewed Johnson before her election four years ago, she said “I don’t know” in response to a question about whether she believed those claims.
After she got the job, Johnson helped usher in changes including the implementation of post-election audits in all South Dakota counties, the results of which helped prove the accuracy of vote-counting machines. She did not pursue other changes, such as shifting from machine-counting to hand-counting all results, and she lost some support.
Four years after delegates at the Republican state convention backed Johnson as their nominee over an incumbent who was perceived as insufficiently devoted to changing election laws, delegates at this year’s convention chose Heather Baxter, a challenger who supports some of those changes, as their nominee over Johnson.
During the June convention, Johnson made it clear she had moved away from some of the positions of her former supporters. She referenced vote-counting machines when she said in a speech, “I fully support the use of secure, tested ballot tabulators.”

Heather Baxter addresses the state Republican convention on June 27, 2026, at The Monument events center in Rapid City just prior to winning the party’s nomination for secretary of state. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)

Then, on Saturday, Johnson endorsed Democratic nominee Terrence Davis to succeed her. Johnson made the endorsement in a written statement published by the South Dakota War College political blog. It’s operated by Pat Powers, a Republican who worked for a previous secretary of state.
Johnson wrote that after serving as an employee in the office and then in the elected post, “I know the difference between campaigning for this office and carrying the responsibility of leading it.”
“I cannot remain silent when I believe the integrity, stability, and professionalism of this office is at stake,” Johnson wrote.
She said her time in office taught her that in response to calls for overhauling election systems, the secretary of state “must consider the law, the information available, the effect on county officials, the security of statewide systems, the rights of voters, the cost and workload created by a change, and whether the proposal can be implemented within the deadlines the law requires. It also requires a willingness to review new information and change course when the evidence supports doing so.”
Johnson did not mention Baxter by name or identify specific concerns about Baxter’s positions but said “South Dakota deserves a Secretary of State who will strengthen confidence through performance rather than provocation; who will support election officials rather than burden them for political effect; who will protect voter access and election security without pretending those goals are enemies; and who will treat the office’s employees, voters, candidates, and business owners with dignity.”
Davis responded by writing on social media that he is “deeply grateful” for Johnson’s support.
“Monae and I come from different political parties. We will not agree on every issue,” Davis wrote. “That is exactly why her confidence in me means so much.”
Davis, a former state trooper, would be the first Democratic secretary of state in South Dakota since the late Lorna Herseth, whose last year in office was 47 years ago in 1979. Davis would also be the first Black person to win a statewide elected office in South Dakota. He advocates policies to make voting easier, including automatically registering all South Dakotans to vote on their 18th birthday.

Terrence Davis. (Courtesy of Davis for South Dakota)

Baxter is a Republican state representative from Rapid City who lost her reelection bid for that office in the June primary election before winning the party’s nomination for secretary of state. She responded on social media Saturday, writing that her win over Johnson at the Republican convention was not the result of “confusion.”
“The letter beside a name is not decoration,” Baxter wrote. “It tells voters what governing philosophy they will carry into the office that runs our elections and business services.”
Baxter also pledged support in her post for “election integrity” measures including voter identification, paper ballots and proof of citizenship — all things that South Dakota already requires. She did not call for hand-counting of votes in her response to Johnson. At the time of her nomination by the Republican state convention in June, Johnson’s campaign website said she wanted to “ensure every vote is counted accurately via paper ballots that are hand counted.” Her website now has modified language, saying she supports “improved hand counting methods.”
The race for secretary of state also includes a Libertarian nominee, Tamara Lesnar.
Besides overseeing elections, the secretary of state’s responsibilities include the management of campaign finance reporting, lobbyist registrations, business corporate filings and concealed pistol permits.
Advance voting for the Nov. 3 general election is underway, and the voter registration deadline is Oct. 19.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trinidad Chambliss and the Rebels put Lane Kiffin in the rearview mirror
description: Mississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss (6) celebrates his team's win over LSU during an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026.
text:
OXFORD — LSU knew better than any other team in America what it was facing in Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss. In this case, familiarity breeds not contempt but respect. Familiarity did not help the Tigers one single bit. The outcome of one of the most anticipated games in Mississippi history was on the line, and Chambliss stepped up and won it.
Rick Cleveland
That’s all he did. He won the game. Chambliss was, as he so often is, magical in the Rebels’ hard-earned 32-24 victory amid one of the most intense atmospheres imaginable. This game was dripping emotion from both teams and more than 70,000 fans.
READ MORE: Shakespeare could have written this LSU-Ole Miss football plotREAD MORE: The Grove, the crowds, the rivalry: Football fans party together, and taunt each other, on LSU-Ole Miss game dayChambliss’s numbers, impressive as they were, tell only part of the story, but let’s get that part out of the way. He did it with his right arm, completing 33 of 48 passes for 363 yards and two touchdowns. He did it with his legs, often racing away from a fierce LSU pass rush to throw perfect darts, and then scoring the winning touchdown on a 14-yard scamper with five minutes, seven seconds remaining.
When Ole Miss needed him most, Chambliss delivered. As Pete Golding said of Chambliss afterward, “He’s just such a fierce competitor. That’s why our guys believe in him.”
Mississippi head coach Pete Golding calls out to his team during the second half of an NCAA college football game against LSU in Oxford, Miss., Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
Lane Kiffin, Chambliss’s coach until Kiffin quit Ole Miss on the verge of the NCAA playoffs last year, called Chambliss “the most dynamic player in college football. … You scheme him up and you make good (defensive) calls, and he just makes plays. That’s why he is who he is.”
“Houdini plays,” Kiffin called them.
If you watched the game you know Chambliss didn’t do it by himself. The Ole Miss defense, especially in the first half, pursued with uncommon speed and aggressiveness. Rebel receivers made big plays, too, especially heretofore little-used slot receiver Traylon Ray.
“Traylon, who?” you might ask, as I did, when Ray kept making big catch after big catch. 
Traylon Ray, who transferred to Ole Miss from West Virginia last year, couldn’t get on the field as a wide receiver and was switched to cornerback because the Ole Miss really needed help at that position. That didn’t work out, either, but he returned to Ole Miss for his junior season when promised a chance to again play wide receiver. He didn’t catch a single pass last year. He caught four for 54 yards in the Rebels’ first two games this year.
And then came Saturday night when the Tallahassee native was targeted eight times and caught seven passes for 115 yards and one touchdown. Chambliss says Rebel fans should get used to it. “He’s great guy and a great player,” Chambliss said of Ray. “He made some really big plays tonight.”
The respect is mutual. “Trinidad has a lot of trust in me and I have a lot of trust in him,” Ray said. “Trinidad’s a gamer.”
LSU head coach Lane Kiffin, left, shows his disappointment to his staff as they lose to Mississippi during an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026. Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
Ole Miss needed players to step up because running back Kewan Lacy, the Rebels’ other superstar, missed the second half with a banged up shoulder after running nine times for 43 tough yards and a touchdown in the first half. JT Lindsey, a transfer from LSU, played well in relief of Lacy, running four times for 20 yards and a couple key first downs.
But let’s get back to Chambliss, who really might be the most entertaining player in the country and is currently in the first sentence of any way-too-early conversation about the 2026 Heisman Trophy. 
Let’s look at the four Ole Miss touchdown drives. On the first, which gave the Rebels a 10-0 first quarter lead, Chambliss completed all four of his passes for 70 yards, setting up Lacy’s five-yard touchdown lead. On the second Rebel TD drive, which put the Rebels up 17-0, he completed four of six passes for 37 yards, including a 21-yard TD strike to Ray.
On the third, after LSU had scored, Chambliss responded by hitting six of eight throws for 75 yards, including a 20-yard touchdown throw to Deuce Alexander for a 24-7 Ole Miss lead late in the first half. By that time, most of the 70,033 fans were dancing in the aisles. Vaught-Hemingway Stadium has rarely, if ever, been so loud.
LSU stopped all that dancing in the second half when the Tigers reeled off 17 straight points to draw even at 24. Momentum had done an about-face. After running only 14 times for 55 yards in the first half, the Tigers went physical and started pushing the Rebels around for 117 rushing yards in the second half, much of it right at the heart of the Ole Miss defense.
So that made the score 24-all and set the stage for the climax of Saturday night’s Trinidad Show. Chambliss drove the Rebels 75 yards in 12 plays, personally accounting for all the yardage. He completed six of eight passes for 62 yards, and then scored the winning touchdown with one of those “Houdini” plays. He faked a handoff to Lindsey and kept the ball around left end for a 14 yards and a touchdown. All but one Tiger bit on the fake, and Chambliss simply out-ran him. This storied old concrete stadium might or might not have shaken at that precise moment.
Mississippi running back JT Lindsey (26) runs into the end zone for a two-point conversion during the second half of an NCAA college football game against LSU in Oxford, Miss., Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
And then Ole Miss pulled one over on LSU, lining up for a two-point conversion. Just when some of us thought the Rebels coaches had gone mad, Chambliss fooled LSU with a hard count and the Tigers jumped offsides. So Ole Miss lined up, looking as if they would go for two again from the one-yard line. And guess what, LSU jumped again. So now, needing only 18 inches, Chambliss really did take the snap and hand the ball to Lindsey for an easy two points.
“We practiced that all week,” Golding said. “With an eight-point lead (and just five minutes left), we knew we couldn’t lose.”
It did get hairy. LSU, as talented as you would expect with a reported $50 million roster payroll, drove to the Ole Miss six. On fourth and goal from there, Kam Franklin batted Sam Leavitt’s pass high into the air and Jaylon Braxton snatched it to seal the deal and set off a lengthy on-field victory celebration.
“Congrats to those guys; they deserved to win,” Kiffin would say post-game.
“I’m just so happy for our guys,” Golding said before trying to set the tone for what comes next for Ole Miss.
“This wasn’t the Super Bowl,” Golding said. “Am I super proud of them? Yes. But this wasn’t our goal. We’ve got a really tough game next week against a really talented Florida team, We’ll celebrate tonight and then get back to work.”
Not to worry, said Traylon Ray, the Rebels’ newest football hero, “Tonight, we celebrate,” Ray said. “Tomorrow when I wake up, it’s back to work.”
The future of the Ole Miss team is filled with wonderful possibilities. That said, for all who bleed Red and Blue, the immediate past will be treasured no matter what comes next. 
Mississippi cornerback Jaylon Braxton (2) secures an end zone interception of a LSU pass during the second half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis

name: VTDigger
title: Towns move forward on regulating short-term rentals
description:
Attempts to regulate short-term rentals in Shaftsbury and North Bennington are on the way.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Towns move forward on regulating short-term rentals.
text:
A property with an AirBnB listing on Intervale Avenue in Burlington seen in Sept. 2023. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Mark Rondeau was first published in the Bennington Banner on Sept. 16, 2026.
Shaftsbury is in the process of developing a short-term rental bylaw, while adjacent North Bennington recently finalized the administrative process for enforcing its short-term rental ordinance.
According to Vermont law, short-term rental “means a furnished home house, condominium, or other dwelling room or self-contained dwelling unit rented to the transient, traveling, or vacationing public for a period of fewer than 30 consecutive days and for more than 14 days per calendar year.”
This does not include annual leases.
Statistics from the Vermont Housing Finance Agency show that available short-term rentals in the state grew from 6,753 in January 2018 to 11,194 in December 2025.
In Shaftsbury, the Planning Commission held a public hearing Sept. 9 on several proposed bylaws changes. After reviewing them again at its Sept. 23 meeting, it will forward them to the selectBoard. The board is required by the state to have two formal hearings on them before it votes. Major changes sought by the selectboard could return any of the proposed bylaws back to the commission.
The bylaw proposal drawing the most comment since Planning Commission Chair Tim Scoggins spoke about them with the selectboard at a meeting in July is the one concerning short-term rentals. Under the proposal, the owner must submit a fee and a copy of the short-term rental safety, health and financial obligations checklist, “a checklist that essentially someone who’s doing a short-term rental has to go through and make sure they’re doing all the right things,” Scoggins said in July.
The state considers renting to be a residential activity and the rental to be a public building and requires it to comply with state building and fire codes, according to the Vermont Short Term Rental Alliance.
The only public comment at the Planning Commission public hearing on Sept. 9 dealt with the short-term rental bylaw.
“Currently, short-term rentals are treated as a home occupation, and this is really no longer adequate given the changes that we’re making and the way the industry has grown, and we want to make sure that we’re not trying to limit anybody’s ability to earn money from a short-term rental,” Scoggins said. “Really, mostly what we’re doing is make making sure that landlords are aware of the current state regulations governing short-term rentals, which are fairly numerous, and collect information on what’s going on in Shaftsbury in terms of short-term rentals, just so we know where they are and how to react if there is an issue.”
The permit would come from the town zoning administrator, he said.
“It would just be a simple come in, fill it out, turn it in kind of thing. We would ask that the owners, when they provide the permit, that they provide a copy of the state’s short-term rental safety, health and financial obligations checklist,” he said. “That just pretty much tells short-term rental owners what they have to do, and it’s a checklist that they should be going through anyway when they’re proposing to do this.”
The original bylaw proposal included a $150 a year fee due on March 1 for a Shaftsbury resident doing business with a short-term rental.
“An owner or manager must be nearby and on call when the short-term rental is active to deal with any issues. The short-term rental owner is responsible for the renter’s compliance with our noise bylaws, and they must provide off-road parking for guests,” Scoggins said. “And currently, in the bylaws, short-term rentals are referenced only in rural districts. We’re proposing that they can happen in any districts.”
Short-term rental owner Art Whitman asked why the checklist had to be submitted every year if nothing changes. He also questioned the $150 fee. Kathy Whitman and Rachel Blumenthal agreed with his objections.
Zoning Administrator Carlyn Mickle, who has since become the town administrator, explained how she came up with that number: $150 is “half of one average night of rental here in Shaftsbury,” she said. “Basically, I looked up all the short-term rentals, made a list with all of their identifying information, and came up with an average of what one night costs, and that’s half of one night on average here in town.”
After the public hearing, Scoggins suggested taking the fee amount out of the bylaw itself and leaving it to the selectboard to decide the amount.
Planning Commission members discussed reducing the fee recommendation from $150 to $50, about the amount needed to cover administrative costs. This would be reduced to $25 if the applicant agreed to be listed in the town’s business directory. This fee is in line with that for applications to conduct occupations in the home.
According to housing data, Shaftsbury had 15 active short-term rental listings in December 2025.
North Bennington
The North Bennington Village Trustees recently voted to adopt an administrative policy for enforcing its short-term rental ordinance. It includes a $100 annual fee. The trustees adopted the ordinance in November 2025 but did not put into place a policy to enact it until this month.
“So, this has been around for a while,” said Trustee Chair Mary Rogers. “If we have an ordinance, it’s only a good idea unless you have some way to follow up and make sure that people are doing what they’re supposed to be doing.”
The ordinance assigns the lead task of administration to the village clerk. The clerk can ask for assistance from the trustees, which then will appoint one of its members to help, she said.
“So first and foremost, I would want to know what our clerk, Lori (Elwell) has felt about this policy and procedure,” Rogers said. “And was this something that you would request help for?”
“I think it’s fine. I don’t foresee it being so busy that I would need to request help,” Elwell said. “But if I do, I will ask one of you.”
Rogers described the administrative tasks involved. They would include accepting the short-term registration form.
“First of all, do the research, look on the VRBO, the Airbnb, whatever those sites are. Find out who is advertising things in North Bennington. Send the registration form, and perhaps a copy of the policy or whatever we need to that individual, and then request the fee,” Rogers said. “And it says that we do this by July 1 of every year.”
The North Bennington ordinance defines a short-term rental “as a furnished house or other dwelling room or self-contained dwelling unit rented to the transient, traveling, or vacationing public for a period of fewer than 30 consecutive days and for more than 14 days per calendar year. This includes both entire units and single rooms if the rental is for a stay of less than 30 consecutive days.”
This does not include month-to-month leases. Officials said that at this time they are aware of just two short-term rentals in the village.
Vermont statistics
In Bennington County, for December 2025, housing data lists the number of active short-term rentals in local towns: 26 for Pownal, 65 for Arlington, 69 for Dorset, 84 for Bennington, 92 for Peru, 201 for Winhall and 228 for Manchester.
According to the Vermont Short Term Rental Alliance, short-term rentals, or STRs, “represent ~3% of Vermont’s housing stock and ~65% of Vermont’s visitor capacity. Over $1 billion in annual economic activity is generated by Vermont’s STRs. More than 500,000 visitors stay at a Vermont STR each year, spending an average of $1,500 per visit at local businesses.”
Regarding short-term rental ownership in Vermont, the alliance states that “80% of owners operate 1 or 2 STR listings; 50% of owners are full-time Vermont residents; 55% of owners are over the age of 55 and are in or nearing retirement; 63% of owners are women.”
In addition, “55% of Airbnb hosts say hosting has helped them afford their homes.”

name: VTDigger
title: The state panel handling labor disputes in Vermont is short on members at a critical moment
description:
Members of the Vermont Labor Relations Board are appointed by Gov. Phil Scott. “I don't understand why the governor is taking so long,” one labor leader said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The state panel handling labor disputes in Vermont is short on members at a critical moment.
text:
State employees enter the state office complex in Waterbury as the Vermont State Employees Association opposes Gov. Phil Scott’s return to work mandate in October 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The Vermont Labor Relations Board, whose members are appointed by Gov. Phil Scott to resolve disputes between workers and their managers, has been down a third of its members for months — and hasn’t been at full strength in nearly two years.
Scott’s office says the governor is making progress on getting the board filled. But labor leaders argue the persistent lack of staffing suggests his administration is not prioritizing what they describe as a key safeguard for unions in the state.  
“It’s not how good government should function,” said Jeff Fannon, executive director of the state’s largest union, the Vermont NEA, in an interview. “It’s somewhat disrespectful — or unfair — to working people and employers who deserve, really, to have their cases heard and have their questions and issues addressed fairly and quickly.” 
The board’s executive director, Judith Dillon, said not since the end of 2024 has the panel had all six of its seats filled. Dillon’s administrative role supports the board’s six appointees, who also oversee union elections, investigate complaints of unfair labor practices and intervene when contract negotiations deadlock, among other roles. 
In the same time period the board has had slimmed ranks, the number of cases it deals with have increased, Dillon said. There were 62 cases filed with the board in 2025, compared to 48 cases in 2024, according to its data.
Among the board’s most high-profile recent decisions was an order in April rescinding Scott’s directive that state employees must return to work in-person three days a week. The panel’s order — which prompted Scott to accuse the board of bias against him — is now being reviewed by the Vermont Supreme Court. A ruling is expected soon.
Beyond state workers, the Labor Relations Board also weighs in on disputes at the University of Vermont and the Vermont State Colleges, as well as at municipal governments, school districts and private employers around the state.
Amanda Wheeler, a spokesperson for Scott, said in a statement that the governor’s office was in the process of appointing a new member to one of the board’s two current vacancies. The position, which has been open since June, should be filled by the end of next week, she said Tuesday. The other seat was vacated just last month.
State law says the governor must fill seats on the board within 60 days after they open up, though the process is not entirely up to him. The law requires the governor to pick from nominees suggested by a separate body, the Labor Board Review Panel.
Fannon, of the NEA, sits on the review panel and said in an email that even as someone who plays a role in the appointment process, “I don’t understand why the governor is taking so long.”
Steve Howard, executive director of the Vermont State Employees’ Association, also questioned the timeline, saying in an interview that it shows fully staffing the labor board “hasn’t risen to the level of priority” for the Scott administration. 
Asked why the governor hadn’t kept the board full, Wheeler pointed to “the added layer of oversight” created by the separate panel and said it can be hard to recruit qualified candidates. 
“It’s also important to note that throughout this process, the Board has maintained a quorum and been able to continue to carry out its work,” she said. 
Beyond the two seats open right now, another recent appointment to the labor board took the Scott administration far longer to finalize. 
Wheeler said Tuesday that Scott had appointed Linda Joy Sullivan, the former mayor of Newport and a former state legislator, to the board effective Sept. 1. Sullivan was appointed to the seat previously held by a member who stepped down at the end of 2024.
The seat is one of two on the board for members whose backgrounds aren’t closely tied to labor or to management, known as “neutrals.” Of the four other seats, two are for members who have more experience in organized labor and two are for those who have served in management.
According to Fannon, the review panel finished interviews for that neutral seat in January, after which he said the Scott administration would have had candidates to choose from.
Even though Sullivan’s appointment took effect Sept. 1, according to Wheeler, it wasn’t until Tuesday, Sept. 15, that the governor’s office informed Dillon that Sullivan had been appointed.
That was the same day VTDigger first contacted the governor’s office asking about the status of labor board appointments. When VTDigger first spoke to Dillon last week, she was under the impression the seat was empty — and that the board had only three current members.
The board has been able to get by with fewer than six members, Dillon said. It needs a bare minimum of three to function, she explained, with a goal of cases being heard by one panelist each from the labor and management perspectives, as well as one neutral.
Still, she said the board members are regular citizens who work part-time and for modest pay. A post last year soliciting applicants cited members making $125 per day. Having fewer members, Dillon said, means more work for each.
Citing the board’s increased workload, Dillon raised concerns to state legislators earlier this year that the board was able to dedicate just three days for hearings in 2025 compared to an average of 14 days over the decade prior.
Operating with just one neutral member for the better part of two years also made it difficult for the board to get its work done, Dillon said. It meant the sole neutral member it had before this month’s appointment, Gwenna Peters, had to attend a number of more meetings and hearings than she would have otherwise.
“We’re very excited,” Dillon said of the new appointment. “The statute was designed and created to have six people, and it’s best to have six people, and we’d love to have six people.”
