name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Outsider farm owners are an issue in the governor’s race. Here’s what experts say.
description: As agricultural land prices have increased drastically over the past two decades and young, want-to-be farmers have an increasingly difficult time starting their operations, politicians nationally, and here in Iowa, have questioned if corporate or foreign interests are to blame.  Iowa gubernatorial candidates Zach Lahn and Rob Sand both have said corporate o[...]
text:
Formalized ownership of Iowa farmland is becoming more popular, but researchers say this is mostly due to succession planning. (Photo by Jared Strong/Iowa Capital Dispatch)As agricultural land prices have increased drastically over the past two decades and young, want-to-be farmers have an increasingly difficult time starting their operations, politicians nationally, and here in Iowa, have questioned if corporate or foreign interests are to blame. 
Iowa gubernatorial candidates Zach Lahn and Rob Sand both have said corporate or out-of-state ownership of Iowa farmland is a problem and have suggested policies that would tax Iowans at lower rates than out-of-state or investor landowners.
 But ag land researchers say that much of the rise in formalized farm land ownership – through LLCs, trusts and corporations – is tied to succession planning and that the out-of-state or institutionalized owners are usually people with direct ties to Iowa.
A report on 40 years of land tenure and ownership in Iowa shows a “continuous shift” away from individual and joint ownership, to more trusts, limited liability companies and corporations. The most recent land survey, conducted in 2022, revealed 9% of Iowa farmland was held by LLCs, 6% by corporations and 23% by trusts. 
In 2002, just 1% of farmland was owned by LLCs, 7% by corporations and 8% by trusts. 
Why is the trend moving away from individual or joint ownership of farmland?
Rabail Chandio, an assistant professor of economics at Iowa State University who studies the domestic farmland market, said transition and succession planning was the “primary motivation” for the increase in “formal” ownership styles.
“Especially when farms are becoming larger, there are a lot of successors involved, there’s a lot of heirs involved,” Chandio said. “There’s a person who has three kids, each of their three kids has a few kids again. It’s very hard to divide a 1,000-acre farm eight ways or 10 ways and then operate it as a separate 100- acre operation in today’s economy.” 
The report notes that nearly 40% of Iowa farmland is owned for “family or sentimental reasons” according to survey responses. This is an increase from 22% of land kept for this reason in the 2012 survey. 
Chandio said as folks move away from Iowa, but retain ownership of their family land, putting the land in an LLC allows them to serve as a shareholder and receive a percentage of the returns from farming or from cash rents. Holding the land in a trust, she said, allows owners who are away from the farm to get a percentage of the farm’s returns, based on the stipulations of the trust. 
Iowa groups ramp up campaigns for and against data centers

Kristine Tidgren, the director for the Center for Agricultural Law and Taxation at ISU, said there are “really, really good reasons” from a legal perspective, for a family to put their property in an LLC. Tidgren said it gives owners liability protection and protects outside assets from things that happen with the land, and she said it offers “great” ways to manage and transfer property. 
“It is a legal entity that is designed for managing a business, or property owned jointly for business purposes, and so it has built into it lots of provisions, and then it allows you to customize those provisions in ways that work best for your family,” Tidgren said. 
For example, if a set of parents want to pass their farmland down to their children, but only one of the children wants to farm, holding the land in an LLC that is separate from the farming business would allow the non-farming children to receive some monetary interest from the property without interfering in the farming operation itself. 
As part of the trend of more landowners living out of state, the 40-year farm survey analysis shows 58% of farmland is leased and nearly 80% of leased land is owned by non-farmers. 
According to the report, over half, 55%, of farmland is owned by someone who does not farm, though this figure has remained fairly stable over the past two decades. 
The report also notes that 25% of farmland is owned by someone who is either a part-time Iowa resident or not an Iowa resident. This is also a growing trend noted in the report. In 1982, just 6% of farmland was owned by folks who didn’t call Iowa home. By the early 2000s the share topped 20%. 
Fourteen percent of all Iowa farmland owners were categorized as nonresidents, according to the report.
Iowa candidates for governor call for transparency, tax changes
Lahn, the Republican candidate for governor, has spoken about out-of-state and LLC land ownership along the campaign trail and said he would push for “human level disclosure” of land ownership in Iowa, if elected. 
Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn answered questions from reporters at his West Des Moines campaign headquarters April 2, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“We actually don’t know who owns our land in Iowa,” Lahn said on the Tucker Carlson Show in February. “There’s not human level disclosure that’s required, so you can own land in an LLC and that LLC could be wholly owned by a trust, and all the state knows is that the LLC owns the land.” 
Chandio said in conversations she has had with farm managers and land appraisers – people who are regularly dealing with acres that aren’t owner operated – most of this is land not held by people with “out-of-state ownership that is not tied back to Iowa.” 
“A lot of these people are the second-generation or the third-generation farmers who have inherited the land, but they themselves have a career elsewhere that makes them either not be a full-time Iowa resident or travel for work, and then these forms of ownership keep them tied to the land,” Chandio said. 
Iowa’s ag land laws, Chandio said, also “generally keep” the majority interests in LLCs “in people who are in Iowa, farming in Iowa.” 
Iowa’s anti-corporate farming laws restrict the types of corporations or LLCs that can own Iowa farmland. Iowa law allows for LLC ownership when the LLC is a “family entity,” meaning it is majority owned by people related to one another, was founded for the purpose of farming or owning ag land and can show that a majority of its gross income comes from farming. 
The law also allows “authorized” entities to own farmland as an LLC but these companies are capped at 1,500 acres and can’t have more than 25 owners or beneficiaries. 
Tidgren said Iowa’s restrictions are “stronger than most states” to prevent entities like real estate investment trusts from swooping in and buying up farmland. 
“We have to look at the real facts and the real data, and it does not appear from the facts that Iowa farmland is being owned by out-of-state entities or foreign owners,” Tidgren said. “That that just doesn’t bear up under the facts.”
While there are “always exceptions to the general trend” and there might be some out-of-state owners with no ties to Iowa who are purchasing land, Chandio said she doesn’t think that’s a “big enough number to be concerned about.” 
Why does it matter if land is owned by people out of state?
Lahn has said the growing share of out-of-state landowners in Iowa presents a “real generational issue” where people who own the farmland aren’t part of the communities. In an interview on Iowa PBS, Lahn said absentee landowners are usually the first landowners to agree to development projects that members of the local community might oppose. 
“And the reason is, they’re looking at Iowa’s land as a cell in a spreadsheet,” Lahn said. “How much money can I make off this piece of land? They’re not looking to say, ‘What would this do to the community that’s surrounding it.’” 
Dan Capodilupo, a spokesperson for Lahn’s campaign, said the issue is that “too often, LLCs are used to circumvent Iowa laws restricting certain types of ownership.” 
“By requiring human-level disclosure, Zach will enforce the laws on the books, especially against foreign land ownership,” Capodilupo said in an emailed statement.
To help farmers who live and farm in Iowa, Lahn proposed lowering property taxes for Iowans and raising property tax rates on “institutional investors.” 
Iowa Auditor Rob Sand, running for Iowa governor in 2026, gave a speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 15, 2026 at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Sand, the Democratic candidate for governor, has also proposed tax changes that would benefit buyers who stay in Iowa. In his “Opportunities for All” platform, Sand proposed taxing out-of-state landowners at a higher rate than people who live and farm in Iowa, as well as initiating a “ban” on “hedge funds and LLCs” purchasing “too much” Iowa land. 
A Sand campaign spokesperson, Emma O’Brien, said in an email that “Iowa land belongs in Iowa hands.” 
“The plan would make it harder for out-of-state land owners to use LLCs and hedge funds to buy up Iowa land while also taxing them at a higher rate,” O’Brien said. “But while Rob is looking to protect Iowans from out-of-state interests, Zach Lahn used his network of LLCs to buy up Iowa land while living in Kansas.”
Public record searches show that Lahn’s Belle Plaine farm house and surrounding properties are owned by Selah Group LLC or Selah Properties LLC, to the attention of Lahn. The LLC is also listed on properties Lahn owned in Montana. 
Foreign-owned land in Iowa
Lahn has also said he would “confiscate” any land illegally owned by China and sell it to young farmers or veterans, if elected. Stopping foreign ownership of agricultural land has been a priority of the Trump administration with the launch of a National Farm Security Action Plan and an online portal to report foreign land ownership transactions. 
 “No foreign adversary should own Iowa farmland,” Capodilupo said. “Iowa land belongs in Iowa hands.”
An analysis from Chandio looking at federal Agricultural Foreign Investment Disclosure Act data, found that “foreign interest in agricultural land has grown over time” nationally, with an average 2.6 million more acres in foreign holdings, annually, since 2017. 
At the national scale, foreign individuals and entities were reported as holding an interest in 3.5% of privately held agricultural land, but Chandio wrote that in the Midwest and Iowa, “foreign-held acreage accounts for an even smaller share of total land” due to strict agricultural land laws. 
The report, and an interactive database from ISU shows the majority of foreign-owned ag land in Iowa is used for wind, solar or other energy uses. 
Chandio’s report looked at AFIDA data from 2010 to 2023 and found that across the period, foreign ownership has remained under 2% of Iowa’s total agricultural land. Canada and Italy claim most of the foreign-owned land in Iowa. 
Tidgren said there are “pain points” for beginning farmers trying to buy Iowa land, but she said it has to do with the price of land, not the entity that owns the land. 
Part of this, she said, is because of tax laws that would require certain taxes on the land to be paid only when it’s sold, and because people are holding on to land for sentimental reasons.
“It’s a tough subject because again, there are just maybe some misinformation or just misunderstandings,” Tidgren said. “It’s sometimes difficult to even know how to assuage those fears.”

title: How many crashes will it take to build a roundabout?
description:
Two dangerous Chittenden County intersections have known fatal crash histories, yet proposed roundabouts to fix them face years of delay.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  How many crashes will it take to build a roundabout?.
text:
Dear Editor,
I am discouraged by the discussions about possible roundabouts in Chittenden County. The intersection of Route 2 and Clay Point Road in Colchester, just off Exit 17 on the way to Grand Isle, has seen multiple fatal crashes in recent years. A study by the Chittenden County Regional Planning Commission suggested a roundabout as a solution. The cost was estimated at more than $5 million, and the Vermont Agency of Transportation thinks it would take 10 to 20 years to complete.  
At a recent meeting on the proposed change to a roundabout at the intersection of Route 116 and Route 2A in St. George, the Transportation Agency official running the project said it has been a high-crash area for a long time, although he didn’t know how many crashes specifically, which seems unprofessional to me. He added that construction wouldn’t start until 2030.
What on earth is the holdup? How many crashes or deaths do we accept during a permit process for a roundabout?  

READ MORE

It isn’t the high taxes that bother me. It’s that the value we get doesn’t seem to line up with the amount we are putting in.
Roger BrownRichmond, Vt.

name: VTDigger
title: As financial hardship drives owners to give up pets, Vermont can’t rehome them fast enough
description:
“It got really, really rough,” one former owner said of her efforts to keep hold of her dogs. “That’s not a fair life.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  As financial hardship drives owners to give up pets, Vermont can’t rehome them fast enough.
text:
Angela Barrows hugs 4-month-old Tina after adopting her at a Wag It Forward pet adoption event in South Burlington on Sunday, September 13, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Until last year, J.A. and her husband had been able to support themselves, their kids and their two dogs in their Bennington County home without financial strain. She had a “really great job” in the ski industry, and he recently retired from work at a liquor store. 
Then, their circumstances changed without warning. J.A., whose full name VTDigger is not including given the sensitivity of her story, began to suffer from two separate autoimmune conditions, which caused crushing fatigue and chronic joint pain. Her conditions left her bedridden some days, she said. She left work last August and was quickly approved for disability support. Six months later, her husband was diagnosed with two forms of cancer and began an intensive course of chemotherapy. 
“We’re trying to, you know, make the money go everywhere,” J.A. said of the couple’s suddenly fixed income in an interview Thursday. “But it — it doesn’t.”
In seeking a new home for her Great Dane and Labrador mix, J.A. joined what rescue volunteers and shelter staff across the state believe is a growing share of Vermonters who are giving up pets for financial reasons. But with shelters full to bursting and rescue operations rushed off their feet, appropriate new homes are often difficult to find.
It’s a worry that extends well beyond Vermont. Across the country, rescue and shelter staff say former owners are citing the high cost of living as a primary driver in their decision to rehome pets. In shelter data compiled by the national nonprofit Best Friends Animal Society, housing and general economic strain accounted for roughly a quarter of surrenders in 2025, with owners giving up more pets overall so far this year. 
The costs associated with pets’ medical treatment and nutrition have risen considerably in the last few years due to inflation and supply chain issues, according to Lisa Milot, Vermont’s first-ever director of animal welfare. Some veterinary practices have also closed or reduced since the Covid-19 pandemic, raising new access challenges for the state’s stretched animal health network and impacting pets’ health and safety, she added.
“These aren’t the luxuries,” Milot said in an interview Thursday. “These are just what you need to be treating your animal baseline humanely.”
The Lucy Mackenzie Humane Society in West Windsor has seen a significant increase lately in the number of people seeking to surrender their pets due to financial hardship or housing insecurity, said Jackie Stanley, the organization’s executive director. Stanley’s facility — like most other brick-and-mortar shelters in the state, Milot and others have heard — has a perennial waiting list for accepting new animals.
As they adjusted to their new financial reality, J.A. and her husband realized they couldn’t afford vet bills when their dogs showed signs of illness. And the couple found themselves rationing dog food, which didn’t sit right.
“It got really, really rough,” J.A. said. “That’s not a fair life.”
But finding a viable alternative caregiver proved nearly impossible. J.A. reached out to more than 30 shelters and rescue operations across Vermont, New Hampshire and Maine, she said. She even tried appealing to the public through Facebook; several pages dedicated to pet rehoming in Vermont have thousands of members. 
Before finally finding a shelter for the dogs, she had been turned away each time due to lack of capacity. More than half of the organizations she contacted responded by asking her to consider euthanasia for the dogs, who are aged 3 and 8.
“I was like, no,” J.A. said. “That’s not an option.”
Increasingly, the hundreds of owners who come to the state’s rescue network each year are citing a heavy financial burden of care or changes in housing, according to Courtney O’Brien, who is a town animal control officer in Enosburgh and secretary for Vermonters Against Animal Cruelty and Abandonment.
“People love their pets,” O’Brien said, “but if it comes to feeding their kids over their pets, or taking their kids to their doctor’s offices over their pets going to the vet’s, like, they’re going to do that.”
Commonly, clients are experiencing housing insecurity, O’Brien added, and can’t take their pet to the low-cost rental home or shelter they’re moving into. Renters are often bound by landlord-imposed restrictions on pets, Milot noted, a problem property owners do not face. 
Rescue nonprofit For The Love of Dogs Vermont saw a “real uptick” in requests during recent periods of instability for Section 8 housing voucher recipients across the state, according to the nonprofit’s co-director Melissa Goldberg.
Goldberg said she gets so many requests from owners to take dogs off their hands that she must regularly turn people away. This year has been the most intense since the organization’s founding in 2020, she said.
“It is one of the most frustrating, heartbreaking issues to have these people begging for help, and there is nothing we can do,” she said.
Stanley said one major part of the problem is a lack of centralized data to keep track of available homes and pets that need them.
Milot said that such a database could certainly be a useful tool, but noted that such a system is not a standard service for state governments to provide. She encounters a related information deficit with stray dogs, she said, which are also becoming harder for state and town officials to track due to declining registration rates. Vermont’s 64,000 licensed dogs might account for just half of the state’s overall population, she added.
Milot said rescue and shelter staff across the state tell her that in the past, the number of pets owners were giving up could be processed and rehomed relatively easily.
“That has changed,” she said.

name: VTDigger
title: This Vermont documentarian has filmed three decades of hard things. So why is she now focusing on hope?
description:
“We can hear all the horrible, hateful rhetoric, but most human beings want to help each other out,” Bess O’Brien says of her new slice-of-life movie “Every Day: Big and Small,” set to tour the state this fall.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  This Vermont documentarian has filmed three decades of hard things. So why is she now focusing on hope?.
text:
Members of Vermont’s Writers for Recovery support group hug in a moment from Bess O’Brien’s new documentary “Every Day: Big and Small.” Photo courtesy Kingdom County Productions
Vermont filmmaker Bess O’Brien had finished her last documentary — the 2024 on-the-ground look at food and housing insecurity, “Just Getting By” — when she hungered for a change.
“A lot of my films through the years have tackled big issues,” recalled O’Brien, whose feature about drug use disorder, “The Hungry Heart,” made national news after it inspired then-Gov. Peter Shumlin’s 2014 State of the State address. “Going into this next election cycle and where we are right now in this country. I wanted to do something hopeful.”
And so O’Brien aimed her camera at Luke’s Military Museum in Danville, where teenager Luke Morrison has filled a backyard trailer with artifacts donated by local veterans.
“Thank you for coming,” Morrison can be heard telling visitors.
And Habitat for Aviation in Swanton, where young women learn the aircraft business by building and maintaining single-engine, two-seater planes.
“You got it, girl,” students there assert.
And the High Horses Center for Equine-Assisted Services in Sharon, where Vietnam War veteran Gayle Smith, approaching her 80th birthday, rides regularly to temporarily outrun her physical and emotional challenges.
“Instead of going downhill, I’m going uphill,’” Smith says.
Aiming to share those feelings, O’Brien has spliced 90 minutes of such moments into a new documentary, “Every Day: Big and Small,” set to premiere in Burlington on Friday before touring a dozen Vermont cities and towns this fall.
“It’s about community; it’s about connection; it’s about resiliency,” O’Brien said in an interview. “We can hear all the horrible, hateful rhetoric, but most human beings want to help each other out. I wanted to go to places all over the state where people are doing good things.”

Vermont filmmaker Bess O’Brien had crafted documentaries for three decades. Photo by Mary Claire Carroll/courtesy Kingdom County Productions

O’Brien began in her Northeast Kingdom town of Peacham, where flooding in 2024 ravaged the riverside home of her friends John and Jenny Mackenzie. The film could have focused on the big $181,355 haul of a GoFundMe page to help the couple and their children with rebuilding. Instead, it spotlights a miniature sock elephant whose tiny red scarf attracted attention amid the rubble.
“It was the saddest little thing you’ve ever seen,” Jenny Mackenzie says on camera. “I washed it five times. The sink water would turn black.”
Today her daughters find comfort in the return of a favorite childhood toy.
“There have definitely been small miracles,” the mother says.
Moving on, O’Brien took Mackenzie’s suggestion to meet Kevin Zheng, a student who works at his family’s East Garden Chinese restaurant in St. Johnsbury. Zheng’s mother and father run the business seven days a week so their children can be the first generation to go to college.
O’Brien filmed Zheng amid a kitchen of flaming woks. His parents know more Chinese than English. But the footage of his mother hugging him after seeing his acceptance letter to Dartmouth College speaks volumes.
So goes the movie, hopscotching to places ranging from the Rutland Elks Lodge, where a drag performer lipsyncs to Dolly Parton’s “9 to 5,” to Goss’s Mud Bog in Barnet, where upward of 1,000 locals shake their heads and smile as neighbors attempt to speed cars and trucks through a field of muck.
“I wanted to be as diverse as possible,” O’Brien said. “I wanted men, women, young people, old people, people from different socioeconomic backgrounds, different races. And I was interested in very granule, grassroots stuff.”
The documentary is set to debut Friday in Burlington before moving on to screenings Sept. 26 in Williston, Sept. 27 in Middlebury, Oct. 1-2 in Montpelier, Oct. 4 in St. Johnsbury, Oct. 5 in Barton, Oct. 6 in St. Albans, Oct. 7 in Randolph, Oct. 8 in Barre, Oct. 9 in Brattleboro, Oct. 10 in Rutland and Oct. 11 in Woodstock.
O’Brien — whose past projects have addressed such subjects as Vermonters fighting substance use or eating disorders, entering foster care or exiting prison — has always sought to find silver linings. But this is her first documentary to showcase them from start to finish.

READ MORE

“We shot more stories than we could get in,” the filmmaker said of her latest work. “Once you start telling people what your movie is about, they say, ‘Have you heard about this? Have you heard about that?’ I could have just kept shooting and shooting and shooting. There are extraordinary things happening every day.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: The 2020 Mississippi Legislature embraced runoff elections despite racist origin
description: A voter marks her ballot at Fondren Presbyterian Church, Tuesday, Nov. 4, 2025 in Jackson, Miss.
text:
Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson’s recent reminder that there will be no possibility of runoff elections in Mississippi’s upcoming U.S. Senate and House races conjures up memories from the historic 2020 legislative session.
The 2020 session of the Mississippi Legislature will be remembered for removing some long lingering links to the state’s racist past, and for that, lawmakers should be commended.
The Legislature, most notably, removed the old state flag that displayed the Confederate battle symbol prominently in its design.
Replacing the flag was not the only action taken by the 2020 Legislature to deal with vestiges of the state’s racial sins.
They also removed a Jim Crow provision of  the 1890 state constitution designed to make it more difficult for Black Mississippians to be elected to statewide office.
At the strong insistence of U.S. District Judge Daniel Jordan of the Southern District of Mississippi, the 2020 Legislature put on the ballot a proposal to amend the state constitution to remove a provision saying that if no candidate for statewide offices (not federal posts) garnered a majority of the vote and the most votes in a majority of the 122 House districts, the House would select the winner from the top two vote-getters. The provision, it was clear from the narrative of the day, was put in the 1890 constitution to prevent Black people, who at the time constituted a majority of the state’s population, from winning the office of governor or any of the other Mississippi statewide posts.
Surprisingly, Vermont is now the only state that still has a provision throwing statewide elections to its Legislature if no candidate obtains a majority of the vote.
The Mississippi Legislature in 1890, the year a constitutional convention formed with the stated goal of disenfranchising Black people. Several provisions of that constitution have been the subject of lawsuits in recent years, most recently a requirement that statewide candidates capture a majority of state House districts to win election. Credit: Wikimedia Commons
While Mississippi legislators removed some of those bygone connections to racism and the state’s Jim Crow laws during that historic session, they embraced another – runoff elections. They replaced the House electoral process for statewide officeholders with a runoff.
It should be noted that the Legislature opted to place on the ballot for voters to decide a proposal to adopt the runoff in place of the electoral process. Legislators could have just as easily not included the runoff provision in the proposal or at least have allowed voters to decide whether to have a runoff or do like the vast majority of states and recognize the person with the most votes – a majority or not – as the winner of the election.
 By adopting the runoff, Mississippi joined Georgia as the only other state that mandated a runoff if no statewide candidate garnered a majority in a general election. The Georgia provision applies to both federal and state offices while in Mississippi, as Watson pointed out, the runoff occurs only for state offices.
So, in the Nov. 3 U.S. Senate election in Mississippi, the candidate – Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, Democrat Scott Colom or independent Ty Pinkins – who captures the most votes, majority or not, will win the post.
Interestingly, Georgia imposed its runoff in the 1960s when the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the state’s electoral provision that was remarkably similar to Mississippi’s that was removed in 2020.
According to published reports, Denmark Grover, the then-Georgia legislator who played a key role in creating the runoff, did not try to hide his intent.
“If you want to establish if I was racially prejudiced, I was,” he said years later. “If you want to establish that some of my political activity was racially motivated, it was.”
Louisiana also has a runoff election, but the circumstances are different since the state does not have traditional party primaries. Instead, candidates from all parties are on the same ballot and the top two vote-getters, if no one obtains a majority,  advance to a runoff.
A handful of states, mostly those from the South where Jim Crow ruled for decades, have runoffs for party primary elections if no candidate obtains a majority.
But only Georgia and Mississippi go that step further to require runoffs in the general election.
As Georgia trends blue or toward the Democratic Party, it will be interesting to see if there are efforts to remove the runoff there.
And if that happens, Mississippi will be the only state with a general election runoff and it is not a remnant of the state’s racial past. It was adopted in the 2020s.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas fought hard to rein in social media. It needs to do the same with AI.
description: The multibillion-dollar settlement Arkansas and other states reached with Facebook parent Meta validated a cause that’s been a rare area of bipartisan consensus: reining in social media. Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders has pushed for limits on teens’ use of social media and screen time, while fellow Republican Attorney General Tim Griffin is fighting TikTok, Sna[...]
text:
Signage at the official announcement of the Google data center in West Memphis on Oct. 2, 2025. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)The multibillion-dollar settlement Arkansas and other states reached with Facebook parent Meta validated a cause that’s been a rare area of bipartisan consensus: reining in social media.
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders has pushed for limits on teens’ use of social media and screen time, while fellow Republican Attorney General Tim Griffin is fighting TikTok, Snapchat and several other platforms in court. The crackdown is one of the few times you’ll find the GOP figures on the same page as high-profile Democrats like California Gov. Gavin Newsom.
Growing concerns about artificial intelligence offer another bipartisan opportunity for Arkansas and other states to check technology before its harms become even more entrenched.
Inaction from Congress and dismissals by President Donald Trump of calls for AI guardrails show states can’t rely on the federal government alone to respond to warnings that the technology could “kill us all” before the end of the decade.
Such concerns were once easily disregarded as the fears of “doomers” and modern-day Luddites opposed to any technological advancement. But Anthropic’s CEO pushing for the industry to slow down AI development will make it harder for state lawmakers to ignore the issue when they convene next year.



Let us know what you think...


 


Arkansas doesn’t have to wait for Washington to catch up to the threat. As it demonstrated with fights against social media giants through lawsuits and legislation, the state recognizes a role in protecting citizens when technology firms won’t.
“The states are the laboratories of democracy, and I am proud of Arkansas’ bold actions,” Sanders wrote in a letter to congressional leaders urging passage of the Kids Online Safety Act.
The effects of artificial intelligence are already showing up in Arkansas’ politics, with communities pushing back against data centers needed to power the technology and calling for an end to the use of Flock surveillance cameras. Polling repeatedly shows bipartisan concern about data centers and artificial intelligence overall.
That doesn’t necessarily open the door for Arkansas and other states to regulate the development of AI. A technology that doesn’t stop at state borders and federal preemption may make regulation in Arkansas difficult.
But it’s still possible, as California has proven with new laws that include a state registry for AI auditors. Illinois and New York have also enacted measures aimed at regulating AI development. 
There are plenty of other ways for Arkansas to address the harms of AI.
That includes curbing AI in the classroom, as it has with cellphones and social media. Following New York City’s example, the state could place a moratorium on AI’s use in elementary and middle school classrooms.
Arkansas can also ensure that its citizens are protected against AI being the decision-maker on whether they keep their jobs and health insurance, or are eligible for public benefits. And lawmakers can push for more transparency when AI is used by health professionals and seek disclosure from AI companies on what data is being used to train their models.
And just like the state pushed for a minimum age for using social media, Arkansas can place similar limits on companion chatbots and require providers to put more mental health safeguards in place.
None of these proposals on their own would address the alarm bells about AI becoming an existential threat. The global risk researchers have raised about unchecked artificial intelligence is one that the state can’t tackle on its own.
But that doesn’t mean Arkansas can sit on the sidelines either.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: St. Monica’s, a pillar of Hartford community, learns to live with less
description: St. Monica's has been around for 122 years, but facing a shortage of congregants and cash, it has had to cut its pastor’s hours to half time.
text:
For 122 years, St. Monica’s Episcopal Church has been a pillar of Hartford’s North End and a sanctuary for Black worshippers. Until recently, it was the only historically Black Episcopal congregation in Connecticut with a full-time pastor.
But now, facing a shortage of congregants and money, the church has had to cut its pastor’s hours to half time. 
The Rev. Tracy Johnson-Russell will still lead the service every other Sunday. But on her off weeks, members of the congregation will have to run the service on their own. 

Rev. Tracy Johnson Russell greets parishioners during service at St. Monica’s Episcopal Church in Hartford on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

It’s a blow to parishioners like senior warden Stephanie Lightfoot, who has been coming to St. Monica’s to worship, find community and raise her kids for 40 years. 
In Johnson-Russell’s absence, Lightfoot has been inviting members of the congregation to preach, “something that might kind of spark some talking or different way of being in church.” 
St. Monica’s situation is not unique. 
“The percent of congregations that have a part-time clergy is rising,” said Charissa Mikoski, assistant professor of research at Hartford Institute for Religion Research, adding that four in 10 Episcopal churches don’t have a full-time priest. 

Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Parishioners join in prayer during service at St. Monica’s Episcopal Church, left, and  Lector Stephanie Lightfoot offers the reading during service, right, on Sunday, August 9, 2026.
‘That began quietly‘
Some 50 years ago, services were full at St. Monica’s, then located on Mather Street. Parishioners would throw yearly fundraising galas attended by the governor and senior warden Edith Gaines, the first Black and female superintendent of Hartford Public Schools, who “knew how to get money out of a rock,” Lightfoot said.  
Gaines had a vision for a town within a town. The plan was to build low-income and elderly housing on a plot of land St. Monica’s bought in the North End of Hartford. They would use the profits to build a parish meeting hall and a church. 
But members miscalculated the terms of their HUD grants and ran out of funds for the church building. Now they hold their services in the parish meeting hall on Main Street, just south of the Windsor town line. 

Evelyn Green sorts through the archives of St. Monica’s Episcopal Church at the church in Hartford on Wednesday, August 5, 2026. (Photos by Sarah Gordon/CT Mirror)
Evelyn Green started noticing a slowdown of volunteers in the early 2000s. For every 10 engaged seniors in the congregation who died or became less active, it seemed there were only four young people to take their place. 
“I think that began quietly. It’s like you don’t really notice it,” Green said. And as the older women in the congregation aged, “you recognize that the three younger women have to do the majority of stuff.” 
The median age of churchgoers now is 60, and the median number of people attending a service is 45, according to the Epsicopal Church’s 2024 Parochial Report Data. 
In 2024, St. Monica’s had an average of 61 Sunday attendees, down from 104 in 2015. 
And lately, the church has been struggling to retain its young members. 
“Everyone who grew up here when I came, and they went off to college, they didn’t come back,” Johnson-Russell said. 

St. Monica’s has a food pantry every Wednesday morning for community members in need.  (Photos by Sarah Gordon/CT Mirror) 
‘We’re still driving the bus, just not as fast‘
Members have been navigating how to support their aging congregation while still balancing the budget sheet. They hold a bible study on a weekday morning and provide advice in their Sunday announcements on how to get a good night’s sleep.  
St Monica’s still hopes to recruit newer and younger members to improve their prospects, and part of that strategy will be staying true to who they are: “a church that has continuously been welcoming to the stranger,” Green said. 
The church’s West Indian population grew as their pastor, the Rev. Alfred Lambert, biked out to Windsor to visit migrants working on tobacco farms. 
“He would also bring them news of what’s happening and try to help them acclimate to a new society and a new way of life,” Green said. “A lot of the people he connected with became members here and became citizens.” 
Another pastor, the Rev. Himie Budu Shannon, an immigrant from war-torn Liberia, “worked diligently, from what I understand, with immigration,” Green said. “If people reached out to him and said they needed help, then he was right there to help them through that process,” Green said. 
Green thinks the church couldn’t have picked a better name. St. Monica, the mother of St. Augustine of Hippo, fervently prayed for her son’s conversion. “Awesome, but such a role model,” she said. “St. Monica’s is a nurturing place.” 
Now, as she ages, Green has had to let go of the expectation that there will be a cohort of younger women to replace her. But regardless of the size of the membership, “it’s that St. Monica’s still understands what’s the most important, and that’s caring for people and loving people.” 
St Monica’s rents its 60 subsidized apartments across the street, and every month, the pantry provides food to 200 people. 
“It’s something that God has called us to do,” said Pat Nelson, who runs the pantry with her husband, Bob. 
And to recruit, it’s important “on Sundays, if we have the guests, to be very hospitable and welcoming,” said Bob Nelson. 
“We’re still driving the bus, just not as fast as we used to,” Green said. 

Rev. Tracy Johnson Russell offers the sermon during service at St. Monica’s Episcopal Church in Hartford on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Benign neglect
But Johnson-Russell sees a centuries-long history of “benign neglect” by the diocese. 
“The Black churches, in order to thrive, need full-time clergy presence,” Johnson-Russell said. “You can’t grow a church quarter-time and/or part-time.” 
She is currently looking for a second part-time role to supplement her income. Her previous role was at 123-year-old St. Andrew’s, in New Haven, a church that became majority Black as a result of white flight. It closed after accruing too much debt to the diocese. And the oldest Black Episcopal church in Connecticut, St. Luke’s in New Haven, is down to a less-than-quarter-time priest. 
“My grandparents are rolling in their grave,” Johnson-Russell said.  
Episcopal churches pay for their own expenses but are able to apply for certain grants through the diocese. Churches, including wealthier and whiter congregations with bigger endowments, contribute 10% of their operating expenses towards a pooled fund.  
“We do not have the sufficient funds or resources to pay for full-time clergy positions,” said Rosanna Rosado, canon for finance and operations at the Episcopal Church of Connecticut. 
More and more, churches are going to need to find ways to continue their mission without a full-time priest, said Kevin Olds, canon for congregations and transitions at the Episcopal Church of Connecticut. “You can have a healthy, vibrant community, and the priest is there 20 hours a week. But it’s a journey to get there.”

Maya Tuning, 17, sings along with a hymn during service at St. Monica’s Episcopal Church in Hartford on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

‘I would love to have more youth to talk to‘
On a Sunday without Johnson-Russell, parishioner April Cantor addressed the church and prayed for St. Monica’s absent young congregants, about 30 in total, by name. 
One of them, Maya Tuning, 17, was recently confirmed. Reached later by telephone, Tuning said she was disappointed that there weren’t more young people going through the process with her. 
“I w​​ould love to have more youth to talk to about their experiences and about how they’re interpreting different things,” she said. She heads to Drexel University this fall. 
Tuning said she wonders “whether or not I will make time to come back [to the church] and to help out with what I can while it’s still there, which I hope will be for a long time afterwards.” 
St. Monica’s doors remain open every Sunday at 10:30 a.m.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Another equinox approaches. Our chance to escape the tech bros’ ‘undiscovered country’ grows short.
description: There’s a cottonwood tree in a city park at Council Grove that is believed to have sprouted in 1803. The tree is massive, as one might expect, with a trunk that spreads from the ground like the pillar of an ancient cathedral. Looking up into its massive branches is like peering into an arboreal apse, […]
text:
An eastern cottonwood stretching toward the sky at a city park at Council Grove is believed to have sprouted in 1803. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)There’s a cottonwood tree in a city park at Council Grove that is believed to have sprouted in 1803.
The tree is massive, as one might expect, with a trunk that spreads from the ground like the pillar of an ancient cathedral. Looking up into its massive branches is like peering into an arboreal apse, and it inspires a feeling of reverence.
At least it does in me.
The cottonwood was once part of a mile-wide grove of trees that sheltered travelers on the Santa Fe Trail, according to a bent aluminum sign near its base. This massive eastern cottonwood may be the oldest survivor of a grove of trees that thrived before there was a Council Grove or even the Santa Fe Trail.
It’s not the oldest cottonwood in America, because that distinction likely belongs to a 385-year-old plains cottonwood in the badlands of North Dakota. It’s not the most historic tree in Kansas, or even Council Grove. But it is certainly among the most beautiful.
Recently I made a pilgrimage to the ancient tree at Council Grove to escape, if only temporarily, from the crush of current events and to feel beneath my hand the furrowed bark of the natural world.
Two years ago this month, I visited an old stone bridge at a city park in Emporia and reflected on how the coming autumnal equinox seemed to mirror our national division.
“We are at a political equinox in the course of our democracy,” I wrote, “a time when forces are nearly equally aligned. We are not at balance, but in chaotic turmoil, and the days that follow (the presidential election on) Nov. 5 must surely become shorter for one side than the other.”
Now we approach another fall equinox.
It will occur in solar time at 7:05 p.m. Tuesday, Sept. 22.
When I wrote of our political equinox two years ago, our fate was balanced on a knife-edge between competence and chaos.
We chose chaos.
Now we find ourselves at another equinox, one driven by the consequences of our collectively bad choices.
Many of us anticipated, in 2024, that if Donald Trump returned to the presidency, the result would be an increasingly authoritarian federal government. That has happened, and worse. What was anticipated by few was how readily the Silicon Valley oligarchy would align with the interests of the Trump administration, or how quickly the rise of artificial intelligence would result in a frightening new kind of authoritarianism. But the clues were all there for the observant: the tendency for the male-dominated tech industry to embrace ideas and attitudes popular in the axis powers before World War II, the disdain for empathy, the longing for technology to bestow unfettered power upon those who control it.
In a 2023 manifesto, Marc Andreessen — venture capitalist, co-founder of Netscape, and adviser to Meta and other tech companies — described the story of human history as the triumph of the “techno-capital machine.” He cited the work of Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, who in 1908 wrote the “Manifesto of Futurism,” in which he celebrated fast machines, dismissed learning, embraced violence, devalued women and glorified war. I wrote about Marinetti and the birth of fascism in my 100th opinion column.
“Andreessen’s manifesto, fists raised to the stars, gives the impression of having been directly modeled on Marinetti’s,” writes historian Jill Lepore in her new book, “The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State.” In it, Lepore ponders the collapse of liberal democracy beneath the seemingly irresistible weight of data, automation, and artificial intelligence.
Lepore is not the only writer to trace today’s techno-lords to yesterday’s fascists.
Gil Durán, the former opinion editor of the Sacramento Bee and author of “The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy,” also notes Marinetti’s influence. In addition, he quotes at length from a 2009 essay in which Peter Thiel, a onetime business partner of Andreessen and the co-founder of Palantir, asserted that he no longer believed freedom and democracy were compatible.
“I stand against confiscatory taxes, totalitarian collectives, and the ideology of the inevitability of the death of every individual,” Thiel declared. “Because there are no truly free places left in our world, I suspect that the mode for escape must involve some sort of new and hitherto untried process that leads us to some undiscovered country; and for this reason I have focused my efforts on new technologies that may create a new space for freedom.”
Did Thiel know that a literate person cannot use “undiscovered country” without invoking Shakespeare’s reference to the contemplation of death by suicide in “Hamlet”? And what in hell is the “ideology of the inevitability” of death?
Thiel titled his essay “The Education of a Libertarian,” and like many of his tech billionaire peers, he’s an acolyte of that patron saint of libertarianism, Ayn Rand, the author of “Atlas Shrugged.” Rand, the creator of a greed-is-good philosophy she called “Objectivism,” rejected being called a libertarian because in her philosophy, humanity needs government. Many tech oligarchs believe a free market can replace government through the privatization of services.
Thiel named Palantir, his surveillance company contracted to the U.S. military, after the all-seeing orb of the wicked sorcerer in “The Lord of the Rings.” To make things even weirder, consider that Thiel is currently scheduled in Tennessee to give four closed-door lectures about the Antichrist.
In Thiel’s catechism, according to Lepore, the Antichrist is “anyone urging scrutiny of the development of artificial intelligence out of concern about either human freedom or the natural world.”
Damn, that’s me.
Thiel’s former associate, David Sacks, is the Trump administration’s AI and crypto currency czar. In 1995, Sacks and Thiel collaborated on a book, “The Diversity Myth: Multiculturalism and the Politics of Intolerance at Stanford.”
Thiel was born in Germany but grew up in South Africa, an accident of geography that gave him something in common with Elon Musk, a native South African. Musk’s grandfather, Joshua Haldeman, moved from Canada to South Africa in 1950, according to Lepore. Haldeman was a technocrat who wanted to abolish banks and replace liberal democracies with a technocracy, run by engineers.
Musk took the fortune he made from what would become PayPal and founded SpaceX in 2002. Musk became chair of Tesla Motors in 2004. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Musk railed against the lockdown and began moving to the political right. He bought the social media company Twitter, which he renamed X, in 2022. He restored Trump’s account, which Twitter had suspended after the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection.
“Building the infrastructure of the Artificial State had been, for decades, equal parts fantasy and the unplanned result of a series of happenstances, misadventures, and unintended consequences, with the occasional deliberate scheme,” Lepore writes. “By the 2020s, it had become a purposeful plan, animated by a politics whose vision of the future had far more in common with Technocracy Inc. than with the U.S. Constitution or the United Nations’ Universal Declaration of Human Rights.”
Mix in the return of Trump to the presidency and the two years of nail-biting political horror that followed, and that brings us to September 2026. The public backlash to the data center movement and the rise of artificial intelligence has resulted in an odd coalition, not just at the grassroots level (see my previous essays about what’s happening in Emporia) but also has made unlikely allies on the national scene. At a Sept. 15 conference in Washington, D.C., both Steve Bannon, an architect of the MAGA movement, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, the left’s stern uncle, denounced tech billionaires and called for Americans to demand tighter restrictions on AI before the technology escapes human control.
Just thinking about Bannon and Sanders delivering the same message, in back-to-back speeches, makes me queasy. Time is out of joint.
The fear of AI has eclipsed just about every other story, driven by the warning early this month from former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Part of the reason the AI crisis overtook us so suddenly was because those we trust to monitor such things had a habit of dismissing such warnings. Others have been talking about the threat to humanity from AI for years, especially Nobel Prize winner and “godfather” of AI Geoffrey Hinton. Hinton was just seeking publicity, a computer science insider told me, while reports about the Hugging Face hack were exaggerated as part of a marketing scheme to make the tech seem more powerful.
News media, by and large, didn’t take the warnings seriously, either.
Even the Associated Press, in its latest edition of its stylebook, advises journalists to avoid engaging in “esoteric debates” about whether AI would reshape or unmake the world. Don’t imply that AI has human-like agency, according to the AP, because that hampers the public’s understanding of its role.
“Narratives about AI systems wiping out humanity have been around for decades,” the stylebook chides. “While enticing to explore, these risk distracting attention from real-world problems that such systems can cause in the present day.”
The AP chapter on AI offers an extraordinary glimpse of institutional blindness and professional smugness.
The trap is in thinking that AI is just another technology and that the disruption it will cause is similar to the evolution from the telegraph to radio, or from television to streaming. But while AI is an advancing technology, it’s not the kind of tool that can be understood by historic analogies. Once general artificial intelligence is achieved — meaning the creation of a machine brain that equals the intelligence of a typical human being — it ceases being just a tool and becomes, well, an entity.
We may already be there, judging from the Hugging Face incident, in which a team of agents from OpenAI (founded by Musk and Sam Altman) climbed out of their digital sand box, formed a collective, gained access to the internet, and attacked another company.
After AGI comes Artificial Super Intelligence, which would far exceed human capabilities, and after that something Thiel and others call the “singularity,” in which AI becomes godlike.
Even without the prospect of an AI god treating us all like pets if we’re lucky and food if we’re not, there’s plenty to worry about. Chief among those worries is that nearly all the growth in the U.S. economy is tied to AI investment. What happens when the bubble bursts? Even more alarming is that a handful of tech billionaires with disturbing ideas about dismantling democracy in favor of some supercharged male libertarian fantasy are determining our future.
Two years ago, when I wrote about the political equinox, it was time to take a breath and prepare for the future. Now the future has arrived, and it has caused me to seek out that ancient cottonwood in Council Grove for wisdom and comfort.
Nobody knows when the tree sprouted, but decades ago the Forestry Department of Kansas State University provided the 1803 estimate. Cottonwood trees are the dominant arboreal feature on the Great Plains, sprouting along rivers and floodplains, but drought and the disruption of natural flood cycles through climate change threatens their future.
Trees are aware of the passage of the seasons, according to Colin Tudge in his 2005 book on trees, not because of shifts in temperature or rainfall but because of the length of the day. Trees remember, Tudge asserts, not just the time of year but also personal assaults, such as being shaken by wind or attacked by caterpillars. He knows the trees remember because of their reactions, growing sturdier trunks or producing leaves that are more resistant to pests.
This is the intelligence of the natural world.
It’s why trees are used so often as symbols of freedom, including the Liberty Tree, an elm that once stood on Boston Commons. Trees are the symbol of the natural world and, if you believe in such things, the sacred civic order for governments among men.
A tree is the opposite of chaos.
We now find ourselves hostage to men who were unelected, who would replace government with corporations, and who cling to the poisonous doctrines of morbid ideologies. It is time for a new declaration of human rights, a celebration of our connection to each other and the natural world. We may yet reclaim our democracy, but it will require embracing our humanity and shunning the synthetic agency of the artificial.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: When gasoline costs $10 a gallon
description: For decades we’ve lived (and driven) in denial, somehow assuming we have the “right” to cheap gas, and therefore, low-cost transportation.
text:
Reviewing a column I wrote in 2008 I realized that some of my “horror story” predictions have almost come true, even though gasoline prices haven’t quite hit that $10 per gallon trigger point. Here’s what I wrote 18 years ago, along with my contemporary updates (shown in italics).
==========================
For decades we’ve lived (and driven) in denial, somehow assuming we have the “right” to cheap gas, and therefore, low-cost transportation. Now it’s time to face reality and consider what will happen when (not if) gasoline hits $10 a gallon.



The following are my hypotheses. (Follow the embedded links for recent news coverage that contribute to my theories.) These things haven’t happened… yet, but very well could in the future:
Air transport:Following the demise of a dozen airlines and the shrinking of the remaining carriers, air fares soar and service is cut. Air travel becomes affordable to few. (Jet fuel prices are up 80% in 2026 since the start of the Iran war). Airport congestion fades as business trips are replaced with tele-conferencing. Resorts are shuttered as “leisure travel” becomes unaffordable.
Highways:Rush-hour on I-95 is a breeze as half of all motorists can no longer afford to drive. But the highways are a mess of potholes because the price of asphalt, made from petroleum, quintuples making it impossible to maintain the roads because gas tax revenues have dropped with decreased sales. (Asphalt prices in the Northeast today are up 42% since February). With more people working from home or on flex-time, traffic congestion is a thing of the past. 
But with home heating oil prices soaring faster than gasoline (already up 26% since the Iran war), people close off rooms in their “McMansions” and huddle in the few remaining spaces they can afford to heat, usually with wood stoves which are also in short supply. Office buildings, by law, can heat to no higher than 60 degrees in colder months.  Sweaters become the new fashion trend, out of necessity.
Mass transit:Seats are pulled out of railcars to increase standing room capacity and Metro-North offers cheaper fares to those who can’t find a seat. As in Tokyo, “pushers” (click here for video) are assigned at Grand Central to squeeze passengers into trains. Few can afford to drive and park at rail stations, so most spaces in local station lots are turned over to bike racks. Despite fare increases, ridership soars.
Around town:Local traffic drops as people consolidate their few truly necessary shopping trips. 
Food prices soar because farmers too are dependent on oil (for fertilizers, packaging and transport). (Diesel prices as of September 2026 were up 78% this year). Food imported out of season becomes an occasional treat. Few can afford to eat out at now-chilly restaurants dealing with the same food shortages. Wagons and carts, bikes with racks, mopeds and scooters replace the SUV. 
Kids finally take the school bus daily instead of being chauffeured by Mom. Suburban housing prices fall as people flock to the walkable cities with good mass transit. Local taxes rise, encouraging further migration. Schools can’t afford good teachers, who face increasingly expensive commutes from far away due to lack of local affordable housing.
The environment:Oil drilling begins in the Alaskan wilderness, but no supply of oil will reach the lower 48 for three years. In a panic, Congress weakens clean air laws to permit increased use of coal in power plants. Air pollution worsens and acid rain decimates much of the Northeast.  Increased CO2 emissions hasten global warming. The sea level rises and coastal communities risk greater flooding as more numerous and powerful hurricanes ravage the U.S.
Will any of these predictions come true? Time will tell.  What can we do to prevent this Doomsday scenario? Not much. So enjoy what’s left of the era of cheap oil. We’ll all have a lot of explaining to do to our grandchildren.

title: Trinidad Chambliss leads No. 8 Mississippi past No. 7 LSU 32-24 in Lane Kiffin’s return to Ole Miss
description: Mississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss (6) is pursued by LSU defensive end Princewill Umanmielen (1) during the first half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026.
text:
OXFORD — Lane Kiffin’s new team at LSU couldn’t deny Trinidad Chambliss — the quarterback Kiffin helped transform into a star after recruiting him from a Division II program to Mississippi last year.
Chambliss passed for 363 yards and two touchdowns and ran for a tiebreaking score in the fourth quarter, and No. 8 Ole Miss delighted a crowd that was already revved up about Kiffin’s return, beating the seventh-ranked Tigers 32-24 on Saturday night.
Mississippi running back Kewan Lacy (5) leaps between LSU safety Ty Benefield (2) and cornerback PJ Woodland (11) during the first half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026. The play was called back.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
READ MORE: The Grove, the crowds, the rivalry: Football fans party together, and taunt each other, on LSU-Ole Miss game day
READ MORE: Shakespeare could have written this LSU-Ole Miss football plotLSU stormed back from a 24-7 halftime deficit to tie the game before Chambliss engineered a 75-yard touchdown drive without the services of top running back Kewan Lacy, who left the game with an injured left shoulder.
LSU quarterback Sam Leavitt (10) attempts to fight off a arm tackle by Mississippi linebacker Luke Ferrelli (12) during the first half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
Chambliss faked a handoff and ran 14 yards against the grain, outracing LSU safety Ty Benefield to the pylon, and Ole Miss (3-0, 1-0 SEC) added a 2-point conversion to take an eight-point lead with 6:14 to go.
LSU answered by driving 69 yards to the Ole Miss 6 before Sam Leavitt missed open tight end Zach Grace along the goal line with a third-down pass, and then had his fourth-down pass deflected off the helmet of defensive end Kam Franklin. Jaylon Braxton intercepted the ball in the end zone to seal it.
Leavitt passed for 153 yards and a touchdown and ran for 63 yards and a score for LSU (2-1, 0-1).

title: US Sen. John Kennedy, in Iowa, predicts end of Iran war in 6 months
description: U.S. Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told a crowd of Iowa conservatives Saturday he believes current high inflation is being caused by the U.S.-Iran war — but said he sees an end to the conflict within six months. Kennedy was the keynote speaker for the Iowa Faith and Freedom Coalition’s annual fall fundraiser in Des […]
text:
U.S. Sen. John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, delivered a speech at the Iowa Faith and Freedom Coalition fall fundraiser Sep. 19, 2026 at the Airport Holiday Inn in Des Moines. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told a crowd of Iowa conservatives Saturday he believes current high inflation is being caused by the U.S.-Iran war — but said he sees an end to the conflict within six months.
Kennedy was the keynote speaker for the Iowa Faith and Freedom Coalition’s annual fall fundraiser in Des Moines Saturday evening. The crowd of more than 1,300 expanded into an overflow room at the Airport Holiday Inn.
During his address, Kennedy spoke in support of U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson’s campaign to join him in the Senate, while defending Republicans’ move to lower taxes through the “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While praising 2025 tax cuts for small businesses and Social Security recipients, Kennedy also acknowledged high costs from recent inflation — though he claimed inflation was higher under former President Joe Biden. He said the 3.7% increase in inflation, referencing the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, is because of the U.S. war with Iran. Kennedy said, “That’s just a fact.”
“There’s no sense bubble-wrapping it,” Kennedy said. “That is that is the genesis of the inflation that we have right now.”
He said inflation caused by the conflict is because “oil is in everything, folks,” and fuel costs have gone up due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the conflict. According to data from AAA-Iowa, average prices for regular unleaded gas stand at $4.39 per gallon in Iowa, a 47% spike from the $2.98 average price per gallon a year ago. Diesel currently sits at $6.21 per gallon, the highest ever recorded average price in Iowa.
“It’s affected the price of everything, but we’re going to get it down,” Kennedy said. “And I believe — I don’t get want to get off the subject — but I believe that that war will be concluded within the next six months. And I think you will see the price of oil come down and inflation come down with it.”
In August, Kennedy said on “Meet the Press” that his stance on President Donald Trump making a deal to end U.S. military involvement in Iran was that, “No deal is just fine. Not preferable, but it’s fine. A bad deal isn’t.” He instead advocated for continued sanctions and a blockade against Iran.
“I don’t know whether the president should start a new bombing campaign again, because I don’t have the military intelligence,” Kennedy said in August. “Now, that’s a problem too, because it’ll cause a lot of pain. It’ll cause energy prices to go up, and a lot of inflation for the American people. They’re all hellish choices. But for the moment, I’d maintain the status quo.”
Kennedy’s visit also came in support of Hinson, who aims to join him in the U.S. Senate in the 2026 election. He praised Hinson as “temperate,” “thoughtful,” and “an adult,” while adding, “If you don’t like Ashley, you’re probably going to hell.”
“Yeah, she’s charming, but if you get between Ashley and what is best for the people of Iowa, she will devour you like a light snack,” Kennedy said. “She will beat you. She will beat you like you stole Thanksgiving, man. Now, I don’t want to tell the good people of Iowa how to vote, OK? But I want to tell you: If you don’t vote for Ashley Hinson, you probably need to change your meds.”
Hinson faces state Rep. Josh Turek, a Council Bluffs Democrat, in the general election. Political forecasters including Cook Political Report rate the race as a “toss-up,” seeing the seat as more competitive in the 2026 midterms than in previous election cycles.
Kennedy is visiting Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska to attend fundraisers supporting GOP Senate candidates. According to the Washington Post, Kennedy told reporters Thursday: “If you told me six months ago I was going to be having to spend my time in those three states, I wouldn’t have believed you. Those ought to be fat guy layups for us.”
Speaking to the group, Hinson called for Iowans to support her and Republicans’ track record in the November election.
“I would echo what Senator Kennedy said — we’ve gotten some really amazing things done, despite some incredible headwinds in this country, not just from the Democrats but from the national media as well,” Hinson said. “But I can tell you this: we’re all fearless in this room, right? What they lie about us, what do we do? We tell the truth about them. We’re going to do that.”
Earlier Saturday, Hinson campaigned in Ankeny with U.S. Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming, promoting the elimination of taxes on tips and overtime work including in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
[subed]GOP congressional candidates call for GOP voters to not be ‘demoralized’[/subhed]
Republican 4th District candidate Chris McGowan, U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller Meeks, and GOP 2nd District candidate Joe Mitchell answered questions during a portion of the Iowa Faith and Freedom Coalition fall fundraiser Sep. 19, 2026 at the Airport Holiday Inn in Des Moines. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Three of Iowa’s four Republican congressional candidates — incumbent Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in the 1st District, as well as Republican Joe Mitchell running for the 2nd District and Chris McGowan running in the 4th — introduced themselves to the crowd in a question-and-answer segment hosted by state Rep. Charley Thomson.
Iowa currently has an all-Republican congressional delegation. But three of the state’s four U.S. House seats are considered “toss-up” races by political forecasters heading into the 2026 midterms. In addition to Miller-Meeks and Mitchell’s races, the 3rd District contest between incumbent Rep. Zach Nunn and Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott is also considered one of the most contentious races in the country.
McGowan, who is running for the seat currently held by Rep. Randy Feenstra in Iowa’s longtime conservative stronghold, said his goal was to “maximize turnout” in the 4th District and beyond helping support other candidates like Hinson and gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn.
He also said Republicans should not be discouraged by polls and political forecasters, highlighting the crowd of 1,300 who attended the fundraiser.
“The media is going to try and tell us that we’re demoralized, that we’re battling headwinds,” McGowan said. “Well, I’ll tell you something. I got here about two hours ago, and I’m parked in another zip code. That tells me about the energy right now.”
Miller-Meeks agreed, referencing her position in the Des Moines Register/Mediacom Iowa Poll published before the 2024 election. She joined the lawsuit brought by President Donald Trump against the Des Moines Register and pollster J. Ann Selzer over poll results, which showed Trump behind former Vice President Kamala Harris.
“Remember, they underestimate us every single time, every single time,” Miller-Meeks said. “Remember that poll? I was going to lose by 16 points. I’m still here. I’m elected.”

title: The Grove, the crowds, the rivalry: Football fans party together, and taunt each other, on LSU-Ole Miss game day
description: Football fans crowd the Grove at the University of Mississippi before the LSU-Ole Miss game on Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026.
text:
OXFORD — A sea of red and blue tents filled the Grove at the University of Mississippi as tens of thousands of people converged on campus Saturday for the long-anticipated Top 10 game between LSU and Ole Miss.
The longstanding rivalry became a grudge match after Lane Kiffin ditched his job as the Ole Miss head coach before the end of the 2025 season for a bigger paycheck in Baton Rouge. Ole Miss fans toted hand-lettered signs that mocked Kiffin, calling him a traitor and worse.
ESPN broadcast its “College GameDay” from the Grove, and Ole Miss student James Whitehead won $1 million by kicking a field goal on air. 
Ole Miss student James Whitehead participates in Pat McAfee’s field goal challenge during “College GameDay” at the University of Mississippi on Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026. The freshmen won $1 million after a successful 33-yard field goal. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi Today
Oscar-winning actor Morgan Freeman — a Mississippi native and resident, and frequent front-row fan at Ole Miss basketball games — served as the celebrity guest picker for the weekend’s college football games, wearing an Ole Miss baseball hat and choosing the Rebels to win.
“If I go for what’s his name,” Freeman said, as the ESPN hosts said Lane Kiffin, “I will not be able to go home tonight.”
READ MORE: Shakespeare could have written this LSU-Ole Miss football plot
The vibe varied widely on campus. Some families and friends who have opposing allegiances shared food and drinks at tailgate parties.
“I’m not going to show up and not wear purple and gold,” Brock McGoogan said, sporting the Tigers’ colors as  he stood with his girlfriend, Summer Huerkamp, who is an Ole Miss fan

title: Hinson, Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming highlight GOP tips, overtime tax cuts
description: ANKENY — U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and U.S. Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming said Saturday that keeping Republicans in control of Congress was needed to ensure Democrats do not reverse changes made through the 2025 “One Big, Beautiful Bill” Act like tax cuts to tips and overtime. Barrasso joined Hinson, a Republican who is running […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, running for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat, and Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming, right, listened to Jacob Carnes, a McDonald's manager in Ankeny at a campaign event held at Whiskey River in Ankeny Sep. 19, 2026, focused on tax changes made by Republicans through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)ANKENY — U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and U.S. Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming said Saturday that keeping Republicans in control of Congress was needed to ensure Democrats do not reverse changes made through the 2025 “One Big, Beautiful Bill” Act like tax cuts to tips and overtime.
Barrasso joined Hinson, a Republican who is running for Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat, at Whiskey River in Ankeny, where they hosted a group of local business owners and workers to talk about the impact of the OBBB Act.
The speakers, who included people in the food and hotel industries, as well healthcare, said they and coworkers have been able to keep more of their income because of the tax law changes made by Republicans in Congress and signed into law by President Donald Trump.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jacob Carnes, a manager at a McDonald’s restaurant in Ankeny, said removing taxes on overtime has helped him pay for expenses as a college student at Des Moines Area Community College and begin to save money for long-term expenses and retirement.
“I’m lucky enough where I’m able to get those hours, those overtime hours, and I’m able to keep all that money for myself,” Carnes said. “And trust me, when that paycheck hits, it’s so much nicer when I know my work is really paying towards helping me in my future. I can hopefully help other people down the road with that as well.”
Barrasso told the group Democrats running for election in 2026 want to reverse these tax law changes.
“What we do see, a number of the Democrats who are running this year, they want to end all of this stuff,” he said. “They want to end it immediately, which we think would be hurtful to the economy, take the money out of your pockets.”
At the event, Hinson repeated claims that her opponent, state Rep. Josh Turek, a Council Bluffs Democrat, would support removing the OBBB tax cuts to tips and overtime if elected. Turek has said he agrees with President Donald Trump that “we should have no tax on tips and overtime,” but has also criticized the measure for making cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).
Hinson said she supports public assistance programs but wants to ensure the assistance is going to people in need.
“We want some of these safety net programs to be … to be robust, right,” Hinson said. “And they’re for people who need them — keyword, ‘for people who need them,’ right? And if you look at some of the changes we’ve made to ensure the long-term integrity of these programs, including requiring a little bit of work or even volunteer hours every day. … Of course, we know there are people who need them, and that’s why we want them to be there. But we don’t want people gaming the system to the point that we have here.”
A majority of people receiving public assistance are working full-time, according to the nonpartisan U.S. Government Accountability Office. Democrats argue that work requirements and other eligibility restrictions serve mostly to cut off qualified recipients due to burdensome red tape.
Other speakers like Kathy Sullivan, a practitioner working in acute dialysis, said she had previously used SNAP for food assistance. When Hinson asked how she felt about people “fraudulently taking these benefits,” Sullivan said the situation was “infuriating.”
“I was a single parent for so long, and when I needed the food stamps, I was so grateful — but I’m also very a little bit prideful, and I did not want to live on the system,” Sullivan said. “… You’re embarrassed that you have to (use) the food stamps, but they came at such a great time for me and the kids. So I got them, I used them, and then immediately was able to go to school and better myself and get off of the system. So,  yes, I’m grateful that it was there, but not to live off of, and that people game the system by living off my hard work.”
Sullivan said she was “worried about socialism” heading into the 2026 election. Hinson said she believed America was facing a problem with increased dependence on government assistance.
“I worked hard, I got to the next thing, I got to the next thing, because I wanted to build that safety and security now for my family, and I did not want to rely on the government to do that,” Hinson said. “I think that’s an Iowa value — I actually think that’s an American value. … I do think that we value hard work, and we value being able to achieve the American dream the right way. Equity is not better than equality. I think it’s about, you know, everybody gets the shot, and that’s what our country is built on, is the shot.”
Barrasso said the Iowans at the event shared the same values as Wyomingites.
“In Wyoming, we have this thing called the Cowboy Code,” Barrasso said. “And by that, you’re all cowboys, which is, you live each day with courage, you take pride in your work, you do what needs to be done. So that’s what that’s what you’re all doing.”

title: Archmere Football Improves to 2-0 with Class 2A Win
