text:
Archmere football lines up on offense at the start of its game against the St. Mark’s Spartans, September 18. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The Archmere Auks (2-0) defeated the St. Mark’s Spartans (0-3), 8-0, on September 18, earning their first Class 2A win of the season and second shutout in as many games.
 
WILMINGTON, DE — Archmere’s junior quarterback, Shane Harding, stood in the shotgun formation with fellow junior, Wyatt Beekley, standing beside him for the third straight play. Beekly ran the ball out of the same formation the past two plays, helping the Auks earn a first and goal opportunity from the St. Mark’s three-yard line with a little less than 10 minutes remaining in the fourth quarter. 
On first and goal, Archmere turned to its trusted running back one more time.
Beekly ran from the right hip of Harding and took the handoff to the left of the center. Beekly looked for a running lane inside, but quickly bounced the run wide of the guard and between the tackle, finding enough room to barrel into the endzone for the first touchdown of the game.
Beekly’s touchdown was the only score in Archmere’s 8-0 win over the St. Mark’s Spartans, Friday night, in the first Class 2A game of the season for either squad.
Beekly finished the game with 58 rushing yards and the one touchdown as part of an Archmere rushing attack that gained over 200 yards throughout the game. Harding led all rushers with 126 yards on the ground and fellow junior, Nathan Blessington, ran for just under 70.
“We just have so many plays that work off each other, like, our plays are all built to like confuse the defense,” Beekly said about what makes Archmere’s running attack so effective. “We have so many weapons outside, inside. Shane’s willing to run anyone over so, I mean, we just have so many weapons that I believe in our offense and we can go as far as we want.”  
The Archmere running game played well throughout the night, but it was the two defenses that made big plays to keep the game close throughout.
The Auks started the game by receiving the kick-off and drove the ball into Spartan territory on the game’s opening possession. Archmere got as far as the Spartan 22-yard line before the St. Mark’s defense earned a sack and forced the Auks into a turnover on downs. Archmere’s next offensive possession was thwarted deep in Spartan territory as were a couple others in the first half. 
Archmere’s defense held the Spartans to their side of the field through the first half. St. Mark’s crossed midfield for the first time on their opening possession of the third quarter — driving to the  Archmere 23-yard-line — before the Auks defense halted the drive. A couple possessions later Archmere scored the game’s only touchdown on a six play drive, all of which were runs. 
“The word of the week we had in practice was finish and at halftime coach was not happy with how we had been finishing the drives, but we finished it at the end so that’s all that matters,” Harding said. 
The Spartans followed Archmere’s scoring drive with a strong drive of their own working their way to Archmere’s 36-yard line. The Auks defense held firm there, stopping St. Mark’s on fourth down and returning the ball to their offense. The Spartans defense did the same on the Auks’ next offensive possession and the Spartans’ offense took over at their own 35-yard line with a little over two and half minutes to play and a chance to tie the game. 
St. Mark’s senior quarterback, Kyle Iudica, connected with fellow senior Ta’Son Wallace for 23 yards on the drive’s first play, but the Archmere defense stopped the Spartan offense on the next set of downs. The Auks defense allowed the offense to gain just two more yards during the drive, successfully keeping the Spartans out of the endzone each time they encroached into Archmere territory.
“I think we got a lot of dogs on the other side of the ball, a lot of guys stepping up, a lot of young guys,” Archmere senior Francis Morda said postgame describing the Auks’ defensive unit. “We have a lot of grit and you can’t teach that, that’s all heart. That’s all it is.” 
The Auks defense finished the game with two sacks and their first shutout against the Spartans since the DIAA quarterfinals in 2021. 
“We look forward to this game every year, we circle it on the calendar, but we got to build off this,” Morda said. “We’re 2-0, but we have a lot of things to fix. We just gotta move forward to DMA and just focus one game at a time.”  
Archmere’s next game will be on September 25, against another Class 2A opponent, Delaware Military Academy. The game will start at 7:00 p.m. and take place at Delaware Military Academy.
The Spartans will play the second game of their two-game home stand against William Penn on September 25. That game will start at 7:00 p.m.

text:

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi oyster industry rebuilds as reefs show signs of growth
authors: Jakira Hunt, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center and Justin Glowacki, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center
description: Commercial fisherman James Miller discusses Mississippi’s oyster industry in Pass Christian. Miller said rebuilding the industry will depend not only on recovering oyster populations but also on restoring demand for Mississippi oysters.
text:
PASS CHRISTIAN — Mississippi’s oyster reefs are showing signs of growth ahead of the 2026-27 season, but for fishermen like James Miller, rebuilding the industry also means finding enough buyers to make getting on the water worthwhile. 
“We’ve just got to get our market moving again,” Miller said. “It’s going to happen. It will take time.” 
At a Sept. 8 stakeholder meeting in Pass Christian, the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources estimated there are just under 400,000 sacks of oysters across surveyed reefs in the Mississippi Sound, up from about 275,000 last year. 
The growth follows a roughly 50,000-sack harvest during the 2025-26 season, which MDMR said was the largest harvest in more than a decade. 
Joe Spraggins, executive director of MDMR, said Mississippi is moving in the right direction. 
“We’ve got big oysters. That’s what started last year, right? That’s all that’s in Mississippi,” Spraggins said. “We can get that reputation back by bringing in 100,000 sacks of market-sized oysters.” 
Reef health
Mississippi’s oyster industry is still rebuilding from the effects of the 2019 Bonnet Carré Spillway openings, which sent large amounts of freshwater into the Mississippi Sound and caused salinity levels to fall. 
MDMR estimated oyster mortality across major reefs in the western Mississippi Sound at nearly 97% following the openings. 
Since then, the department has used reef monitoring, cult placement and other restoration efforts to rebuild oyster populations. 
Jason Rider, director of MDMR’s Shellfish Bureau, pointed fishermen toward Henderson Point and St. Joe, where population estimates increased and harvest pressure was relatively low last season. 
Fishermen and Mississippi Department of Marine Resources officials gather for an oyster stakeholder meeting Sept. 8, 2026, in Pass Christian, Miss. Jason Rider, director of the MDMR’s Shellfish Bureau, walks up the aisle prior to his 2026 reef report.  Credit: RHCJC News
“We’re seeing the growth across nearly every size class with the spats. That’s picking up significantly,” Rider said. “That’s really encouraging for us. That’s a really good, strong sign of growth.” 
Other reefs did not see the same gains. 
According to MDMR, the density of market-size oysters at Pass Christian Dredging declined from 19 oysters per square meter, or per 10.76 square feet, in 2025 to 8.2 in 2026. At Pass Christian Dredging, density dropped from 2.7 to 1.2 oysters per square meter. 
MDMR officials said Pass Christian Tonging, Pass Christian Dredging and Pass Marianne were among the areas affected by heavy rainfall and lower salinity this summer. 
Rider said the department will continue monitoring the reefs and investing in restoration efforts. 
This summer, MDMR placed limestone and shell, known as cultch, across 236 acres of oyster habitat. Much of that work was concentrated on reefs affected by the heavy rainfall.
Managing the harvest
MDMR plans to maintain a 30% harvest quota for individual reef areas this season. Because the quota is based on oyster population estimates, the number of sacks available for harvest can increase or decrease as populations change. 
During the 2025-26 season, harvest exceeded the 30% quota in several areas. MDMR reported harvests of roughly 41% at Pass Christian Tonging, 37% at Pass Christian Dredging and 34% at Pass Marianne. Henderson Point and St. Joe were much lower, at about 8% and 1%, respectively. 
A pile of oysters sits on the deck of the vessel Royster in Pass Christian, Miss. The stateestimates nearly 400,000 sacks of oysters across surveyed reefs in the Mississippi Sound ahead of the 2026-27 season.  Credit: Justin Glowacki/RHCJC
Miller said he believes individual reefs should be closed once they reach the 30% quota to prevent too much harvesting in one area. 
“They keep the reef sometimes open too long in areas,” Miller said. “Once they meet their quota, they need to shut it down.” 
The Roy Howard Community Journalism Center has reached out to Rider for more information about why harvest exceeded the 30% quota in some areas last season and how MDMR plans to manage the quota this season. Rider has not yet responded. 
MDMR also plans to maintain last season’s daily commercial limits of 15 sacks per tonging vessel and 20 sacks per dredging vessel. Those daily limits are separate from the 30% seasonal harvest quota. 
Miller supports keeping the daily limits in place. He said allowing fishermen to bring in more oysters would do little good if there are not enough buyers. 
“If you can’t sell them, why bring them in?” Miller said. 
Rebuilding the market
The 2026-27 oyster season is scheduled to open Oct. 1, nearly two weeks earlier than last year’s Oct. 13 opening. 
Miller, a lifelong fisherman from D’Iberville, supports the earlier opening because he said lower rainfall in the fall can give fishermen more opportunities to harvest before river conditions lead to reef closures. 
He said the commercial market remains another challenge after years of limited Mississippi harvests. 
“When you’re off for five years, your market is slowly progressing, coming back,” Miller said. 
He said oysters from other Gulf states, including Louisiana and Texas, have filled some of the demand that Mississippi fishermen previously served. 
“We’ve got a kind of show that we do have a good oyster for them to buy, and we can boost our market back up,” Miller said. “It’s going to take time.” 
Operating costs are another concern. 
Miller said fuel costs have cut into his income from fishing and shrimping. He estimated he has recently spent $3,500 to $4,000 a week on fuel while working on the water. 
Still, Miller said he believes keeping harvest limits in place while Mississippi rebuilds both its oyster populations and commercial market is the best approach. 
“We had a good thing last year,” Miller said. “It’ll be a good thing this year.”

name: VTDigger
title: The Upper Valley’s widening tick-borne disease problem
description:
Researchers at Dartmouth have identified a critical link between alpha-gal syndrome — a tick-borne allergy — and potentially fatal anaphylactic reactions during blood transfusions for type O patients.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The Upper Valley’s widening tick-borne disease problem.
text:
Paul Guyre looks at photos of his wife Veronica on display at his home in Lyme, N.H., on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

This story by Molly Hughes was first published in the Valley News on Sept. 18, 2026.
Paul Guyre got home from his lab one evening about 15 years ago and found his wife, Veronica, covered in hives from head to toe. She was too weak to get to her inhaler.
“She lived to tell about it,” Guyre said. “But it was really horrible.”
The culprit: She had eaten meatloaf four hours earlier. She was suddenly allergic to meat.
Guyre is a professor emeritus of microbiology and immunology at Dartmouth’s Geisel School of Medicine, and even he didn’t connect his wife’s condition to her meal right away. That’s the puzzling part about alpha-gal syndrome, a tick-borne allergy to red meat and nearly everything else that comes from a mammal. The reaction arrives hours after the meal.
“The key thing about alpha-gal is you don’t connect the dots so easily,” Guyre said.
What happened to Veronica is far more likely to happen to an Upper Valley resident today than it was 15 years ago. The tick that carries the allergy is the same one that carries Lyme disease, and Vermont counted more ticks and more of their diseases in 2025 than in any year on record. The CDC estimates as many as 450,000 Americans may have alpha-gal, most undiagnosed. This summer, Dartmouth researchers found that the same antibody can turn a routine blood transfusion into an emergency.
Alpha-gal is a sugar found in beef, pork, lamb, dairy and the gelatin that coats many pill capsules. Humans are the only mammals that don’t make it, so our immune systems already treat it as foreign. A tick bite can push that reaction into overdrive: some ticks carry alpha-gal in their saliva, and in a minority of people, the immune system responds by producing IgE, the antibody class behind allergies. After that, a hamburger can trigger a life-threatening reaction hours after the sugar has been digested.
Guyre was able to identify what was happening because he was an immunologist. Their primary care doctor had never heard of the condition. That hasn’t changed as much as it should have. In a 2023 CDC survey, 42% of the health providers surveyed had never heard of alpha-gal syndrome. Diagnosis has sped up: a 2025 study from the CDC and a North Carolina allergy clinic found recent patients were diagnosed in about a month, whereas a decade earlier it took more than five years. A third of patients still waited over a year.
No treatment existed back then, and none exists now. Instead, Guyre and his wife used what he called a “tincture of time.” Some people’s antibody counts drop low enough over time that the reactions stop. Veronica did not eat meat for seven years. Some can never eat meat again.
Veronica was a nurse and an avid hiker, paddler and skier, and she took the diet in stride. She died recently of pancreatic cancer, unrelated to any of this.
“She was tough. She said it wasn’t a big deal,” Guyre said. “And she was actually rubbing my nose in the fact that I had a healthier diet now.”
Her reactions in those years didn’t come from the dinner table.
“It was due to gelatin-containing pharmaceuticals,” Guyre said. “That’s, I guess, how we learned that that was a problem.”
Guyre suspects a deer tick did it, the ordinary kind common across the Northeast, not the Lone Star tick usually blamed for alpha-gal. That is no longer a fringe idea.
That matters here, because the deer tick is the one the Upper Valley has in abundance.
The woods, and who lives near them
When Dr. Jeffrey Parsonnet arrived at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in 1990, ticks this far north mostly carried nothing. Lyme was still a coastal problem.
Today, “most ticks harbor the organism all the way up to the Canadian border,” said Parsonnet, an infectious disease specialist.
Vermont counted 2,246 cases of Lyme disease in 2025, the most it has ever recorded, according to the Vermont Department of Health, which says its three most common tick-borne illnesses all hit record highs that year. Anaplasmosis, which produced three or fewer cases a year as recently as 2010, had more than 700. More than half the blacklegged ticks the state has tested carried at least one pathogen. Across the river, New Hampshire has one of the highest rates of Lyme disease in the nation, according to the CDC, though the state’s own counts for anaplasmosis and babesiosis are incomplete for the last two years.
Alpha-gal syndrome is the newest entry on that list, and the only one that isn’t an infection. The CDC counted more than 110,000 suspected cases nationally between 2010 and 2022 and estimates as many as 450,000 Americans may have it, most undiagnosed.
What makes this more than an inconvenience is who lives here. Windsor County’s median age was 48.5 at the 2020 census, and nearly a quarter of residents were 65 or older. Parsonnet said he generally resists alarmism, then said this is a case where concern is earned.
“Babesiosis can be severe, especially in people with compromised immune systems and in the elderly,” he said. And when clinicians say elderly, he added, they aren’t describing frail 85-year-olds. Immune function starts slipping in a person’s 50s and 60s.
He put alpha-gal and babesiosis above Lyme on his own list of worries. Lyme is treatable. Alpha-gal has no fix.
“What is this going to do to our eating habits?” Parsonnet said. “What’s it going to do to the beef industry and the pork industry?”
It is common enough on Martha’s Vineyard that restaurant menus mark safe dishes “AG,” and when patients tell Parsonnet they’re spending the summer there, his advice is blunt.
“I say no. Don’t do that. Go swimming in the Amazon,” Parsonnet said. “That’s much safer than going to the Cape.”
The patient on the table
That was the version of alpha-gal syndrome doctors understood: a food allergy, frightening but manageable once you knew what to avoid. This summer, Dartmouth researchers described a second risk. It doesn’t come from a plate. It comes in a bag of platelets, and the people at risk have no idea they’re carrying the allergy at all.
In 2025, a man was on the table for heart surgery at Dartmouth Hitchcock when he “got a Group B platelet product,” said Dr. Richard Kaufman, a pathologist at the hospital, “and immediately dropped his blood pressure in the operating room.”
He was having a severe allergic reaction. His surgeons brought him back. Nothing they had done explained it.
His blood was type O. The sugar that marks blood as type B is so similar to alpha-gal that his antibodies couldn’t tell the difference. Kaufman ordered the test that confirmed it: the patient was positive for alpha-gal IgE. The reaction “was consistent with an anaphylactic, a really severe allergic reaction,” he said.
The patient had a history of tick bites. But he had never had trouble eating red meat, the usual sign of alpha-gal syndrome, so no one had thought to test for it.
Kaufman knew what to look for because Dr. Michael Knudson, a pathologist at the University of Iowa, proposed in 2022 that alpha-gal antibodies might cross-react with type B blood after a few case reports pointed that way. Knudson would become a co-author of the Dartmouth study.
The researchers looked for a pattern: if the hypothesis held, reactions to type B products should cluster in regions where tick bites have sensitized many people and stay flat everywhere else.
Kaufman, with Dartmouth colleagues Nancy Dunbar and Anne Hoen, pulled records of more than half a million platelet and plasma transfusions from 40 hospitals in five countries, sorting the hospitals in advance by whether alpha-gal syndrome is common nearby. Reactions were rare: about three in every thousand transfusions.
They weren’t evenly spread. At the nine U.S. hospitals in regions where alpha-gal syndrome is common, a group that included Dartmouth Hitchcock, type O patients given type B or AB units were nearly four times as likely to react as type O patients given type O units, according to the study published Aug. 24 in JAMA Internal Medicine. At the 15 U.S. hospitals in places where the ticks don’t live, most in the West, and at the hospitals overseas, the pattern was absent.
The study is epidemiological, Kaufman said, and can’t prove the mechanism. It shows a pattern that matches what the hypothesis predicted.
He suspects the transfusion risk reaches more people than the meat allergy does. Only about 1% of those carrying the antibody ever react to meat. Of the nine transfusion cases in the literature, most of the patients, like the man at Dartmouth Hitchcock, could eat a steak without trouble. They had no reason to know.
“It’s just that you’re much more likely to eat a hamburger than you are to get a platelet,” Kaufman said.
What hospitals are doing
Platelets and plasma have never worked the way red blood cells do. A type O patient needs type O red cells, but platelets and plasma could go to anyone, which is how blood banks avoided throwing out units that expire in five days.
“We’ve gone a step further at Dartmouth to say, okay, if someone’s type O, we’re just going to avoid giving them any B or AB platelets or plasma unless we absolutely have to,” Kaufman said, with an exception for bleeding emergencies. Dartmouth Health announced the change alongside the study. Other hospitals have made similar changes.
The cost is waste. “We may end up having to discard some platelet units because we can’t just give them to anybody like we had been doing,” Kaufman said.
The product hospitals now need most is the one already hardest to keep on the shelf. “Type O, O positive and O negative, tend to be in greatest demand,” said Jennifer Costa, regional communications director for the American Red Cross, which supplies about 40% of the nation’s blood, “and so those are typically the first to be depleted.”
Platelets are the harder ask: a two-and-a-half- to three-hour process at a donation center, with a needle in each arm, for a product that lasts five days. “Those platelets have such a short shelf life that there’s always a greater need than the donations coming in,” Costa said.
Kaufman said Dartmouth Hitchcock’s own supply has held, helped by multiple suppliers and a hospital-based donor program.
What nobody knows yet
How many people in the Upper Valley carry the antibody is anyone’s guess. Fourteen states now require doctors and labs to report alpha-gal cases, and six more accept reports voluntarily. Neither Vermont nor New Hampshire does either, and alpha-gal was left off Vermont’s list of reportable diseases when the state revised it in June. Massachusetts began a one-year trial of mandatory reporting on April 1.
There is no alpha-gal support group in the Upper Valley. The nearest in-person groups are on Martha’s Vineyard and, as of this month, in Branford, Connecticut.
No one knows what share of antibody carriers would react to a transfusion.
“For this allergy related to blood transfusion, we’re just defining the problem now,” Kaufman said.
Guyre’s wife had an immunologist in the house. The man on the operating table had a surgical team that happened to include a pathologist who had read the right paper. Neither of them had any way of knowing before the hives, or the crash, that a tick had changed how their bodies worked.
For everyone else, the signal is the delay. Hives, stomach cramps or trouble breathing that arrive in the middle of the night, hours after a dinner of beef, pork or lamb, are the pattern doctors look for, especially in someone who spends time outdoors and has pulled off ticks.
If you think you may have alpha-gal, ask your doctor for the antibody blood test by name. If you already have it, tell your surgeon before an operation. If a reaction reaches your throat or affects your breathing, call 911.
In the Upper Valley, the only way most people find out is the hard way.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Why the Beacon Hill transparency debate gets it all wrong
description: The problem is not that the public lacks crucial information about its government; it’s that its government lacks crucial information about the public -- and has little motivation to care about that.
text:
FOR THE PAST few years, one of the central debates in Massachusetts politics has been the fight over transparency. From the Democratic state auditor to  progressive advocacy groups to the Republican gubernatorial nominee, critics argue that we suffer from an opaque state government, and if we just knew more about what happens inside the State House, we would get better policies. 
Unfortunately, this diagnosis is flawed, so the prescriptions are the wrong medicine for what ails our body politic. 
Fundamentally, the problem is not that the public lacks crucial information about its government; it’s that its government lacks crucial information about the public — and has little motivation to care about that. Members of the Legislature don’t actually know what their constituents want – at least, not on a systematic basis – and worse, they don’t need to care. 
Sunshine is no cure-all. I should know. From 2006 to 2012, I led a Massachusetts-focused civic engagement organization. I was part of a coalition that brought online voter registration and voting machine audits to the Bay State, and I collaborated with community leaders on the 2011–12 legislative and congressional redistricting, arguing not just for better lines, but for deep public participation.  
I got a lesson in the limits of the value of public disclosure when I was advocating for Election Day registration a decade ago. I learned that a listed cosponsor of the bill (a person now long retired) had signed on precisely so his name would be publicly listed – right out in the sun – and we advocates would praise him. All the while, he was quietly opposing the measure in the rooms where it mattered. Would posting this person’s office spending or his committee votes have made a difference? Of course not.  
Activists argue that increased transparency will boost the power of everyday citizens. They recorded a big win in 2025 when new rules were adopted by the Legislature that mandate streaming every hearing and posting every committee vote. Yet citizen volunteers do not have the bandwidth to sit through every meeting or analyze thousands of votes. Professional lobbyists do.  
Journalists, activists, and even AI bots can help. They can go through the newly open data and report it to the public. But most Bay Staters aren’t reading local newspapers regularly to begin with (if there is even still a robust local paper serving their community), nor are we actively participating in community organizations at the levels that characterized earlier generations. This means, unfortunately, there aren’t enough readers for these new transparency reports. The reform might be a win, but it will not be transformative. 
And there are tradeoffs involved in making public every step of the legislative process. It is essential that many meetings are held in public. But public meetings also incline leaders to perform for the cameras, preventing them from asking colleagues key questions like, “Let’s say I give a little on topic A that I’ve been so committed to – what would you give me on topic B?” Those kinds of freewheeling discussions are essential to finding commonsense solutions and necessitate some limits on transparency.  
None of this is an argument against making more information available to the public. But if the goal is to have a Legislature that is more responsive to constituent views, what we need most are better ways for lawmakers to know what voters want and incentives that increase legislators’ accountability for addressing those concerns. That is, the Legislature will work better when voters have effective channels to tell legislators their preferences, backed up by consequences that kick in should they consistently ignore those preferences. 
Legislators, it is true, pay attention to their districts. But they are imperfect observers.  
In 2014, political scientists David Broockman and Christopher Skovron asked thousands of state legislative candidates and sitting legislators to estimate their constituents’ views and then compared what they said to what the voters themselves reported. By and large, legislators considered their constituents to be significantly more conservative than they actually were.  
Related research by Alexander Hertel-Fernandez, Matto Mildenberger, and Leah Stokes showed that senior staff in Congress consistently misjudged constituent opinion.  
Why? One reason might be that the neighbors most likely to show up at community meetings, to head up to the State House, to make political donations, or to be represented by lobbyists tend to be systematically wealthier and better educated than their neighbors who don’t, and their policy preferences aren’t representative. 
It is hard to serve people well when you do not know what they want.  
To fix this problem, polling can help—but not polling on what the average Massachusetts voter thinks. Information on statewide voter preferences is almost meaningless if you are elected to serve the people of a few neighborhoods in Boston, a town or two on the South Shore, or several rural communities in Central Mass. The solution is district-level opinion data. In a promising experiment in 2008, political scientists gave district-level polling data to legislators in New Mexico and watched them vote more closely with their districts’ actual opinion than a control group that didn’t get the data.  
Bay State polling firms and nonprofits, its news media, and university pollsters should upgrade their work to routinely offer poll numbers for all 200 legislative districts. This used to be prohibitively expensive, but new data analysis tools, modeling techniques, and online panels can bring the costs of this kind of survey data into a reasonable range. Philanthropists who want more responsive government should invest to make this happen. 
Still, high-performing government requires more than clear information channels. It requires consequences for performance that fails to address public concerns. 
To increase consequences, the essential task is to convince more people to run for the Legislature. In 2024, according to Ballotpedia, only one in five Massachusetts legislative districts featured a competition with candidates from both major parties—the lowest rate in America. The state has ranked last in Ballotpedia’s competitiveness index for five straight election cycles. 
It’s common sense: In a state with so little competition, challengers serve voters just by showing up. Incumbents who face no challengers act differently than those who do. Even token challengers make incumbents work. Frequently, after defeating a challenge, incumbents will adopt some of their opponent’s issues.  
Ballot initiatives and state constitutional amendments also add consequences. Legislators, of course, would prefer that the Legislature be, for all intents and purposes, “the room where it happens” when it comes to public decisions that matter. If they haven’t acted in a prior year, putting a measure on the ballot is a powerful prod. The Bay State’s first-in-the-nation comprehensive health care law passed in 2006 in part because civic leaders had gathered enough signatures to threaten the Legislature’s primacy in policymaking with both a constitutional amendment and a ballot initiative.  
This year will see a bumper crop of nine ballot questions. But ordinary citizens can be hard-pressed to understand what ballot language actually means and might be persuaded by whichever side has better advertising and deeper pockets. 
A Massachusetts Ballot Initiative Institute might help. It could house a Citizen Initiative Review Commission, a jury of randomly selected citizens, who could listen to the sides for and against current initiatives facing voters and create short, plain-language video explainers. This is a logical 21st-century upgrade to supplement the dated but helpful paper guides that the Commonwealth mails to every voter. (A pilot in Oregon shows this model is worth exploring.)   
Such an institute could also work proactively. By bringing together ordinary citizens, community groups, businesses, and nonprofits across economic strata and social and political divisions, the group might aim to formulate thoughtful and innovative potential future ballot measures and offer them to the Legislature for action – and to the public, the press, and the philanthropic community for follow-through should the Legislature fail to act. 
The path forward is long. Yet whether you would give today’s Legislature a grade of A+, F, or anywhere in between, we can all agree that improvement is possible, and worth it. Improving state legislative performance could mean a better social return on the state’s $60 to $70 billion annual budget, and more effective lawmaking on issues that shape our economy and our communities.  
As a reformer, I thought the fix was making the Legislature visible to the people. Fifteen years later, I see that making the people visible to the Legislature is equally crucial, if not more so. 
Avi Green is a policy consultant and philanthropic advisor.

title: Governor, EPA administrator tout cleanup, development actions at Columbia Falls Superfund site
description: COLUMBIA FALLS — A new subdivision is under development within the boundaries of a federal Superfund site, the first use of the Columbia Falls Aluminium Company plant property since the plant closed in 2009.  The 78-acre development by Mick Ruis will bring more than 400 housing units, and eventually commercial development, to the site, and […]
text:
Gov. Gianforte (center) and Administrator Zeldin (center left) hosting a press conference at an EPA Superfund site in Columbia Falls. (Courtesy photo)COLUMBIA FALLS — A new subdivision is under development within the boundaries of a federal Superfund site, the first use of the Columbia Falls Aluminium Company plant property since the plant closed in 2009. 
The 78-acre development by Mick Ruis will bring more than 400 housing units, and eventually commercial development, to the site, and on Thursday, Gov. Greg Gianforte and Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin praised it as part of a successful future for the blighted area. 
“One of the most exciting steps of the Superfund process is being able to delist a project at the end of it, to be able to get an important vision not just started, but completed,” Zeldin said during a press conference. “Fortunately, we are at a very important milestone moment here in Columbia Falls, where there is just so much incredible progress imminently ahead on this project.”
The Columbia Falls Aluminum Company, known as CFAC, began operation in the 1950s, importing alumina and converting it into aluminum, supporting thousands of jobs in the Flathead Valley, but creating hazardous waste byproducts from the smelting process. 
In 2016, the site received official Superfund designation from the federal Environmental Protection Agency, and this year a $57 million cleanup agreement was reached between CFAC, owned by the Swiss commodities firm Glencore, Ltd., and the federal government. 
Touring the property on Thursday, Zeldin and Gianforte both complimented the work by Ruis, a major developer in the Valley, who purchased a huge swath of the property that has been controversial among local residents. 
Residents and city officials have raised issues of having a major development in a wildlife corridor, straining city services, and whether there are additional health and safety concerns due to the proximity to a federal Superfund site. 
But the development has been approved by the city and both the EPA and Montana Department of Environmental Quality have said the site does not require cleanup and is cleared for development, according to local reporting. 
During the plant’s productive years, hazardous waste materials like cyanide, fluoride and arsenic were deposited in repositories around the CFAC site, which can be picked up by groundwater as it moves towards the Flathead River. 
A major part of the cleanup process includes constructing a slurry wall that will be injected below the repository site to prevent further groundwater contamination. 
Constructing the slurry wall is expected to be completed in 2029. 
The cleanup will also include lining a nearby overflow ditch, adding a landfill to contain contaminants without having to transport them off site, and long-term monitoring of the remedy’s effectiveness. 
“Our main goal with cleanup is to protect the Flathead River and cut off that clean groundwater from encountering the waste source,” said plant Superfund Project Manager Allie Archer.
In his comments to the press, Gianforte echoed Archer’s sentiment and highlighted the agreement signed between the EPA and Montana Department of Environmental Quality detailing what the cleanup plan would be, an agreement that followed years of scrutiny by watchdog groups.
“This is going to address the contamination, hazardous materials, and eliminate exposure to prevent contamination of groundwater and the Flathead River, which is right over here, near and dear to my heart,” Gianforte said, adding that he and First Lady Susan Gianforte recently camped on the banks of the Flathead River. “It’s great to see the cleanup efforts underway today to address the hazardous contaminants and return the site to productive use.”
Montana has nearly 20 federal Superfund sites, and DEQ administrator Sonja Nowakowski said the state is seeing progress at “nearly all of them right now.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Theme of this year’s South Dakota ballot issues: Let’s make life tougher
description: As they cast their ballots now through Election Day on Nov. 3, voters will decide on four constitutional amendments, all courtesy of the South Dakota Legislature. Three of the amendments reflect their origins in a Legislature that’s top-heavy with Republicans. Those three deal with popular Republican topics: tinkering with voting rights, looking to squeeze o[...]
text:
A voter drops a ballot in the ballot box at a Brandon polling place during the runoff election for the South Dakota Republican nomination for governor on July 28, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)As they cast their ballots now through Election Day on Nov. 3, voters will decide on four constitutional amendments, all courtesy of the South Dakota Legislature. Three of the amendments reflect their origins in a Legislature that’s top-heavy with Republicans. Those three deal with popular Republican topics: tinkering with voting rights, looking to squeeze out expanded Medicaid and making it tougher for citizens to have their say in changes to the state constitution.
Here’s a look at the four amendments:
Amendment K: Everyone must love it
Each election year, the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office produces a Ballot Question Pamphlet that includes an explanation from the attorney general as well as “pro” and “con” arguments about the measure. Amendment K would create a trust fund for unclaimed property. It sailed through the House and Senate in 2025 without a negative vote. Maybe that’s why the Secretary of State’s Office couldn’t find anyone to write a “con” statement about the amendment.
In an age when no one seems squeamish about sharing their opinions, you’d think that there would be someone, somewhere who thinks that the trust fund is a bad idea. Secretary of State Monae Johnson could have turned to one of the proponents of Amendment I, which seeks a method for repealing expanded Medicaid coverage. One of them could tell her that the state’s financial arrangements should never be enshrined in the constitution, because that’s what they’ve said about expanded Medicaid.
Amendment I: Taking another swipe at expanded Medicaid
After successfully authorizing a work requirement for expanded Medicaid in the last election, proponents of Amendment I are seeking to blame the federal government for their need to put in place a mechanism to roll back the program.
The federal government pays for 90% of the insurance coverage. Amendment I says that the state constitutional requirement to offer coverage would end if the feds drop their share below 90%. As an example, they say that for every 10% drop in federal assistance, South Dakota will have to pay an additional $36 million per year. Their theory is that things are so bad in Washington, D.C., that it’s likely the federal government will need to cut its share of Medicaid financing.
That sounds like a scare tactic all dressed up as sound financial management.
Amendment J: For those times when a federal law just isn’t enough
Amendment J seeks to make it clear that noncitizens aren’t allowed to vote in South Dakota elections. The fact that there’s already a law banning noncitizens from voting doesn’t seem to matter to the amendment’s backers.
While Amendment J seems like a well-intentioned, if redundant, way of making the state’s voting laws clearer, there is a downside. The author of the amendment’s con argument offers the reminder that it’s now the law of the land in South Dakota that any registered voter may challenge another voter’s registration by claiming that they’re not a citizen.
Passage of Amendment J would add one more obstacle to citizens facing the challenge of proving their citizenship within the confines of Election Day or being barred from voting.
What the amendment’s backers would have you believe is that it’s a way to protect election integrity. In reality, the amendment takes a backhanded swipe at naturalized citizens and people of color — many of whom have been known to vote for Democrats.
Amendment L: Welcome to minority rule
Currently, for an initiated amendment to be enacted, it needs approval by a simple majority of voters. Amendment L would change that threshold, requiring 60% of voters to approve of an amendment in order for it to be added to the state constitution.
Backers of the amendment say changing the constitution should be held to a higher standard. Apparently they are unaware of the irony that, if approved, it would only take a simple majority of voters to require that all future amendments meet the 60% threshold.
Similar attempts to raise the voting threshold in 2018 and 2022 failed. Voters saw those for what they were — more attempts by the Legislature to keep citizens from messing with the constitution.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Activists have chosen constitutional amendments as their best vehicle for getting issues before the voters, because they still remember what the Legislature did to Initiated Measure 22 in 2017. Approved with 51% of the vote, IM 22 was a flawed, likely unconstitutional, attempt at policing corruption in government. Rather than wait for the court system to work its magic, legislators scrambled to dismantle IM 22 with the speed and efficiency of a NASCAR pit crew.
True, the measure was flawed. However, the ease with which lawmakers disregarded the will of voters still stings. Ballot measure organizers see initiating change via a constitutional amendment as the safest path because the Legislature won’t be able to touch it for two years and must attempt to make any changes at the ballot box.
All four of this year’s amendments have been offered by the Legislature rather than citizens. That’s a testament to all the restrictions the Legislature has put on petition drives. Those restrictions include petition deadlines, circulation requirements and allowing signatures to be taken off petitions.
Lawmakers continue to enjoy an easier path to getting amendments on the ballot, having to just convince a simple majority (ahem) of their colleagues that it’s a good idea. This is a means of working the system, using their role as legislators to get their issues before voters without going through all the mess and fuss of having to collect petition signatures.
Study your own copy of the 2026 Ballot Question Pamphlet to help you decide how to vote. From here it sure looks like these amendments reflect Republican-centric issues. Their passage would make life tougher by implementing unnecessary restrictions on voting, adding mystery to the prospect of getting Medicaid coverage and allowing a 41% minority to decide if the constitution will be changed.
Not only that, but thanks to the lackluster effort of the secretary of state’s office, there’s no one out there to tell us if the unclaimed property trust fund is a bad idea.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi midterms: In 4th District race, Ezell touts FEMA and Coast Guard wins. Hulum bets on Trump backlash
description: Candidates for Mississippi's 4th District congressional seat are, from left, Carl Boyanton, Jeffrey Hulum III and Mike Ezell.
text:
An incumbent Republican who’s a former sheriff, a Democratic retired military officer and an independent businessman and perennial candidate are vying to represent southern Mississippi in Congress for the next two years. 
State Rep. Jeffrey Hulum III of Gulfport is the Democratic challenger trying to oust incumbent Republican Rep. Mike Ezell, despite the Gulf Coast congressional district having remained solidly conservative for nearly two decades. Independent Carl Boyanton of Diamondhead is making his fourth run for the seat.
Hulum told Mississippi Today during an episode of “The Other Side” podcast that he decided to run because the area needs a unifying figure to combat divisiveness, support K-12 public education and support veterans.  
“We’re too divided as a country,” Hulum said. “We’re too divided as a community. But we need a unifier. Someone who’s going to bring people together, be more neighborly and look out for the well-being of one another.” 
If elected, Hulum said he would consult constituents on major policy issues, instead of blindly supporting a political party or political figure. 
“We have to put the will of South Mississippi before anyone’s political agenda or aspirations,” Hulum said.
Hulum is attempting to become the first Democrat to win the southern district since 2008. He currently represents Gulfport in the Mississippi House of Representatives, and he served in the U.S. Army for 22 years, retiring as a sergeant major. If elected, Hulum would be the first Black person to represent the 4th Congressional District. 

Hulum hopes that President Donald Trump’s unpopular decision to escalate the military conflict in Iran and enact additional tariffs on Canadian goods imported to the United States will cause South Mississippians to rethink their voting for the GOP. 
A native of Pascagoula, Ezell defeated former Republican U.S. Rep. Steven Palazzo in 2022. Before entering Congress, Ezell was the Jackson County sheriff. He serves on the Natural Resources Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee. 
Ezell told Mississippi Today in an interview that he wants to run for reelection to steer more federal resources to southern Mississippi infrastructure projects and build on recent funding increases in the U.S. Coast Guard, which he believes has been chronically underfunded in recent years.
If reelected, he wants to introduce legislation that rolls back unnecessary federal regulations at the Federal Emergency Management Agency to make it easier for state and local governments to receive relief after natural disasters damage Mississippi communities. 
The Republican incumbent over the next two years also wants to rework some of FEMA’s flood maps because homes located within the flood zone have higher home insurance costs. 
“Insurance is just over-the-top expensive,” Ezell said.  
Ezell said that some of the president’s decisions on tariffs and the military conflict in Iran may be unpopular nationally. But he defended the military action as necessary to prevent Iran from having access to a nuclear weapon, and he said Trump’s tariffs are needed to correct trade imbalances between America and other countries.  
“Americans have been ripped off by European nations and Canada because of the way they do business,” Ezell said. “It’s time to get some payback.”
Boyanton has vowed to fight inflation and lower the cost of living by reining in government spending and the national debt. He vows to combat fraud, waste and abuse, which he said is widespread in government. He has also been a proponent of term limits for Congress.
The midterm elections are Nov. 3.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri election officials begin mailing ballots as they await ruling on congressional map
description: Missourians living overseas began receiving their ballots Friday despite continuing uncertainty over which congressional candidates should be listed on them. Military personnel and other eligible Missourians outside the United States can receive ballots electronically or by regular mail, with military members in combat zones able to return voted ballots dire[...]
text:
Absentee voting for people who cannot get to the polls begins Tuesday in Missouri. Election officials are waiting for a ruling from the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to find out if they must work overtime to change congressional districts for voters in 28 counties (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).Missourians living overseas began receiving their ballots Friday despite continuing uncertainty over which congressional candidates should be listed on them.
Military personnel and other eligible Missourians outside the United States can receive ballots electronically or by regular mail, with military members in combat zones able to return voted ballots directly through a portal maintained by the Secretary of State’s office. 
Federal law directs election authorities to send the emails and post the envelopes by Friday, the last business day before the 45th day before the election.
And while those deliveries were going out, and other work necessary to conduct the election continued around the state, officials in 28 counties were looking to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in St. Louis for a decision on the congressional district map. A three-judge panel on Thursday heard arguments from U.S. Rep. Bob Onder, state Sen. Rick Brattin and Secretary of State Denny Hoskins that the correct map for November is the gerrymandered plan drawn in 2025 to favor Republicans in seven of Missouri’s eight districts.
Federal court weighs whether it’s too late to revive Missouri’s gerrymandered map

Brattin is the GOP nominee in the 5th District, the one targeted by Republicans. A lawsuit filed Thursday in Jefferson City seeks to kick him off the ballot because the district lines changed, but no action is scheduled in the case until after the election.
The 8th Circuit did not rule Friday. Any decision it does reach is certain to be appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. The nation’s highest court has already acted twice to sustain the Missouri Supreme Court’s ruling that the legal map for November is the one passed in 2022 and used for two most recent elections.
The gerrymandered 2025 map was used in the Aug. 3 primary. But the Missouri Supreme Court’s Sept. 3 ruling that the referendum petition from the political action committee People Not Politicians was legal, sufficient and timely meant the 2022 map would govern the general election. The court said the 2025 map “is not the law and has never been the law.”
The referendum will be Proposition A on the Nov. 3 ballot. Republicans will say it reflects the state and seek a “yes” vote while People Not Politicians will call it a power grab and ask for a “no” vote.
Through a flurry of legal filings and hearings in state and federal court, election officials and voters waited in limbo. The district lines changed three times, from the 2025 map to the 2022 map, back to the 2025 map and, currently, to the 2022 map, between Sept. 3 and Sept. 10. 
Missouri Supreme Court finds Denny Hoskins ‘was in contempt’ over congressional maps

A fourth, or even a fifth change, would mean about a week of overtime to catch up, election officials said Friday.
St. Charles County Elections Director Kurt Bahr is still behind because he had to wait until Sept. 10 to give directions to the vendor that prepares his ballots and get other preparations completed. Military personnel who vote through the portal received notices Friday that their ballots were ready, while the emails and envelopes will go out Monday, Bahr said.
If the district lines change again, he said, it will switch about 80,000 voters back to the districts used in August, he said. And it means there is no chance that he will be ready for absentee voting to begin on Tuesday, as required by state law.
Working in a rush, Bahr said, the county’s vendor “said he would expect it to take five to seven days to get a turnaround for all of his customers across the state.”
St. Charles County is split between the 2nd and 3rd districts. If the 2025 map is used, all St. Charles County voters would be in the 3rd District. Onder is a resident of St. Charles County. He advocated for a map that put the whole county in one district as a state senator and got the ear of President Donald Trump in July 2025 to begin the push to redraw district lines.
The later an order to change maps comes, Bahr said, the bigger the issues become. Ballots will be mailed Tuesday to voters with a standing request for an absentee ballot. That is the day that local election authorities across Missouri must be ready to accept voted ballots from people who know they will not be able to get to the polls on Election Day.
Officials can notify anyone who has already received a ballot that a replacement is available, Bahr said. But ballots that have been cast cannot be uncast.
“If somebody gets a ballot quickly, responds and votes quickly, once it’s received by the elections office, that vote is cast,” Bahr said. “At that point they don’t have an opportunity to vote the correct ballot.”
Next door in St. Louis County, about 60,000 voters would change between the 1st and 2nd districts in a late order reviving the 2025 map. The county Board of Election Commissioners sent about 1,500 ballots to overseas voters, said Eric Fey, Democratic director of elections.
He’s not sure how the county would react to an order to change maps, he said.
“We’d have to figure out a way to communicate with them and speak with our legal counsel about what, if anything, we could do,” Fey said.
The delays before the map returned to the 2022 lines on Sept. 10 taught the board how quickly it could get new ballots ready if voters had to be switched between districts, Fey said.
“We learned if we work expeditiously, we can program the election and get it proofed and ready to go in about four to five days,” Fey said.
In Boone County, where about 50,000 voters would move from the 3rd and 4th districts to the 3rd and 5th districts, the total of overseas ballots sent Friday was 115, County Clerk Brianna Lennon said.
Running an election is more than making a document and printing a ballot, Lennon said.
The machines that read ballots and tabulate the votes, the computer codes that link addresses to voting districts, and, finally, mass printing of ballots, all must be ready before the first votes are cast Tuesday, she said. That is the day that absentee voting begins for people who know they will not be able to get to the polls on Nov. 3.
“My concern is, now that we’re to the point of having the ballots, all of those processes that we did are really hard to undo and redo,” Lennon said.
Even if officials can alert anyone who receives a ballot that it is no longer valid, it doesn’t help anyone who votes immediately, Lennon said.
“You cannot pull a voted ballot back out of a tabulator and redo it,” she said. “You have voted your ballot; you are done.”
Most voters don’t follow the back-and-forth over the map, Fey said. They want the issue settled so they can focus on the candidates, he said.
“The public is a little bit baffled and frustrated by this whole process,” he said. “Most people are not totally plugged into all the inside baseball of what actors did what in this case, and what courts did what. It just seems chaotic to a lot of regular voters.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: John Stinner: Careless budget decisions threaten state’s stability
description: In my time as a state legislator and chairman of the budget-writing Appropriations Committee in the Nebraska State Legislature, I encountered the extremes, both feast and famine.  When times were good, my fellow appropriators and I diligently crafted budgets that took care of the state’s needs while tackling pressing issues, like property tax reform. When […[...]
text:
Image via Getty ImagesIn my time as a state legislator and chairman of the budget-writing Appropriations Committee in the Nebraska State Legislature, I encountered the extremes, both feast and famine.  When times were good, my fellow appropriators and I diligently crafted budgets that took care of the state’s needs while tackling pressing issues, like property tax reform. When times were bad, we buckled down, weighed the options and worked within the constraints, ensuring first and foremost that the state would continue to provide for its most basic obligations.
That’s why I’m so dismayed by today’s budgetary disaster. There’s no recession driving it. Rather, it’s been a series of careless decisions overturning decades of good budgeting practices. No business would or, more importantly, could ever run its finances the way the state has been; the business would fail.
Let’s start with the basics. The budget is a numerical presentation of the state’s priorities, which have been established over decades. Education makes up the biggest portion of general fund spending, some 41%, supporting K-12 and higher education. The next largest slice of the pie is made up by programs that provide aid to individuals, which I’ve always considered the “have to” spending. These are mostly administered by the Department of Health and Human Services, which makes up about 37% of the budget. The largest program is Medicaid, and much of it is dictated by federal regulations and mandates. The third priority is public safety, about 13% of the budget, and includes corrections, the court system and state patrol. That leaves about 9% for everything else, including operations at many other state agencies. The work of the Appropriations Committee is to ensure efficient operation and effectiveness of all of these agencies. Underfunding operations is neither efficient nor effective.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Separate from these priorities are initiatives, which may reflect the priorities of the current administration or legislators. Cutting income taxes for individuals and corporations was an initiative. Property tax relief is an initiative. Importantly, initiatives can only be funded when the priorities are taken care of. However, that’s not how the budget has functioned in recent years, instead funding initiatives (wants) at the expense of priorities (needs).
In order for an initiative to be successful, it must have sustainable, predictable funding. Legislators leveraged a one-time budget surplus as the basis for cutting income taxes, which was never going to sustain the roughly $900 million annual reduction in tax receipts, even with widespread sweeps of existing cash funds, overreliance on the cash reserve and deep cuts to state agencies. The effect of the income tax initiative has been a swift dismantling of the budget’s structural integrity.
Property tax relief, the costliest initiative, is funded through excessive use of a budget tactic that bypasses the state general fund altogether. In fiscal year 2022-23, these “transfers out” totaled $518 million, which included $310 million of property tax credits. Fast forward to FY 2026-27, and transfers out now account for $1.76 billion, an increase of 239%. Less than $1 million of that money will go to something other than property taxes.
This has not been reported as an increase in spending, but should absolutely be analyzed as such. When you look at the spending that includes transfers out, cash fund sweeps, department-level cuts and depletion of the cash reserve, Nebraska has seen an increase of around 60% in total expenditures over the last four years. The explosion of spending on transfers out for the property tax initiative has forced budgetary moves that would get any businessman laughed out of the boardroom.
Taken together, cutting revenue and increasing spending through two major initiatives have left the state’s priorities high and dry. Structural integrity, now a distant memory of a seemingly bygone era, has disappeared altogether, and agencies are continually asked to cut spending at a time when they’ve already sustained cuts and had their cash funds raided.
Any good business manager knows that it is much cheaper to retain an employee than it is to replace one. Continual cutting of department budgets will inevitably result in an exodus of top talent from state agencies and higher education. Losing top talent defies gravity. Asking state employees to sleep in their cars on state travel is not a serious retention strategy.
I’ve always supported diligent tax reform – look no further than my record – but any business run like the state has been in recent years would be destined for failure.
This is no way to run a business and certainly isn’t the way to run the state.

title: The value of a college degree can’t be measured by salary alone
description: Ask whether college is worth the cost, and the conversation will quickly turn to jobs. Will graduates find employment? How much will they earn? Will their salaries justify what they spent or borrowed to attend? These are necessary questions. College is expensive, and students deserve honest information about whether a degree will improve their economic […]
text:
(Getty Images).Ask whether college is worth the cost, and the conversation will quickly turn to jobs. Will graduates find employment? How much will they earn? Will their salaries justify what they spent or borrowed to attend?
These are necessary questions. College is expensive, and students deserve honest information about whether a degree will improve their economic circumstances. Institutions should be accountable for helping students graduate and preparing them for meaningful work. But in our effort to prove that college pays, we have begun to treat earnings as though they are the only return that matters.
That increasingly narrow definition of value is becoming embedded in public policy. In June, the U.S. Department of Education issued new accountability regulations tied to whether graduates of undergraduate programs earn more than the typical adult with only a high school diploma. Earlier this year, Missouri lawmakers considered going further. Senate Bill 1617, which advanced from the Senate Education Committee but did not pass before the legislative session ended, would have prohibited public colleges and universities from using state funds for programs classified as producing “low-earning outcomes” under the federal standard.
This policy direction reflects a legitimate expectation: Students should not invest years of their lives and thousands of dollars in programs that leave them worse off financially. The concern is not that employment and earnings are being measured. It is what happens when those measures become the primary basis for deciding which forms of education deserve public support. Earnings can be counted, compared, and displayed on a dashboard. They appear to provide an objective answer to a complicated question: Which degrees are worth supporting?
But a measure can be precise without being complete.
A graduate’s earnings reflect more than the quality or value of an education. They also reflect geography, local labor markets, economic conditions, and how society compensates different kinds of work. Teachers, social workers, school counselors, and other professionals serving the public good perform work that communities depend on, even when their salaries do not reflect its value. When earnings become our primary measure of educational value, we risk turning labor-market inequities into judgments about educational worth. Chronic underpayment is treated as evidence not that society undervalues essential work, but that the programs preparing people to do it are unworthy of public support.
We also risk judging an education by what happens immediately after graduation rather than what it makes possible across a lifetime. A first job is one moment in a career that may span four or five decades. During that time, industries will change, technologies will evolve, and some occupations will disappear. The lasting value of an education must include the ability to continue learning, evaluate new information, communicate across differences, and adapt when familiar answers no longer work.
Those capacities matter beyond the workplace. At its best, college gives people structured opportunities to examine difficult questions, test their ideas against evidence, and encounter perspectives different from their own. Students may reconsider assumptions they have long held or discover that a problem appearing simple from a distance becomes more complicated when viewed through another person’s experience. Few institutions create sustained space for that kind of development.
This does not mean attending college automatically makes someone more thoughtful, engaged, or compassionate. People develop these qualities in families, workplaces, faith communities, and many other settings. Nor does every college provide every student with the support needed to realize education’s broader promise.
Yet recent research reflects a more complicated picture than earnings alone provide. In the 2026 Gallup-Lumina State of Higher Education study, 71% of alumni said their education was worth the cost, even as only 11% of bachelor’s degree holders believed colleges charge fair prices. Graduates can recognize the value of their education while still questioning the price they were asked to pay.
That value may also extend beyond graduates themselves. A Gallup-Lumina analysis found that educational attainment remained associated with voting, volunteering, and charitable giving after accounting for demographic differences. These associations do not show that college alone produces civic engagement, but they point to contributions that an earnings measure cannot capture.
Economic mobility and human development are not competing purposes of college. Students should not have to choose between preparing for a livelihood and preparing for a life. The same abilities that help people become thoughtful members of their communities—critical thinking, communication, intellectual curiosity, and a willingness to revise conclusions—also help them navigate a changing economy.
None of this excuses higher education from addressing its problems. Colleges must become more affordable, communicate costs and outcomes clearly, eliminate barriers to completion, and ensure that students can translate learning into opportunity. Defending the broader value of college cannot become a reason to dismiss concerns about debt, completion, or employment. It should lead us to build a more complete definition of accountability.
As the Postsecondary Value Commission has argued, higher education should contribute to both a better living and a better life. We should ask whether graduates achieve financial security. We should also ask whether they can think critically, work across differences, contribute to their communities, and respond to a changing world. The answer is not to abandon measurement, but to avoid assuming that only the outcomes most easily counted are valuable.
Higher education faces legitimate questions about affordability, outcomes, and public trust. It needs people willing to confront those shortcomings while protecting its capacity to expand opportunity, deepen understanding, and serve the public good.
A good job is one important outcome of college. But education’s most significant returns may emerge over decades—in the questions people ask, the choices they make, the communities they strengthen, and the possibilities they imagine for themselves and others. Those outcomes may be difficult to capture on an earnings dashboard. They are no less worthy of public investment.

name: WyoFile
title: UW research values Wyoming’s elk, mule deer and pronghorn at a stunning $6B
description:
‘Natural wealth’ valuation takes into account all the benefits and costs from the hundreds of thousands of ungulates that call the Equality State home.  
The post UW research values Wyoming’s elk, mule deer and pronghorn at a stunning $6B appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
One way to comprehend the value of Wyoming’s elk, deer and pronghorn is to relate it to the state’s permanent mineral trust fund. 
The corpus of that account, which sits at over $13 billion, is fed by severance taxes on oil, gas and mineral extraction and its investment income funds an impressive share of Wyoming’s government. 

Jake Hochard, a Knobloch associate professor and natural resource economist with the University of Wyoming’s Haub School of Environment and Natural Resources, poses in his office in February 2026. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

“For wildlife, it’s very similar,” said Jake Hochard, a Knobloch associate professor and natural resource economist with the University of Wyoming’s Haub School of Environment and Natural Resources. “The corpus is that [wildlife] biomass on the landscape. And the return is that we’re able to hunt every year, and we maintain and responsibly manage that value for the future.” 
While the mineral trust fund is financial wealth that creates a financial return, the state’s ungulates are a form of “natural wealth” that create return in “ecosystem services,” Hochard said.  
The collective value of that natural wealth for Wyoming’s three most common ungulate species — elk, mule deer and pronghorn — isn’t trivial. Together, the hundreds of thousands of wild ungulates dwelling across the Equality State’s 62 million acres are worth nearly $6 billion, according to the UW professor.  That’s about the same overall market value as some well-known national businesses, like footwear and clothing companies Crocs and Abercrombie & Fitch. 
Hochard stresses that his research is different from the more common type of economic impact studies that have been conducted, for example, on Wyoming’s hunting and fishing, and broader outdoor recreation industry. While those industries generate billions annually, the associated studies overlook the costs, which is a factor Hochard’s natural wealth estimate takes into account. 
“Wildlife is managed,” Hochard said. “Game and Fish has a budget. That’s not free. Ungulates are hit by vehicles. We’re not just looking at revenue generated or economic impact.”
The $6 billion estimate accounts for overall value added to society and factors in those costs, now and in the years to come. He likened the state’s ungulate populations to a bridge used by vehicles. Both are valuable now, but they also generate value streams for decades into the future. 
“So, if we invest in a migration corridor today,” Hochard said, “that’s going to create some additional value every year going forward.” 
Hochard’s database of valuations for the state’s big three ungulate species is detailed enough that it produces estimates down to the herd level. And it also tracks how values change along with ungulate populations and other factors over time. 
Wyoming’s mule deer and pronghorn numbers, for example, have fallen significantly in recent decades. Elk, though, are the most valuable species and wapiti populations have fared much better — they’re even at nuisance levels in some areas. As a result, overall ungulate values are growing. 
“We’re seeing that the appreciation of value is pretty steady across the state,” Hochard said. 
Mule deer populations that include this group of six above Pinedale in April 2026 are valued statewide at $1.2 billion, according to new University of Wyoming research. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
According to the most recent estimate, Wyoming’s elk are valued at $3.9 billion, mule deer at $1.2 billion and pronghorn at $916 million. So far, values have held up better than populations. Over a recent span that mule deer populations struggled and fell by more than half, values declined by only 6%. 
In some cases, steady population declines aren’t abrupt enough to halt appreciation. The historically significant Jackson Elk Herd is one example: Over a recent roughly two-decade period, the crown jewel herd fell in population by 32%, but the value of the herd as an asset grew by 25%, from $104 million to $131 million. 
Values of the Jackson Elk Herd, in red, have risen over decades while the herd’s population has declined. (Jake Hochard)
Hochard plans to introduce his valuations on Wyoming elk, mule deer and pronghorn to a broad audience at the National Assembly of Sportsmen’s Caucuses conference in Oklahoma City this December. If a peer-review process goes smoothly, he’ll also make a portal of his valuation data public around that time. 
Much sooner, Hochard is sharing his research with the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission. He’s scheduled to present at 3 p.m. Monday at the commission’s meeting in Evanston. Readers can tune in remotely via Zoom.

title: Community meeting planned about controversial plant planned for Kanawha County
description: Organizers opposing a controversial “advanced recycling” facility planned for eastern Kanawha County will host a community meeting about the project this week. A forum about the proposed Clean Seas-West Virginia plant is scheduled for 6 to 8 p.m. Tuesday, Sept. 22 at the Belle Town Hall gym, 1100 E Dupont Avenue in Belle.  The plant […]
text:
Eric Caruthers, a Belle resident who is concerned about the proposed Clean-Seas project, speaks at the Kanawha County Commission meeting on July 23, 2026. Caruthers — along with several of his neighbors — delivered a petition signed by nearly 1,000 residents opposing the pyrolysis plant to Commissioners Ben Salango and Natalie Tennant. (Photo by Caity Coyne/West Virginia Watch)
Organizers opposing a controversial “advanced recycling” facility planned for eastern Kanawha County will host a community meeting about the project this week.
A forum about the proposed Clean Seas-West Virginia plant is scheduled for 6 to 8 p.m. Tuesday, Sept. 22 at the Belle Town Hall gym, 1100 E Dupont Avenue in Belle. 
The plant — which would be located at the old 84 Lumber building near Belle — would burn plastic feedstock to create pyrolysis oil, synthetic gas and solid residue to be used and sold for petrochemical manufacturing purposes. 
While the company has marketed the process as a “clean” and a “sustainable energy solution” for the world’s ongoing plastics crisis, experts and organizers have said the technology is a rebranding of plastic incineration, which has been shown to harm the environment and public health while contributing to climate change. 
Organizers have invited dozens of federal, state and local elected officials as well as company representatives to the meeting, said Eric Caruthers, a Belle resident who has led opposition efforts to the facility.
A large meeting about the plant last April had a large turnout and sparked interest in taking further action against the facility, Caruthers said. He said organizers wanted to host a second large forum to make sure residents know that since the state issued the facility an air quality permit, the company is free to finish construction and start operations. 
“We wanted to open up the forum just to make sure that everyone is aware of what’s happening,” Caruthers said. “We sent out personal invitations to 168 elected officials and community leaders to bring them into the conversation, and I think the goal is to get more people aware of what’s happening, and also maybe motivate some more people to join in with our efforts as we go as we move forward.”
Eastern Kanawha County residents have raised concerns about the emissions the plant could cause, and its proximity to nearby Riverside High School, Midland Trail Elementary School and residential neighborhoods.
“The most concerning thing for me is having this facility right beside where my nephew goes to high school,” Caruthers said. “He’s on the track team. He’s in the band, so he’s going to be running right beside this in track season. And he actually got up and spoke at the DEP meeting too. He was quite the hit.”
The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection last month issued a finalized air quality permit to Clean-Seas West Virginia, allowing the company to move forward with plans for the plant, despite opposition from residents there. 
Despite the permit, Caruthers said organizers are still working to oppose the plant. They’re partnering with Fair Shake Environmental Legal Services to appeal the permit, he said. 
Organizers collected nearly 1,000 signatures from residents opposed to the plant, asking Kanawha County commissioners to hear their concerns. Kanawha County officials say a policy implemented 40 years ago prevents the agency from enforcing zoning in unincorporated areas, including most of eastern Kanawha County.
Caruthers said organizers want to revisit the issue with the commission. He said no one has been able to find the actual law that prevents the county from enforcing zoning. 
“And so we are planning — I’m not sure when, but we are planning to go back to the commission and say, ‘Hey, you said that there was a law in place preventing you from taking action on our behalf, but no one can find it. So, what were you talking about?’”
They also hope that towns and officials in the area also join efforts to oppose the facility. The town of East Bank has already done so, he said. 
“We are campaigning around to the local area municipalities, requesting that they issue resolutions, so that as a Kanawha Valley, we can all stand together and tell this company that we don’t want them here,” Caruthers said.
