name: Kansas Reflector
title: How to know if you can trust an artificial intelligence chatbot’s answer to your pressing question
description: I recently typed a simple question into Google search: How much screen time is too much for teenagers? Instead of presenting links, as Google had been doing for many years, it gave me an AI-generated answer. The artificial intelligence agent cited a number, then complicated that reply, noting that quality and balance of time could […]
text:
An AI answer to a search query can fit one of several types, writes our columnist today. (Photo by Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images)I recently typed a simple question into Google search: How much screen time is too much for teenagers? Instead of presenting links, as Google had been doing for many years, it gave me an AI-generated answer. The artificial intelligence agent cited a number, then complicated that reply, noting that quality and balance of time could matter more than the number of hours, and that “too much” time could depend on a teenager’s sleep, exercise, school demands and mood.
I tried another search: Should I take a daily aspirin? This time the AI answer presented me with medical information, warned about risks and offered more tailored guidance if I provided my age and medical history.
These were good replies. What interested me was that they were different kinds of replies.
Debate about AI answers has focused on accuracy: Did the system get the answer right? That matters, but accuracy is only one test. Each kind of answer requires a user to judge something different.
I find it useful to sort AI answers into an “answer typography” of four broad types: factual, interpretive, constructive and strategic. A factual claim can often be checked against a source. An interpretation can be accurate and still reflect choices about which evidence matters. A construction can be well reasoned and still be wrong for the person receiving it. A beautifully written strategic document may not be true. Yet AI presents all four types of answers in much the same fluent, authoritative form; the differences are easy to miss.
I’m university librarian and dean of libraries at the University of Virginia who leads national efforts to develop AI competencies for library professionals, and I consult widely on AI literacy. I first proposed the typography in the Journal of Academic Librarianship.
The four categories are not airtight boxes. A response from an AI agent can reflect several types. That said, I describe each type of answer below, and offer guidance for deciding whether a reply is ready to use or needs more investigation.
 
Which answer is Google giving you?
A factual answer makes a claim that can, in principle, be checked against evidence. When was the University of Virginia founded? What is the chemical symbol for gold?
To determine whether a factual answer is robust enough for you to use, verify the claim against an appropriate source. If the answer cites a source, follow that link instead of simply treating the answer itself as proof.
An interpretive reply is built on evidence, but there is not a single takeaway. How much screen time is too much for a teenager? Does remote work raise productivity? The answer depends on what evidence is included, what is left out and how disagreement is understood.
Google’s initial answer to my screen-time question indicated that two hours was a limit for teenagers. Then it noted that pediatric guidance puts more weight on the quality and context of screen use than on simple hours. The American Academy of Pediatrics says there is no exact recommended amount for teens and emphasizes the kind of screen use and what activities it might be displacing. A question that looked numerical turned out to require interpretation.
To assess interpretive answers, do more than check facts. Ask yourself what evidence the system emphasized, what it left out and whether another defensible interpretation exists. A useful follow-up question to present to the search engine is: “What is the strongest evidence for a different conclusion?”

Constructive answers are made rather than discovered. Ask AI to draft a cover letter, write a eulogy, suggest a lesson plan or reorganize a paragraph — there is no single correct result.
You can judge the response by considering purpose, audience and voice. A eulogy can be grammatically perfect and still sound nothing like the person delivering it, or it may land flat on family members hearing it. It may not capture the deceased person well, either. Consider these kinds of effects as you read.
Strategic questions ask what to do. Should I take a daily aspirin? Should I buy the house? The answers combine information with judgment about goals, risks, trade-offs and personal circumstances.
My aspirin search shows why context matters. Google warned about risks, told me to consult a medical professional and offered more tailored information if I provided my age, cardiovascular history and risk of bleeding. That caution matches the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force guidance. It says the decision to start low-dose aspirin for prevention of heart attacks and strokes should be individualized and weigh cardiovascular benefit against bleeding risk.
For strategic answers, ask what the system would need to know before its advice could reasonably apply to you individually. Consider the stakes, the alternatives and whether a qualified person should be involved. For the aspirin question, a useful follow-up would be: “What details about my age, medical history or bleeding risk could change this advice? What should I discuss with my doctor before deciding?” The final judgment remains yours because you are the person who has to live with the outcome.
 
The first question after an answer
My questions began as ordinary Google searches. I did not open a chatbot. The AI-generated responses simply arrived, and links were appended.
The responses were useful. Google added context, acknowledged complications and offered tailored guidance if I supplied additional information. Within each response, though, the type of answer could change. Reporting what a medical guideline says is different from deciding how it applies to a particular person. A fluent response can move between those types of answers without a noticeable change in voice.
As a user, try to recognize what kind of intellectual work the AI agent did for a response you receive. Consider whether the interpretation is persuasive or the advice fits your circumstances.
Before asking whether an AI answer is right, ask a more basic question: What kind of answer is this? The type will tell you what to do next.

Leo S. Lo is dean of libraries and university librarian at the University of Virginia, where he also serves as adviser to the provost for AI literacy and professor of education. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. title: Andrew Young, Eric Holder reflect on the state of civil, voting rights after court decisions
description: When Andrew Young rose from his motorized chair and took his seat on stage Friday, he received rousing applause. U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, an Alabama Democrat, recounted Young’s storied journey. Pastor. Mayor of Atlanta. Congressman. U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. Civil rights icon. Working alongside the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., Young played a [[...]
text:
From left to right: Andrew Young, Eric Holder and Rep. Shomari Figures (D-Ala.) participate in a panel discussion Friday at the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation's 55th annual legislation conference in Washington, D.C. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)When Andrew Young rose from his motorized chair and took his seat on stage Friday, he received rousing applause.
U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, an Alabama Democrat, recounted Young’s storied journey. Pastor. Mayor of Atlanta. Congressman. U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. Civil rights icon.
Civil rights icon Andrew Young poses for pictures Friday at the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation’s 55th annual legislative conference in Washington, D.C. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Working alongside the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., Young played a key role with other civil rights leaders in securing support for Congress to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights of Act of 1965. At age 94, Young is among the few surviving members of King’s inner circle.
“One thing I really want to make sure that everybody understands. That we are in the presence here of a legend, and all that I’ve been able to do, all that Shomari has been able to do, all that Congresswoman (Terri) Sewell has been able to do, is as a result of the great work, the sacrifices, the commitment, the determination and the courage of this man,” said former U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder, the nation’s first Black attorney general.
But the landmark legislation that Young help draft has been damaged by legal challenges with the U.S. Supreme Court, recently dealing the Voting Rights Act a blow. In April, the nation’s highest court ruled in Callais decision v Louisiana  that the state’s use of race-based redistricting amounted to an “unconstitutional racial gerrymander.”
“What worries me about this moment now is that this administration aided by this Supreme Court is bound and determined to take us back to a time that I thought, that we all thought, that might have been behind us,’’ Holder said. 
Said Young: “I don’t know where we are now.”
Young, Holder and Figures shared a conversation about civil rights Friday at the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation’s 55th annual legislative conference in Washington, D.C.
A  New Orleans native, Young’s work in voting rights began as an elementary student. He recalled that students were instructed to write a letter to their parents on why they needed to vote.
“You wrote to your own parents and took the letter home and gave it to your parents about why they should vote,” he said. “Even in segregation, we were being taught the struggle.”
Although he had studied Gandhi as a young man, he said his father taught him how to endure racism, a lesson that carried him through his work in the movement. 
“My daddy said, ‘Look, you’re never going to be able to be big enough to beat everybody, but you can outthink anybody,’” Young said. “He said, ‘Don’t get mad. Get smart. If you lose your temper in a fight, you lose the fight. Your mind is the most valuable weapon you have, and if you get emotional, you cut your mind off.’ And so that’s the way I was raised.”
Young said he first met King at Talladega College in Alabama in the late 1950s. Young was studying at Hartford Theological Seminary in Marion where he would meet his first wife, Jean Childs Young. “We were both newly married, and we talked more about our baby daughters than we did about civil rights, and we talked about growing up,” he said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Youngs moved to Atlanta in 1961, where he joined the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), eventually becoming its executive director and working alongside King.
In 1972, Young made history when he was elected to Congress as the first Black representative from Georgia since reconstruction. Five years later, President Jimmy Carter appointed him ambassador to the United Nations in 1977. Young also served two terms as Atlanta mayor and would work to bring the Olympics to the city in 1996.
He and Jean Childs Young were married for 30 years before she passed away in 1994. He is married to Carolyn Young.
Young is credited with helping draft the landmark Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act, barring racial discrimination.
Holder, a New York native, was 14 when Congress passed the Voting Rights Act in 1965 and acknowledged it was the impetus for his work as an attorney. 
“I lived through the struggles, observing them from New York on television, to see the passage of the Voting Rights Act, to see the flowering of Black political power in the South and to see attempts to undo that history. As I  matured and to be able to be in these positions, it became my determination that not on my watch would we see a retrenchment, to go back to the America that existed before the great work that Ambassador Young and all those great heroes, heroines did before me,’’ said Holder, who became the nation’s first Black U.S. Attorney General under President Barack Obama, the first Black president.
Former U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder poses for a picture Friday with James Field IV of Mobile, Ala., at the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation’s annual legislative conference in Washington, D.C. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
But civil rights advocates have lamented decisions by the Supreme Court in Shelby County v Holder in 2013  and the Callais decision in April that they say have gutted the Voting Rights Act.
Holder also connected some of the past struggles to what the Trump administration is pursuing, including attempting to add President Donald Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center and the Iran war. He called those running the country having “intellectual deficits.”
Watching the conversation and attending his first Congressional Black Caucus conference, James Fields IV, 23, of Mobile, Ala., said the panel was his favorite.
“I think this was my favorite panel because it had a mixture of knowledge,” said Fields, who works as a community liaison for Birmingham City Councilmember Crystal Smitherman. “I’m learning from their footsteps, and also I think being able to hear their mistakes allows us the opportunity to know what we should and should not do as young people. I’m just blessed and I’m honored.”

title: Georgia school system abruptly bans Toni Morrison’s ‘The Bluest Eye’
description: Georgia’s second-largest school district is once again at the center of a political controversy over the appropriateness of school materials. Cobb County Schools Superintendent Chris Ragsdale announced the district is removing copies of Nobel Prize winner Toni Morrison’s “The Bluest Eye” from school library shelves. The novel tells the tragic story of a youn[...]
text:
Cobb County School District Superintendent Chris Ragsdale, 2023 file photo. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderGeorgia’s second-largest school district is once again at the center of a political controversy over the appropriateness of school materials.
Cobb County Schools Superintendent Chris Ragsdale announced the district is removing copies of Nobel Prize winner Toni Morrison’s “The Bluest Eye” from school library shelves.
The novel tells the tragic story of a young Black girl dealing with racism, poverty and abuse.
In a speech during a school board meeting Thursday, Ragsdale read aloud from a scene in which the protagonist is raped by her father.
“The words speak for themselves,” Ragsdale said. “Both as a father and as a superintendent, I think about a parent having to explain to their sixth-grade daughter after she encounters explicit descriptions of child incest and rape in a book provided at school, without parents’ knowledge. As the superintendent responsible for the instruction of 100,000 students, I do not have the luxury of making that decision for other parents and their children.”
Library and free speech advocates reject the removal.
Georgia Library Media Association advocate and retired school librarian Nan Brown said the district appears not to have followed the proper procedure under a 2022 law which created pathways for removing books that start with guardian complaints and must follow a review process.
“The Cobb County Schools superintendent seems to be saying, ‘I don’t have to go by policy,’ she said. “If I was a Cobb parent, I would be very concerned because if he is going to bypass that policy, what other policies will he be comfortable bypassing?”
Under the district’s library rules, “Only a parent or legal guardian of a student currently enrolled in a District school” may initiate a request for materials to be removed, but during the school board meeting, Ragsdale said the district became aware of the book “through conversations with superintendents in Georgia and across the country.” A district spokesperson did not immediately respond to questions about the procedures that led to the book being removed.
In 2022, Forsyth County removed eight books, including “The Bluest Eye,” but ended up returning it and most of the others after a review process and after the feds launched an investigation into whether the district was creating a hostile environment for students.
Brown said the book did not meet the standard three-pronged test for obscenity called the Miller Test: whether the work taken as a whole appeals to a prurient interest, whether it depicts sexual conduct or bodily functions in a “patently offensive way” and lacks serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value.
Brown said “The Bluest Eye” is widely recognized as having great literary value and the scene Ragsdale focused on treats the rape as a brutal act.
“It’s violence,” she said. “It’s not titillating. It’s violence.”
Some Cobb County parents expressed bewilderment at the way the district announced the ban, reporting that they received notifications on their phones that contained the explicit passage Ragsdale referenced with a content warning.

Former Attorney General Treg Taylor, at right, speaks at a Sept. 9. 2026, forum held by the Last Frontier Republican Club at the Petroleum Club of Anchorage. Next to him, from left, are two of the other three gubernatorial candidates: former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, and former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)On the day that his campaign announced it had accepted hundreds of thousands of dollars in donations from employees of a California-based artificial intelligence company, Democratic governor candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins said that if elected, he will seek to temporarily ban new computing data centers in Alaska.
As Americans grow frustrated with artificial intelligence software and concerned about the side effects of data centers, they have become a major issue in this year’s midterm elections. Alaska’s gubernatorial race is no exception, particularly since the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority announced plans for a development that could include data centers in Southcentral Alaska. 
All four candidates — Republicans Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor and Bernadette Wilson and the Democratic Kreiss-Tomkins — have staked out different policy positions before Alaskans vote this fall.
Data centers need reliable connections to the internet, cheap electricity and a cooling method. Currently, the North Slope is the most promising location for all three. 
One $500 million proposal on the North Slope intends to burn local natural gas for power and use the natural cold air of the Arctic. 
Another shipping-container-sized plan involves a gas-powered data center processing Bitcoin.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Current Gov. Mike Dunleavy has backed data centers, saying they could be an economic driver — they would create construction jobs and demand for infrastructure that would enable further development. 
Dunleavy is term-limited and cannot run again this year. Four candidates remain in the race to replace him.
“I’m a big believer in data centers. I know that might be unpopular with some folks here,” said Bronson at a candidate forum hosted by Commonwealth North in Anchorage on Thursday.
A former Anchorage Mayor, retired Air Force pilot and former director of the state’s largest airport, Bronson said he sees economic opportunity if data centers are built in Alaska, and he would like to encourage them.
“The logistics (are) minimal, and there’s a lot of money in data centers, but you’ve got to deal with the noise. You’ve got to deal with the cooling, and you’ve got to deal — certainly — with the electricity. And the groups that I’m talking to, they said we’re not going to take your electricity because it’s not reliable. … We will produce our own, and we will move, and we will build our own data centers. That’s good for us. That’s a very strong revenue source,” Bronson said.
At a Sept. 8 forum in Anchorage, Taylor — the state’s former attorney general — offered a similar perspective.
“I think we need to embrace it,” he said of data centers. 
“We have all the makings of a great place for a data center to thrive and produce good-paying jobs for Alaskans,” Taylor said.
He added that electricity costs are his biggest concern. Any data center must “bring their own energy,” he said, and if a data center then sells excess power it generates, it could be a benefit to Alaskans if it is cheaper than other power available nearby.
“It doesn’t have to drive up costs if you do it correctly. It can produce a net savings to the ratepayers in Alaska,” he said.
Bronson and Taylor each said they see data centers as the future and fear that Alaska will miss out if it doesn’t embrace them.
“It’s a service everybody’s using and everybody has to adapt to and use, or you’re going to get left behind,” Taylor said.
Kreiss-Tomkins is advocating a temporary pause on data center development in the state.
“I support a moratorium on data center development in Alaska until the Legislature can pass a comprehensive regulatory framework for that development in Alaska,” he said during a Sept. 8 forum in Anchorage.
Any limits on development would be decided by negotiations between himself and the Legislature, he said.
While Kreiss-Tomkins’ campaign has received large donations from people employed by the AI company Anthropic, those employees have tended to recommend restrictions on AI development as well.
This year, the Alaska Senate voted 14-5 to pass a data center bill, but the House failed to take it up before the end of the legislative session. That bill would have regulated how data centers can use electricity from public utilities and would have required them to create decommissioning plans. 
The sponsor of the bill, Sen. Löki Tobin, D-Anchorage, will return to the Legislature next year, and the coalition majority that passed the bill is also likely to return, meaning that the next governor will likely be confronted with similar legislation.
Kreiss-Tomkins has also endorsed legislation that would ban AI-generated fake images intended to mislead the public and a bill that would require political advertisers to disclose AI-generated content. 
Wilson, asked about her position by text message, criticized Kreiss-Tomkins’ campaign for accepting large contributions from AI company employees.
“Unlike Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins — better known as Chat JKT — our campaign is not funded with hundreds of thousands of dollars from California AI companies hoping to own our governor and exploit our state,” she said before explaining her position. “Our administration will make independent decisions that are in the best interest of Alaska, not big donors from the Lower 48. I will never allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers that take our resources and spoil our lands. Our natural beauty, environment and quality of life matter to every person who calls Alaska home and my job is to represent them, not big tech liberals.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Black astronauts tout space exploration at CBCF legislative conference
description: There have been fewer than 20 Black astronauts in NASA history, but two of them were on a Washington stage Friday for the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation conference, touting space exploration and encouraging Black youth to think about careers in space.
text:
NASA astronaut emeritus Victor Glover, center, speaks Friday at the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation’s legislative conference in Washington, with retired NASA astronaut Jeanette Epps and Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-4th). (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)There have been fewer than 20 Black astronauts in NASA history, but two of them were on a Washington stage Friday for a discussion as part of the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation’s annual legislative conference.
Jeanette Epps and Victor Glover were on hand for “Ad Astra: African Americans in Space Exploration,” hosted by Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-4th), honorary co-chair of the 55th annual conference this year. Ivey, whose district includes the Goddard Space Flight Center, said the panel was to not only tout space exploration, but to encourage younger Blacks to enter what Ivey called a multitrillion-dollar industry “that’s just going to keep growing.”
Glover, a pilot with the rank of captain in the Navy, completed a 10-day mission in April on the Artemis II that traveled around the moon, taking humans farther from Earth than they had ever traveled. That led Ivey to point at Glover and quote the opening lines from the original “Star Trek” TV show, “To boldly go where no one has gone before.’ He really did.”
Glover, who spent a total of 178 days in space in his career, said one of his inspirations to become a pilot was when he attended college and saw a Black man in a Navy uniform.
“Thinking about my future, I wound up having a mentor come to campus … and he was in his Navy uniform,” Glover said. “And from a young man who did not believe he had any place in the federal government, but especially in the military, that changed that myth instantly by seeing this Black man in that Navy uniform, and I would join the Navy a couple of years later.”
Retired NASA astronaut Jeanette Epps responds to a question at the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation’s legislative conference Friday. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Epps spent 235 days in space as a mission specialist on the International Space Station. What was supposed to be a six-month mission ended up being almost eight months in space, when delays in launching a return vehicle extended her crew’s stay. She became the Black astronaut with the most time recorded in space.
“I had a wonderful eight months in space. It was glorious,” she said Friday. “I saw a solar eclipse in space, which is amazing because all you see is a shadow of Earth. I saw hurricanes, some of the most beautiful auroras you can think of. Nothing would take away my joy.”
Dozens showed up for the hourlong panel discussion, after which both Glover and Epps were asked how they maintained their mental health being in space for several months.
Glover said NASA provided resources such as strength and conditioning professionals, and even a nutritionist. For behavioral and mental health support, Glover said NASA had “operational psychologists.”
But he said mental preparation must be part of your lifestyle before a trip to outer space begins.
“If you don’t have healthy habits on the ground before you go on mission, it is not going to get better in space,” said Glover, who now works at California Polytechnical State University.
Epps, who resides in Prince George’s County, said she would communicate with her family on “WhatsApp” and turn her iPad toward the window so they could see space.
“I wanted to make sure everybody I knew got a chance to see what I was looking at every day,” she said. “I called my family every day, every night before I went to bed.”
Before the panel discussion began, both said in a brief interview that talking with younger people about space exploration begins at an early age. They also acknowledged NASA hosts programs for the public, including one coming up in November called “MAX POWER.”
“We’re going to talk about rockets. We’re going to talk about airplanes and the technology behind them,” Glover said. “What the [NASA] administration is doing now is quite impressive. Could we do more? Of course, but I don’t think people realize all of the things that we’re doing now, and this administrator’s vision is the right direction.”

title: Tom Osborne becomes the first living member of the Nebraska Hall of Fame
description: Husker legend Tom Osborne’s bust was unveiled as he was recognized as the first living member of the Nebraska Hall of Fame.
text:
The statue of former Husker football coach Tom Osborne is unveiled in the Nebraska State Capitol Rotunda on Sept. 18, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Husker legend and former congressman Tom Osborne’s bust was unveiled Friday as he was recognized as the first living member of the Nebraska Hall of Fame. 
“I think everyone in this room is guilty: We love Tom Osborne” Pillen said during a press conference at the Capitol rotunda.
Osborne was inducted into the Hall of Fame thanks to a push by state lawmakers, at the governor’s request, in the last legislative session to change state law so Osborne could be inducted while alive. 
Some lawmakers raised a possible constitutional concern about “special legislation” because the original language would have made Osborne the only eligible candidate. The proposal was tweaked to be a little broader. The governor-appointed Nebraska Hall of Fame Commission unanimously approved Osborne as the next member in July. 
Osborne spoke briefly to thank those in attendance. 
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, left, with his former Husker football coach, Tom Osborne, before a ceremony honoring Osborne as the first living inductee of the Nebraska Hall of Fame in the Nebraska State Capitol Rotunda on Sept. 18, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
During his speech about Osborne, Pillen said he spoke with President Donald Trump about awarding Osborne the Presidential Medal of Freedom. 
The Presidential Medal of Freedom is the highest award a civilian can receive in the United States.
In a short press gaggle after the event, Pillen went into more detail about the conversation with Trump. He said the meeting focused on beef. 
“It was rather intense because I explained to him Nebraska livestock producers’ — cattlemen’s — perspective. He asked questions. I was using my hands a lot because I was defending Nebraska. … We got finished. I said, ‘Hey, Mr. President, [got] time for one more subject. He said, ‘Yeah, what’s that?’ I said, ‘Tom Osborne,’” Pillen said. 
Pillen told the Examiner that while he and the Trump administration are working out the details, they are planning something next month.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska federal judge nominee dodges 2020 election, Jan. 6 questions in confirmation hearing
description: An Alaska nominee for federal judge joined other nominees in a joint confirmation hearing before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee on Wednesday and declined to answer some questions about the 2020 election and Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol.  President Trump nominated Kyle Reardon, a federal magistrate judge and former prosecutor, to fill […]
text:
Alaska federal judge nominee Kyle Reardon (right) is sworn in before a confirmation hearing before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Hearing on Sep 16, 2026, along with nominees Trevor Pemberton for the Eastern District of Oklahoma (center right), Courtney Coker for the Northern District of Texas (center left) and Richard Bennett for the Southern District of Texas (left) and Daniel Ballou for the Eastern District of Kentucky and Zach West for the Northern District of Oklahoma (not pictured).  (Screenshot of U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee livestream)An Alaska nominee for federal judge joined other nominees in a joint confirmation hearing before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee on Wednesday and declined to answer some questions about the 2020 election and Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. 
President Trump nominated Kyle Reardon, a federal magistrate judge and former prosecutor, to fill the last of three federal judge seats for the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska in August.     

Alaska federal judge nominee Kyle Reardon answered questions from senators at a confirmation hearing before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee on Sep. 16, 2026. (Screenshot of U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee livestream)
 

Reardon was endorsed by Alaska’s Republican U.S. Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan to fill the vacant seat, after former judge Joshua Kindred resigned in disgrace in 2024.  
If confirmed by the U.S. Senate, Reardon would be one of three federal judges in Alaska serving lifetime appointments. 
Reardon appeared before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee for a nomination hearing along with nominees Daniel Ballou for the Eastern District of Kentucky, Richard Bennett for the Southern District of Texas, Courtney Coker for the Northern District of Texas, Trevor Pemberton for the Eastern District of Oklahoma and Zach West for the Northern District of Oklahoma.
Nominees answered a variety of questions from committee members, including their views on the administration of justice, impartiality, diversity, abortion access and the 2020 election. 
President Donald Trump has continued to falsely deny that President Joe Biden won the 2020 election by claiming election fraud without evidence. Biden won both the popular vote and the majority of Electoral College votes in 2020. 
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Connecticut, posed the questions to the six nominees on the topic. He also asked whether the U.S. Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021. The event was widely documented and reported — Trump supporters attempted to interfere with Congress’ certification the 2020 election results in a violent attack that caused significant damage, dozens of injuries and at least five deaths. 
When asked who won the 2020 election, Reardon answered that Joe Biden did. 
But when Blumenthal asked the nominees who won the popular vote in 2020, he gave a different answer. 
Nominees from Kentucky and Texas answered before Reardon. Daniel Ballou from Kentucky responded: “I believe it’s inappropriate under the canons of judicial ethics to weigh in on matters of political controversy.” 
Reardon agreed, and said “I have the same answer.” Coker, Pemberton and West said the same.
Blumenthal then asked if the U.S. Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6.
Richard Bennet of Texas responded before Reardon and declined to call it an attack.
“I saw some of the coverage and the violence, the vandalism and the trespass, and I condemn those,” he said. “But characterizing it as an attack, I believe, weighs into a matter of political controversy, and it’s inappropriate for me to comment on that under the canons.”
Reardon agreed with Bennett’s response: “Senator, I concur with Judge Bennett’s characterization,” he said. 
Following the exchange, Blumenthal questioned the judges’ independence. “The failure to answer the question of who won the 2020 election again, I think, indicates that you would be unwilling to stand strong against political influence, particularly from the White House, which has asserted that it wants to dominate the Department of Justice and our entire justice system,” Blumenthal said. 
Blumenthal said he would oppose their nominations for that reason: “Right now, we’re in a very perilous time, and I would have expected more from nominees of the United States District Court.” 
Reardon was not available Friday, according to his clerk’s office, to comment on his reason for declining to answer the questions or on Blumenthal’s assertion it indicated an unwillingness to stand against political influence.
Alaska U.S. Sen. Murkowski strongly condemned the attack on the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6 and called for Trump to immediately resign, just weeks before Biden’s inauguration. She also condemned Trump for issuing blanket pardons last year for roughly 1,600 people criminally convicted for their involvement in the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. 
On Thursday, a spokesperson for Murkowski responded to Reardon’s responses, and whether they were a sign of unwillingness to stand up to political influence as Blumenthal said. 
“President Biden won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election, and the U.S. Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021. These are facts, despite the controversy that has come to surround them,” said Joe Plesha, communications director for Murkowski, in an email. 
“During multiple interviews and conversations with Mr. Reardon, Senator Murkowski was impressed by his professionalism, judgment, and independence,” he said. “Based on those interactions and his record of public service in Alaska, she expects Mr. Reardon to demonstrate those qualities as a District Judge for Alaska should he be confirmed.”
Sullivan also condemned the violence on the U.S. capitol. Later he voted to acquit Trump at a subsequent impeachment trial saying, in part, that Trump was already out of office. Sullivan declined to comment on the blanket pardons of those involved in Jan. 6 but said publicly that Trump had promised on the campaign trail to do so. 
On Thursday, a spokesperson for Sullivan declined to comment on Reardon’s responses at the hearing because the senator was traveling. The spokesperson pointed to an August post on social media congratulating Reardon on the nomination. 
Both Alaska senators have endorsed Reardon’s nomination. At the hearing, Murkowski spoke in support of Reardon, praising his career in public service and on the bench in Alaska. “This is an individual that is not only qualified for this position, he is ready to hit the ground running as a U.S. District Court judge,” she told senators. 
In an opening statement, Reardon grew visibly emotional while thanking his family members for their support. He also thanked President Trump and Alaska’s senators for the nomination, saying “it is a professional honor of a lifetime.”
Reardon has served as a federal magistrate judge in Alaska since 2021, a role which oversees a variety of judicial proceedings. His career in the judicial system includes serving as a federal prosecutor as an Assistant U.S. Attorney in Alaska and California, clerking for two federal judges, and serving as a Judge Advocate in the U.S. Army, according to his questionnaire submitted to the committee.  
There is no set schedule for the judiciary committee to vote on confirming the nominees. The judges were asked to answer additional questions from senators in writing before a committee vote, then their nominations go to a vote before the full U.S. Senate, expected in the coming weeks.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah’s strategy to fight invasive reeds at the Great Salt Lake? Play the long game and look upstream
description: State lawmakers got an update on efforts to remove invasive reeds from the Great Salt Lake and what it will take to keep up the progress.
text:
Crew members work a controlled fire to get rid of invasive phragmites around the Great Salt Lake. (Utah Fire Info) Floods of four decades ago wiped out native plants and left the Great Salt Lake vulnerable to an expensive problem: tall, invasive, thirsty reeds crowding out other plants and covering up habitat for migratory birds. 



This article is published through the Great Salt Lake Collaborative, a solutions journalism initiative that partners news, education and media organizations to help inform people about the plight of the Great Salt Lake — and what can be done to make a difference before it is too late.


The good news is getting rid of the weeds in and around the lake could yield an estimated 82,000 more acre-feet of water, state land managers told legislators at the Utah Capitol this week. That’s more than enough to meet the yearly, indoor needs for a community the size of West Valley City.
Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle on the Legislative Water Development Commission agreed Thursday that killing the phragmites is “low-hanging fruit” in the state’s ambitious goal to deliver almost 10 times that amount — 800,000 more acre-feet of water — each year.
Administrators in the Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands pointed to Utah Lake as a success story. There, similar efforts reduced the reeds’ cover of the lake bed by nearly 90%, said Keith Hambrecht, restoration manager with the Division of Forestry, Fire, and State Lands. 
As for the Great Salt Lake, Utah’s gained ground against the invasive plants across thousands of acres, Hambrecht said. But the work will take more time and funding. 
Each year, $800,000 in state money goes toward that effort, and lawmakers set aside $2.2 million this year. Hambrecht said if the state keeps up its financial commitment, it could remove the majority of the reeds around the lake in the next decade.
But further from the lake’s shore, there’s more work to be done, especially when it comes to controlling upstream sources — work that is logistically more challenging and likely much more expensive, Hambrecht said.
“We’ve done a really good job in the wetlands, but phragmites is throughout the watershed,” Hambrecht said. “It’s in ditches, canals, streams. It’s all over the place.”  
A tributary to the Great Salt Lake at the Ogden Bay Waterfowl Management Area is pictured on Monday, Nov. 25, 2024. The U.S. Geological Survey installed a stream gauge on this tributary, and 13 others, to monitory water flow into the Great Salt Lake. (Kyle Dunphey/Utah News Dispatch)
The panel floated ideas for stepping up a response throughout the watershed, including greater coordination among counties, with help from the Great Salt Lake commissioner.
Success in tackling phragmites also depends on weather and drought: In dry years, the herbicide the state uses is less effective, so the state prioritizes those treatments in wet periods.
“We probably need to just be aware that we can do a lot of damage on these phragmites if we’re if we’re paying attention and get the money at the right time,” said Sen. Mike McKell, R-Spanish Fork.

title: Arkansas finance secretary urges lawmakers to keep Medicaid fully funded after $400M spending hike
description: Arkansas spent $400 million more on Medicaid between July 1, 2025 and June 30, 2026 than the previous year, Finance and Administration Secretary Jim Hudson told lawmakers Friday. This increase was just above the amount in the Department of Human Services’ operating plan for fiscal year 2026, agency spokesperson Gavin Lesnick said in an email, […]
text:
Arkansas Finance and Administration Secretary Jim Hudson and Human Services Secretary Janet Mann answer questions about Medicaid funding from the Arkansas Legislative Council on Sept. 18, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas spent $400 million more on Medicaid between July 1, 2025 and June 30, 2026 than the previous year, Finance and Administration Secretary Jim Hudson told lawmakers Friday.
This increase was just above the amount in the Department of Human Services’ operating plan for fiscal year 2026, agency spokesperson Gavin Lesnick said in an email, but Hudson said state officials did not anticipate the spike in insurance claims that contributed to the spending increase.
“We had an unfavorable year, in terms of experience,” Hudson told the Arkansas Legislative Council.
The council approved a request from Hudson and Human Services Secretary Janet Mann for $200 million in restricted reserve funds to cover the state’s required match for Medicaid, the federally funded, low-cost insurance program for low-income people and people with disabilities.

Sept. 2026 PEER E. restricted_reserve 
Medicaid covered nearly 840,000 Arkansans at the end of fiscal year 2026, costing more than $9.8 billion. Mann wrote in her funding request to Hudson that she expects similar cost and enrollment for fiscal year 2027.
The $200 million allocated Friday will not last the rest of the current fiscal year, which ends June 30, 2027, Hudson said. He urged lawmakers to keep Medicaid fully funded, find ways to increase recurring revenue from the program and ensure the state’s Medicaid trust fund is “adequately capitalized to deal with any surprises that occur in the future.”
As of Aug. 31, the Medicaid trust fund had more than $120 million, Lesnick said.
Republican Sen. Scott Flippo of Bull Shoals asked Hudson “how healthy” he considers the Medicaid trust fund.
“I won’t put a healthy or sick label on it,” Hudson said. “This is math, right? I think what we have to look at is the total resources that we have available as a state to meet our obligations, and we have more than adequate resources to be able to do that.”
Hudson also said Arkansas needs to have enough reserve funds to contribute to Medicaid if need be. The state finished fiscal year 2026 with a $655 million surplus and about $4 billion in reserves.
State lawmakers will meet several times throughout October to discuss the fiscal year 2028 state budget, and Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders will reveal her formal budget proposal in November.
Hudson and lawmakers agreed that Medicaid funding discussions will continue in the budget hearings leading up to the 2027 legislative session beginning in January.
The future of Arkansas Medicaid is expected to be one of the session’s highest priorities. The federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services verbally denied a five-year extension of Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion model in July, and in August the state requested a two-year grace reprieve to keep Medicaid recipients covered while officials come up with a new model.
The Department of Human Services has not yet received a formal notification of the denial, nor has it received a response to the agency’s request for the two-year grace period, Lesnick said Friday.
Mann told lawmakers last month that she expects the federal government to approve the two-year grace period and that the Department of Human Services does not plan to stop administering Medicaid.

name: WyoFile
title: Sikh truck driver stabbed at Wyoming rest stop, suspect faces attempted murder charge
description:
Authorities say there is no known motive for the attack, which has caused concern within the broader Sikh community.
The post Sikh truck driver stabbed at Wyoming rest stop, suspect faces attempted murder charge appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A Punjabi Sikh truck driver suffered multiple stab wounds when a man attacked him with a knife in the bathroom of a western Wyoming rest stop, authorities say.
The driver told police the man attacked him from behind at about 3:30 a.m. Sunday at the Bitter Creek Rest Area along Interstate 80 east of Rock Springs. The assailant stabbed the man multiple times, including twice each in the neck and chest, according to investigators with the Sweetwater County Sheriff’s Office.


The crime drew national attention after NPR and other news agencies reported about the attack and the fears it had spurred within the Sikh community amid a national rise in vitriol directed at immigrant truck drivers. The Sikh faith has about 30 million members worldwide, with several hundred thousand adherents in the United States. About 20% of U.S. truckers are Sikhs, according to the North American Punjabi Trucking Association.
“Everyone deserves to feel safe,” said Jasjit Singh, an attorney and director of legal services for Jakara Movement, a California-based organization that supports the Punjabi Sikh community. “I think the fact that this was an unprovoked attack is just a reminder of how dangerous things have gotten for folks as the rhetoric continues to grow.” 
Authorities in Sweetwater County say they don’t yet know the motive for the attack. County and Prosecuting Attorney Daniel Erramouspe cautioned against making assumptions about the assailant’s motives at this stage in the investigation. 
“I don’t understand the reason why everyone wants to find a motive on this other than to satisfy their own political theories,” he told WyoFile on Friday. “The investigation is still ongoing. We still have a long ways before trial. And so assumptions don’t get anyone further in this case.”
In an interview with NPR, the victim indicated he doesn’t know why he was attacked.
“I don’t know why this happened,” said the man, who NPR identified only by his last name of Singh due to his safety concerns. He is a resident of Sacramento, California.
The Bitter Creek Rest Area along Interstate 80. (WYDOT)
Witnesses at the rest stop heard sounds of an altercation and then saw a man run from the building and leave in a semi-truck headed east on Interstate 80, according to an affidavit filed by sheriff’s investigators. Those witnesses photographed the semi, which was later located by the Wyoming Highway Patrol in Rawlins. The driver, identified as Andrew Kris Bzdak, was taken into custody. 
Prosecutors charged Bzdak with attempted first-degree murder on Monday. Bzdak, a 44-year-old man who lives just east of Los Angeles, is now being held on $1 million bond at the Sweetwater County Detention Center in Rock Springs.
Rhetoric and concern
After the attack, Singh, and a family who also happened to be at the rest stop, called for help. He was later flown to Wyoming Medical Center in Casper, where he was treated for 17 lacerations.
He is recovering well, Jasjit Singh told WyoFile in a Friday interview. Jasjit Singh flew to Wyoming earlier in the week to visit the driver as he received treatment in a Casper hospital. He is in good spirits, Jasjit Singh said.
“There’s a concept in the Sikh faith of being in Chardikala — Chardikala refers to being in forever rising spirits, always trying to keep a positive outlook on life. And he had that, right, despite being stabbed 17 times and literally almost losing his life.

The truck driver, identified only as Mr. Singh, was stabbed multiple times, including twice each in the neck and chest. (Jakara Movement)

“There’s a lot of people who ended up being great people, right? Whether it’s the Latino family that ended up helping him or the troopers who came to his aid or the helicopter that … flew him all the way to Casper.” 
The driver Singh has worked as a trucker for nearly four years, and traveling through Wyoming was normal for him, Jasjit Singh said. 
“You know, someone asked him, ‘What do you think about Wyoming?’ And he’s like, ‘It’s a beautiful state,’ right? Beautiful place to drive through, calm, quiet. And it’s unfortunate that this is his experience right now.”  
In his interview with NPR, the driver Singh said he sensed another man following him as he walked into the restroom. The assailant beat and then stabbed him before fleeing. 
Speaking to WyoFile, Jasjit Singh noted that the attack occurred four days after a post on X by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security that showed the Transformers’ leader Optimus Prime facing off against a Sikh man. The agency later said that man was Harjinder Singh, a truck driver from India facing felony charges for a crash that killed three people in Florida. “America for Americans. Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh,” the post said.
“And that was top of mind for our community,” said Jasjit Singh, whose own father is a retired trucker who immigrated to the United States and drove through 48 states during a 42-year career. “The day that post came out a lot of people were condemning it and doing other things. But the fear is no [amount] of condemning something like that is going to stop the damage from being done for someone who may use that as a green light to take things into their own hands for whatever purpose, and that’s kind of our fear for that. 
“Although they’re saying there’s no motive right now, it’s still unprovoked. And unprovoked, what has caused this person to think that it’s OK to do such an attack?” 
Authorities in Sweetwater County told WyoFile they’ve received a slew of recent press inquiries from news outlets in other states since the attack. Erramouspe, the county prosecutor, questioned the motivations of out-of-state outlets focusing on this case, when stabbings were also occurring in their home communities.
“They are trying to make political points, and I’d rather they’d stuck to their own backyard,” he said.
Witnesses and camera footage
A family who was also at the rest stop early Sunday reported the attack to authorities. A woman was using the female restroom at the time, and heard grunting and screaming coming from the men’s restroom, her son told a detective with the Sweetwater County Sheriff’s Office. She ran to the family’s vehicle, and a short time later, they saw two people — identified as the suspect and the victim — leave the building.
The suspect, the family told authorities, ran to his truck, which they followed as it headed east on Interstate 80 until they were able to photograph it. 
Camera footage from a semi-truck that was parked nearby depicted a scene that resembled the family’s description. A detective who reviewed the footage said Singh casually walked into the bathroom. A short time later, another man could be seen walking to the restroom “in a quick manner,” according to the affidavit. 
That man matched a photograph of Bzdak that was later taken by a Wyoming Highway Patrol trooper, according to the affidavit. 
Soon after, the man that authorities say is Bzdak was recorded running out of the building. Singh was then seen leaving the bathroom. He lost his balance and fell or lost consciousness at least once, according to the affidavit.
“Everyone deserves to feel safe. I think the fact that this was an unprovoked attack is just a reminder of how dangerous things have gotten for folks as the rhetoric continues to grow.”Jasjit Singh
The sheriff’s affidavit does not offer details about Bzdak’s arrest, nor does it state whether he spoke with investigators after being taken into custody. 
The next day, prosecutors charged him with first-degree murder, which carries a penalty of life behind bars. Court records show Bzdak made his initial court appearance in Rock Springs on Thursday. 
Bzdak filled out a form that indicated he lived in San Gabriel, California, and had a prior felony conviction for assault with a deadly weapon. Los Angeles County Superior Court records reviewed by WyoFile show that a man with the same name faced that charge in a 2005 case that eventually led to a conviction. The records do not include a description of the crime. 
Bzdak is set to next appear in court for a preliminary hearing on Sept. 24, court records show.
The post Sikh truck driver stabbed at Wyoming rest stop, suspect faces attempted murder charge appeared first on WyoFile .

name: VTDigger
title: Jurors to begin deliberations after closing arguments Monday in attempted murder trial
description:
Both the prosecution and defense closed out the presentation of evidence Friday in the case against Jason Eaton, accused of shooting and wounding three Palestinian college students in Burlington.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Jurors to begin deliberations after closing arguments Monday in attempted murder trial.
text:
Judge John Pacht speaks from the bench during the trial of Jason Eaton, who is charged with attempted second-degree murder, in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Friday, September 18, 2026. Pool photo by Paul Heintz/Boston Globe

BURLINGTON — Jurors have heard the evidence in the trial of a Burlington man accused of shooting three Palestinian students but won’t begin deciding his fate until next week. 
The judge sent jurors in the Jason Eaton trial home early Friday afternoon after all the evidence in the case had been presented. 
Both sides had rested their cases by midafternoon Friday. Rather than start the expected lengthy closing arguments and then jury deliberations, Judge John Pacht decided it was best to wait until Monday morning.
“We will start promptly at 8:30,” the judge told jurors Friday before allowing them to leave Chittenden Superior criminal court, adding that they must avoid media coverage of the trial or talking with others about the case. 
Eaton, 51, faces three counts of attempted second-degree murder, accused of shooting and wounding the three students on the evening of Nov. 25, 2023, as they walked on North Prospect Street near an apartment where Eaton had been living. 
Eaton’s lawyers have raised the insanity defense, with psychiatric experts for the prosecution and defense offering differing views during the five-day trial on whether he met the standard to be considered not criminally responsible for his actions. 
Eaton, in a recording made shortly after he was arrested five days after the shootings, said he had been hearing voices through his FM radio from either the CIA, the Israeli Mossad or God, directing him to carry out the act. 
The jury on Friday heard testimony by Emily Eckel, a clinical mental health counselor with a medical care contractor for the state Department of Corrections. Eckel, called to the stand by the prosecution, told jurors that Eaton was screened after he was arrested and incarcerated shortly after the shooting. 
She said Eaton did not appear to be psychotic at the time. She said he did report being a daily marijuana and alcohol user.
Initially, Eckel added, Eaton had been placed on regular mental health checks, also referred to as suicide watch. She said it wasn’t necessarily due to his mental state, but was done because he had reported a past suicide attempt, he was charged with serious crimes, and it was first time being incarcerated.  
In a meeting a few days later, Eckel said, she reported that Eaton appeared to be in good spirits, though she added that he expressed concern that he might be assaulted while incarcerated because of how public his case had been.
Also Friday, the attorneys discussed with the judge the instructions to the jurors to help guide them on matters of law during their deliberations. 
In addition to the testimony of the psychiatric experts, the jurors heard earlier in the week from a firearms examiner who matched a handgun seized from Eaton’s apartment to casings recovered at the scene.
The three men Eaton is accused of shooting — Hisham Awartani, Kinnan Abdalhamid and Tahseen Aliahmad — were all U.S. college students visiting relatives of one of them in Burlington over the Thanksgiving weekend in 2023.  
They were all treated for their injuries at hospitals, and Awartani’s lower body remains paralyzed. 
Awartani has attended the trial daily, seated in a wheelchair along the front row of the courtroom gallery directly behind the prosecutors. 
If convicted of even one of the attempted second-degree murder charges, Eaton faces up to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Kosta Diamantis sues to keep pension after fleeing to Greece
description: Konstantinos Diamantis on Friday sued state officials who announced that they were cutting off his state pension payments.
text:
After fleeing the country to avoid being sentenced Thursday on federal corruption charges, Konstantinos Diamantis on Friday sued state officials who announced that they were cutting off his state pension payments.
Diamantis, who previously served as a deputy budget director in Gov. Ned Lamont’s budget office, filed a federal lawsuit against Connecticut Comptroller Sean Scanlon and Attorney General William Tong, alleging that they illegally cut off more than $70,000 in annual pension benefits.
Connecticut law gives the Attorney General the ability to file a case in state Superior Court to either revoke or reduce a person’s pension if they are convicted of or plead guilty to “any crime related to state or municipal office in state criminal or federal criminal court.”
The Connecticut Attorney General’s office has used that law more than 30 times since 2008 to petition a judge to cut off or reduce pension payments to former public officials, including former Hartford Mayor Eddie Perez and Bridgeport’s former police chief Armando Perez.
It’s not a guarantee that someone’s pension will be revoked or reduced just because the Attorney General’s office requests it. It’s up to a state judge to decide if that action is warranted. The law specifies that the judge needs to take into account multiple things, including the severity of the crime, the amount of money that was lost and the degree to which the crime violated the public trust. 
Diamantis’ attorney, Norm Pattis, argued in the federal lawsuit, however, that state officials did not follow the correct process before they announced that they were revoking the pension payments for his client.
Diamantis was convicted by a federal jury last year on 21 counts of bribery, extortion, conspiracy and lying to federal investigators. He was found guilty of soliciting multiple bribes from several construction contractors that he oversaw as the head of Connecticut’s school building office.
But Pattis alleged on Friday that the jury verdict alone was not enough to cut off the payments.
“Connecticut law establishes a judicial procedure for revoking or reducing the pension of a public official convicted of specified corruption-related offenses. A jury’s guiltyverdict, standing alone, does not constitute a final judgment of conviction or automatically result in pension forfeiture,” Pattis wrote. 
It wasn’t a state judge or the attorney general’s office that announced the immediate cutoff of the pension payments to Diamantis, who is also a former state Democratic lawmaker. Instead, it was Scanlon, whose office is responsible for issuing checks and making the direct deposits to state retirees. 
After it was announced on Thursday morning that Diamantis fled the country, Scanlon issued a statement announcing that he was unilaterally cutting off his pension payments.
“This morning, upon confirmation that Kosta Diamantis did not appear at his sentencing and has fled the country, I have discontinued the direct deposit of his monthly pension payment. No one who has been convicted of defrauding the taxpayers and is now fleeing justice should continue receiving a pension,” Scanlon said. 
The press release did not state what legal authority Scanlon was relying on in order to discontinue those payments, however. The state law that allows state or municipal pensions to be revoked doesn’t mention the comptroller’s office.
The comptroller’s office did not clarify what authority they were using to end the payments to Diamantis on Friday, but in a statement, they argued that they were within their rights to end the benefit payments. 
“We are confident in our authority to determine the manner in which pension payments are issued, and we will gladly defend that authority in court on behalf of Connecticut taxpayers,” Madi Csejka, a spokeswoman for Scanlon, said.
Under the state law, it is up to the Attorney General’s office to file a motion seeking to permanently end or reduce pension payments after a conviction, but as of Friday, no such filing has been posted in state court. 
Tong, who has served as Attorney General since 2019, issued a statement on Thursday acknowledging that it was up to his office to make such a filing, but the statement said Tong’s office was still reviewing its legal options. 
“Kosta Diamantis abused the public trust and will be held accountable. His disappearance this morning is a shameful insult to every person in Connecticut and will not deter our efforts to fully protect the state’s interest and taxpayer dollars. State law requires that my office take action to revoke or reduce the pension of state or municipal officials convicted of corruption-related charges. We are reviewing all legal options to fully enforce the law,” the statement reads.
Without going through the proper channels, Pattis argued, Connecticut officials were violating Diamantis’ due process rights.
“Plaintiff does not seek to relitigate the jury’s guilty verdict or obtain a federal adjudication of whether his pension ultimately should be revoked or reduced. Rather, plaintiff challenges the actual or imminently threatened interruption of an existing pension entitlement without constitutionally adequate notice and an opportunity to be heard,” Pattis added.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Feds end oversight of MBTA that began in 2022
authors: Colin A. Young I State House News Service
description: The Federal Transit Administration officially closed its safety management inspection of the Department of Public Utilities' safety oversight management of the MBTA.
text:
THE FEDERAL OVERSIGHT of the MBTA that began amid a series of incidents including derailments and the death of a Red Line passenger has come to an end, Gov. Maura Healey announced Friday.
The Federal Transit Administration issued a letter on September 11 officially closing its safety management inspection of the Department of Public Utilities’ safety oversight management of the MBTA, the governor’s office said. The FTA also transferred its direct oversight of the MBTA that began in 2022 to the DPU.
“With the FTA’s role overseeing special directives concluded, we have officially closed the book on the serious safety issues we saw four years ago,” DPU Commissioner Staci Rubin, who oversees the DPU’s transportation divisions, said. “We made a commitment to invest in the Rail Transit Safety Division, strengthen technical expertise, and build more rigorous oversight processes—and we delivered. This was made possible thanks to our dedicated rail safety staff and support from the Legislature. The DPU is well positioned to ensure safer T operations in the years to come.”
In its letter, the FTA said the DPU has added 13 full-time staff since 2022 and “implemented a comprehensive technical training plan to provide staff the training and qualifications required to perform critical safety oversight activities.” DPU also updated its process for overseeing MBTA safety investigations, safety rules compliance, fatigue management, and safety management.
The announcement came the same week that Healey defended MBTA General Manager Phil Eng, who she hired in 2023, amid reporting on a since-dismissed complaint filed with the Massachusetts Commission Against Discrimination alleging a pattern of inappropriate behavior. The T is paying a $500,000 settlement in connection to Eng’s admission to pulling an employee’s hair.
Healey said he “absolutely” still has confidence in Eng, who is also serving as interim state transportation secretary.
“Those were allegations. That was a matter that was settled. Phil, you know, owned up and was accountable for his conduct. He said that, you know, he regretted his behavior and, you know, he’s, we’ve all moved on from this and there was a resolution there. And, you know, the thing that I like about Phil is he’s a real stand-up guy,” Healey said on GBH Radio. She added, “When I started as governor, we had trains on fire. People were jumping out of trains. Since then, under Phil’s leadership, we got rid of slow zones. We have faster service, more reliable service. Is it perfect? No, not yet. But every day we’re working that way.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New report digs into whether state investments in kids are paying off
description:
New Mexico has made some major investments aimed at improving the lives of kids around the state,
but a new report from New Mexico Voices for Children takes a deeper look at the impact of those investments.
text:
From left to right, U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Dahveed Torres and Gabrielle Uballez, executive director of New Mexico Voices for Children, discuss ways the state can ensure their recent investments in children's well-being make a tangible difference for everyday people, during a Sept. 9, 2026 roundtable. (Daniel Montaño/KUNM)New Mexico has made some major investments aimed at improving the lives of kids around the state. Just this year the Legislature passed and the governor signed into law free universal childcare, which came a year after creating a trust fund specifically dedicated to early childhood.

This story originally appeared on KUNM.

But a new report from New Mexico Voices for Children takes a deeper look at whether or not any of those are actually making a difference on a day-to-day level.
They call it the Children’s Roadmap. The report brings together formerly disparate data on education, health care and family economic security, and makes recommendations for how to make those policies work for everyday people, no matter where they are.
Emily Wildau, director of policy for Voices, said since passing the laws and making the headlines, the state now has a real challenge on its hands.
“At the same time,” she said, “there is the very unsexy work of implementing well.”
That means making sure programs that already exist, as well as anything coming down the pipe, actually reach the families that need them.
Wildau said health care is a good example, as the state has stepped in to cover Affordable Care Act subsidies that were cut by the Trump Administration, and have kept costs low while expanding the number of people covered.
“But do people even have a place to use their health insurance?” she said.
There are some counties that completely lack pediatricians, school-based health centers and OB-GYNs.
The problem comes up elsewhere too, like childcare.
Gabrielle Uballez, executive director of Voices, said the state has added about 10,000 new childcare slots over the last year. But she said the state needs to learn how to expand that coverage to more rural areas while maintaining a high quality.
The report makes policy recommendations for ensuring students get support, addressing health care workforce shortages, and increasing family security by increasing incomes, and expanding access to public benefits and tax credits.
That’s why they’re hosting a series of roundtable discussions around the state.
“This isn’t everything, and not every answer is here,” she said. “But there are a lot of provocative pieces of information that will help us find new solutions to all these issues.”
U.S. Sen.Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) attended the first roundtable on Sept. 9, which was hosted in the same building as NM Voices for Children headquarters in downtown Albuquerque. He said he was inspired by the discussion, which included representatives from several other nonprofits and advocacy organizations, and even the University of New Mexico School of Medicine.
“The only way that we are going to really invest and see the results that we want to see in our greatest asset, which is the next generation,” he said, “is if we start working together across all of those silos.”
The next roundtable will take place in Farmington on September 25 — details are available online — and they’re hosting a virtual event in October.
Support for this coverage comes from the W.K. Kellogg Foundation.
