title: Visit Nebraska leader touts tourism impact, Buffalo County growth
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska’s Buffalo County, buoyed by development in Kearney, stood out as a growing state tourism magnet during an event Friday spotlighting the economic impact of travel to the Cornhusker state. Of Nebraska’s five most populated counties, Buffalo reportedly outpaced peers with its 7% growth in direct travel spending in 2025 compared with 2024. Onl[...]
text:
"Nebraska. All Heart" is the marketing brand of  Visit Nebraska, also known as the Nebraska Tourism Commission. Leaders Friday talked about a newly released report on the economic impact of travel in the state. (Courtesy of Visit Nebraska)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s Buffalo County, buoyed by development in Kearney, stood out as a growing state tourism magnet during an event Friday spotlighting the economic impact of travel to the Cornhusker state.
Kearney’s SportsPlex, a 209,000-square-foot facility that attracts regional athletic events, is among newer developments in Buffalo County. (Courtesy of the City of Kearney)
Of Nebraska’s five most populated counties, Buffalo reportedly outpaced peers with its 7% growth in direct travel spending in 2025 compared with 2024.
Only one of the top five lost traction in tourism-related spending. Sarpy County’s dollar growth reportedly dipped 0.5% during that time frame. Douglas grew by 4.4%; Hall by 3.5% and Lancaster by 2.2%.
Those and other details are included in a 127-page report newly released on behalf of Visit Nebraska, also known as the Nebraska Tourism Commission. It looks largely at 2025 compared with 2024 and breaks down impact in the state’s 93 counties.
Jenn Gjerde, Visit Nebraska’s executive director, was joined by Paul Younes of Kearney at the Friday media event hosted by Gov. Jim Pillen, who said he was putting on his “chief bragging officer” hat for the occasion.
 Praising ‘Passport’ program 

Among the report highlights were that the direct travel spend in Nebraska overall rose by more than 2%, led to about 760 additional jobs and generated about 5% more in local and state tax revenue in 2025 compared with the year before.
Nebraska Tourism Commission Director Jenn Gjerde, left, with Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“To break that down for the everyday Nebraskan, that means every household saved $412 on their taxes last year because of tourism in this state,” Gjerde told reporters.
The economic impact study was researched by Portland, Oregon-based Dean Runyan Associates, which Gjerde said has compiled the travel report for two decades. Findings are based on data collected from various public and private sources.
Officials said the travel industry represents a key component of Nebraska’s economic prosperity, as related spending generates jobs and taxes.
Pillen praised Visit Nebraska’s Passport program,  which guides Nebraskans and out-of-state visitors to “hidden gems” across the state, and pointed out various attractions around the state. 
“We have extraordinary draws and places that we can brag (about), that we can enjoy,” he said. “Tourism is really making progress.”
Norfolk’s Farmers Market hosted the launch of the 2025 Nebraska Passport season. (Courtesy of Visit Nebraska)
Much of the state’s tourism impact was in those most populated counties, with direct travel spending in Douglas County reportedly reaching $2.16 billion last year. That was nearly half the amount attributed to the entire state. Direct travel spending measures purchases and taxes paid by travelers during their trip.
According to the researchers, the statewide direct travel spend increased 2.6% in 2025 over 2024 — nearly $118 million, for a total of $4.72 billion. However, they noted that considering reduced purchasing power of the dollar due to recent inflation, the “true quantity of goods and services purchased by travelers” increased 2.1% or $95.3 million.
Direct travel spending in Buffalo County was reported to be about $184 million, in Hall County, $180 million; in Lancaster, $725 million; in Sarpy, $257 million.
Joslyn Art Museum in Douglas County reopened in late 2024 after a major expansion and overhaul. (Courtesy of Visit Omaha)
Gjerde credited Younes with boosting development in Kearney. She said he started out washing dishes and worked his way up in the hospitality industry. He lobbied successfully to get a “good life district” designation in Kearney, which opens the door to a public tax incentive.
Kearney expansion
The good life district is being developed on 200 acres of Younes Landing, a large-scale project by Younes and Maggie Younes-Holz, who own the Kearney-based Younes Hospitality. Kearney was the state’s fifth and final good life district. Related legislation allowed half of the state sales tax generated within the designated district to go toward defraying development costs in the district boundaries.
At Younes Landing, the Kearney SportsPlex and Kearney Partnership Building opened last year. Other entertainment and retail venues are expected.
Younes said visitors may come to the development or his hotels but also look to grow businesses elsewhere in the area and create jobs and spend money.
Kearney businessman Paul Younes, left, with Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen on Sept. 18, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“It’s going to generate more sales tax for everybody. The city, the county, the state, everybody will benefit,” he said. “All of us in Kearney work together.”
Among other highlights of the report:

Travel spending generated 41,990 jobs in 2025, an increase that year of about 760 jobs, which was a 1.8% annual growth.
Direct earnings of employees and business owners attributable to travel spending went up 6.7% to $1.1 billion in 2025 over 2024.
Direct tax receipts collected by state and municipalities, as levied on travel purchases such as hotels, food, retail goods and gas, went up 5% to $339.5 million in 2025 over 2024. (State tax revenue rose by $14 million and local tax revenue by $2 million.)
Nebraska welcomed 12.7 million overnight visitors in 2025, a 1% increase from the year before. About half stayed in a hotel, motel or short-term vacation rental. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: VTDigger
title: School districts assigned to new merger discussion groups
description:
Districts across the state were reorganized into 18 merger study committees after districts requested changes. Committees are still expected to hold first meetings within the next month as school board leaders say they lack clear guidance on the process.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  School districts assigned to new merger discussion groups.
text:
Harwood Union High School in Duxbury in August 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

School districts across the state have been assigned to new groups to consider mergers after 13 districts requested changes ahead of groups’ first meetings, set to happen in the coming weeks. 
Those requests, school board leaders say, are representative of districts exercising local control early in a process they say is still muddied by unknowns. 
The new assignments announced Friday group the state’s 119 districts into 18 committees. The arrangement is different than previously outlined under this year’s sweeping education reform law, Act 170, which divided districts into 20 committees. 
The new groupings grant districts’ requests, according to a press release from the Vermont Learning Collaborative, an educational services agency hired by the state to facilitate the committees. 
“These groupings reflect a starting point, not a final decision,” the press release said. School board leaders can provide their input on the changed committees until Sept. 23, according to the release, which sets a Sept. 25 goal to finalize the groups. 
While school districts are not mandated to merge with each other under this year’s law, they are required to participate in study committees in “good faith” — just one of the law’s provisions that school board leaders say has yet to be defined. 
The change in assignments comes just weeks before committees are expected to hold their first meetings, which must occur by Oct. 15. 
A regional facilitator hired by the Vermont Learning Collaborative is set to helm the committees within a region. Those seven facilitators are instructed to remain impartial as they help districts interpret guidance from the state. 
A single statewide lead facilitator, Younce, is tasked with overseeing the seven regional leaders. 
Facilitators have so far been charged with interpreting ambiguities in the state’s mandate, according to Younce, and were tasked with reviewing districts’ committee reassignment requests.
Vermont’s effort to consider district and school consolidation comes as states across the country face declining enrollment, according to News From the States, a national news site. Preliminary data shows that more than 1,000 public schools closed nationwide during the 2025-26 school year, the site reported. 
A list of requests 
Flor Diaz Smith, president of the Vermont School Boards Association, said in an interview this week that she wasn’t surprised districts requested to change committees before work gets underway. It’s emblematic of school boards wanting local control in the fast moving process, she said. 
Although all school districts were assigned to a study committee by the Legislature, Act 170 gave districts the authority to request a reassignment with their school board’s approval. 
The law says that districts in a committee should collectively enroll at least 2,000 students, and districts can only move to committees that are geographically adjacent to their assigned committee. 
“‘Thumbs up’ is kind of the default for me, unless it violates the law,” Younce said in an interview last week, because it’s early on in the process. 
Younce declined to say which 13 school districts submitted requests to him. 
One district, Harwood Union Unified School District, requested a committee reassignment because it was originally grouped with schools in the Barre and Montpelier area, which board members said were more urban and separated from Warren and Waitsfield by a mountain range, according to the Waterbury Roundabout. 
Instead, the district was more interested in merger conversations with Mount Mansfield Unified Union School District, the news site reported. 
The new committee assignments announced Friday reflect changes like the one requested by Harwood. 
Along with making requested changes, facilitators had to shuffle districts to keep committees above the law’s 2,000 student threshold, the press release said, which resulted in two fewer districts. 
Facilitators also had to accommodate the requests of districts that wanted to be paired with others in their county, according to Younce. Those four districts appear to be in Franklin County, based on the list of new committees. 
Diaz Smith said earlier this week that she isn’t surprised that districts want to change committees so early on. 
“Because the process is different from a completely mandatory merger, some districts might try to preserve as much local agency at the very beginning,” Diaz Smith said. 
The fact that it’s an election year adds uncertainty to the process, Diaz Smith explained. 
Gov. Phil Scott previously advocated for a forced merger process, until he compromised with legislators who characterized the idea as politically impossible. With the governor up for reelection in November, Vermont could see a new executive leader — along with new legislators. 
“Who gets elected for governor is going to have a big impact,” Diaz Smith said. 
Upcoming Deadlines
While the uncertainty of an election looms, committees are instructed to begin work under a tight timeline — and now in new groups. Under Act 170, school districts will vote on mergers on Town Meeting Day in 2028. 
But they’ll have to meet a number of deadlines before then. 
Facilitators must submit a report to the state on Feb. 1 with an update on committee work, Younce said. Then each study committee has to submit a final report to the state in September 2027 detailing which of its members — if any — are merging. 
As committees get underway, Younce said their meetings will run like local school board meetings. They will be open to the public, with minutes and agendas posted online. 
The regional facilitators, who will help districts make the best decisions they can with informed data, are paid $150 an hour, with a $50,000 limit for the entire committee process, according to Younce. 
Younce said that committees will begin work with districts mapping their assets, such as school buildings, buses, extracurricular activities and technical education programs. Then, districts will begin thinking about resources they want but don’t have, Younce said. 
Identifying what districts both have and want will direct districts’ decisions, he said. 
It’s still unclear though how districts should decide about merging, Diaz Smith said. She said the Vermont Agency of Education needs to issue more guidance on how to collect and understand data — and how that data should guide districts’ decision making. 
Definitions desired 
Parts of Act 170 remain unclear for school boards, according to Diaz Smith
Younce said that in his conversations with state authorities, “it’s become clear” that any undefined parts of the law are up to the facilitators to determine. 
For example, Younce said he’s in the process of refining a standard for what “good faith” participation means. He’s been consulting with lawyers and state officials and aims to publicly announce statewide guidance by the end of September.
Act 170 also says that school districts will have committee representation that’s proportional to the number of students enrolled in their district. But the law doesn’t specify what proportional membership should look like. 
Younce, though, said committees will have options and the ability to exercise discretion. 
To start, school boards will appoint only one member each to a study committee, Younce said. Then each study committee will decide its own respective approach to achieving proportional membership, he added. 
Younce anticipates two common models will emerge. Committees that start with more members, meaning they represent more districts, may limit their size and instead make each member’s vote weighted based on their district’s student population. 
Alternatively, committees that have fewer districts may want multiple representatives from each district. In that case, the number of members would be proportional to the student size of each district, Younce said. 
Diaz Smith said that her organization has been fielding many questions from school boards on proportional representation. She said she just wants “ clear guidance on how things would work.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Three Georgia counties flagged by Trump administration for using non-English election materials
description: At least three Georgia counties were listed on an internal memo of jurisdictions across the country that offer election materials in languages other than English, according to internal records from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Gwinnett, Cobb and DeKalb counties were all listed in the report, which was emailed to a number of top […]
text:
A sign directs Gwinnett County voters to the polling station ahead of the 2025 general election. Gwinnett County has been required to distribute ballots in Spanish and English since 2016, and it voluntarily translated sample ballots into languages like Korean, Mandarin and Vietnamese. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderAt least three Georgia counties were listed on an internal memo of jurisdictions across the country that offer election materials in languages other than English, according to internal records from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
Gwinnett, Cobb and DeKalb counties were all listed in the report, which was emailed to a number of top officials at the department in December, though the memo noted there could be other jurisdictions in the state that translate election materials. The email said the list was “outlining requirements for prosecution of voter related charges,” and was signed by the department’s acting director of border policy, though the official’s name is redacted.
The documents were first reported Friday by NPR and obtained independently by the Georgia Recorder. 
Recipients of the memo include undersecretary for the office of strategy, policy and plans Rob Law, assistant secretary for border security and immigration Eric Ruark and former election activist Heather Honey, who now serves as deputy assistant secretary for election integrity for the Trump administration. The list was obtained as part of a public records request filed by the Democratic National Committee.
Lawmakers consider how to protect voting access for people with disabilities, non-English speakers

Only U.S. citizens are allowed to vote in American elections, but advocates for immigrant communities in Georgia say some naturalized citizens may struggle to understand ballots written in English. Section 203 of the federal Voting Rights Act requires local jurisdictions to offer ballot access in languages besides English whenever there are either 10,000 residents or more than 5% of the population who speak a given language and lack English proficiency. 
Gwinnett County, where U.S. Census data shows more than 38% of residents speak a language other than English at home, has been required to distribute ballots in Spanish and English since 2016, and it has voluntarily translated sample ballots into languages like Korean, Mandarin and Vietnamese. Athens-Clarke, Cobb and DeKalb counties also voluntarily translate certain elections materials.
The list from the DHS raises new questions about whether President Donald Trump’s administration may be planning to deploy federal agents at polling places during the upcoming midterm elections, though voting rights advocates say efforts to do so would be illegal. Trump has repeatedly attempted to change election rules ahead of the midterms, citing unfounded claims of widespread noncitizen voting to attempt to restrict the use of mail ballots and urge Congress to pass the SAVE America Act.
Trump’s Justice Department revives lawsuit seeking sensitive voter data in Georgia

Department of Justice officials also filed a lawsuit earlier this year seeking Georgia’s unredacted voter data after Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican, refused to hand the information over voluntarily. The case is currently pending in federal court.
State election officials say that noncitizen voting is incredibly rare, with a 2024 audit from the secretary of state’s office finding only 20 noncitizens on Georgia’s voter rolls out of 8.2 million registered voters. Only nine had ever cast a ballot. Still a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said federal officials would work to find and arrest any noncitizen voters.
“Aliens who illegally vote in U.S. elections should not be able to use a purported lack of knowledge of the English language as an excuse to avoid prosecution,” an unnamed DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens.”
But advocates for naturalized citizen voters say language accessibility requirements are a core part of voting rights laws and necessary to ensure that all U.S. citizens have access to the ballot box.
Gigi Pedraza, executive director of Latino Community Fund Georgia. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“The role of the government is to make sure that all its citizens are protected and able to exercise the right to vote,” said Gigi Pedraza, executive director of the nonpartisan Latino Community Fund, adding that counties should be encouraged to increase language access to their ballots.
“It’s just unfortunate that instead of encouraging people to participate in democracy, we make it look like it’s something that can put them in harm’s way,” she said.
Anar Parik, the policy manager at the nonprofit Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta, said that fears of immigration enforcement activity near polling places could have a chilling effect in the midterm elections. She added that naturalized citizens are already required to provide extra documents to verify their citizenship and residency in Georgia.
“The threat of immigration enforcement at polling sites exacerbates all of those barriers to voting that already exist,” she said.

title: Coast Guard icebreaker Healy cancels fall voyage to Arctic Ocean after mechanical problem
description: The Coast Guard icebreaker Healy will not sail to the Arctic Ocean this year. The Healy is one of only two active Arctic icebreakers in the Coast Guard’s fleet and had been scheduled to return to service this year and sail to the Arctic after an overhaul, but during a post-shipyard voyage in July, it […]
text:
The U.S. Coast Guard icebreaker Healy is seen on Nov. 7, 2022, in Juneau, Alaska. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)The Coast Guard icebreaker Healy will not sail to the Arctic Ocean this year.
The Healy is one of only two active Arctic icebreakers in the Coast Guard’s fleet and had been scheduled to return to service this year and sail to the Arctic after an overhaul, but during a post-shipyard voyage in July, it suffered a severe mechanical breakdown off the coast of Washington state. 
The website gCaptain, which reported on the incident at the time, cited unnamed sources who said one of the ship’s crankcases had exploded. 
In July and again this week, the Coast Guard declined to answer questions from the Beacon asking to confirm that account. 
In a written statement, a Coast Guard spokesman said only, “The Coast Guard continues investigating the cause of the engineering casualty onboard Coast Guard Cutter (CGC) Healy. CGC Healy will not complete its planned 2026 high-latitude summer mission. However, the Coast Guard is developing repair plans and evaluating the feasibility of additional operations.”
The Coast Guard did not answer multiple followup questions, including how long the Healy’s repair will take and whether the Coast Guard will seek to have another icebreaker take the Healy’s place.
This is the second major problem aboard the Healy in two years. In 2024, an electrical fire aboard the ship canceled its fall voyage into the Arctic. 
Without the Healy, the Coast Guard’s sole Arctic icebreaker is the former oilfield services ship Storis, which was commissioned into Coast Guard service last year and is not yet fully operational to Coast Guard standards.
The heavy icebreaker Polar Star is operational but is committed to service in Antarctica and is thus unavailable for Arctic service.
The Storis is less effective in ice than the Healy, which has reached the North Pole several times, and does not have dedicated science lab space, as the Healy does. 
Earlier this year, the Coast Guard awarded construction contracts for 11 new icebreakers of two different designs. The first four ships — two from each design — are being built in Finland and are scheduled for delivery by 2028. 
In the meantime, the Coast Guard has been using non-icebreaker ships in the Arctic. This summer, the CGC Munro monitored two Chinese research ships operating in the Arctic off Alaska.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Massachusetts is already putting its untapped talent to work
description: The administration is working across state agencies and with workforce partners to remove obstacles that prevent people from entering—and staying in—the workforce.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS’S ABILITY TO compete is anchored by our greatest asset – our people – and ensuring jobseekers, current workers, and future workers can pursue a path to good jobs in growing industries across all regions of the state. 
Recent commentary in CommonWealth Beacon rightly focused attention on the residents whose skills and potential remain underutilized. And they’re right that our economic future depends not only on attracting and retaining talent, but on making sure the talent already here can access good jobs and growing industries. 
However, the suggestion that Massachusetts has overlooked that opportunity is incorrect. In fact, it is at the center of the Healey-Driscoll administration’s workforce agenda focused on attracting, retaining, and developing talent; leading by example; and improving infrastructure to connect employers and talent.  
Massachusetts has both enormous economic strengths and real workforce pressures. Our labor force participation rate has surpassed its pre-pandemic level, with nearly 80,000 more people participating in the labor market than before COVID. Yet, with more than 215,000 jobs posted in June, alone, Massachusetts employers are still looking for skilled talent.   
That is why talent attraction cannot be tied to job creation alone. In addition to upskilling and developing talent, talent attraction strategies must reduce barriers that often prevent talented people from securing employment. 
The administration works across state agencies and with workforce partners to remove obstacles that prevent people from entering—and staying in—the workforce. From delivering a more affordable child care system and other caregiving initiatives to investing in English language learning contextualized for work, the administration continues to advance proven strategies to reduce barriers for employment. The most recent move to do so features the launch of “Massachusetts Advancing Pathways for International Talent” or MAP-IT, with a call for proposals from workforce partners to translate the skills of work-authorized immigrants with international credentials for careers in Massachusetts.   
We have also prioritized upskilling our existing workforce, ensuring workers today can maintain competitive skills that, in turn, help employers operate in efficient and productive ways. Since January 2023, through the Workforce Training Fund Program, the administration has awarded $100 million to train and upskill more than 82,700 existing workers employed by nearly 4,000 Massachusetts employers. The Workforce Training Fund offers an effective model to reskill and retain existing workers across industries experiencing disruptions in technology, from advancements in manufacturing to the introduction of AI in the workplace.  
Since Gov. Healey took office in 2023, the administration has invested nearly $235 million, through the Workforce Competitiveness Trust Fund (WCTF), Career Technical Initiative (CTI), and programming on re-entry, young adult with disabilities programs, and youth employment programs—all helping to prepare our future workforce. For the $129.7 million invested in WCTF and CTI, both tied to industry-recognized credentials and certificates, the administration has trained over 14,335 residents with a 74 percent average employment placement rate. Training should not conclude with a credential and a hope that a job exists. It should be informed by employers, connected to hiring needs, and designed to lead to a career with strong demand, family-sustaining wages, and opportunities for advancement. 
One example is our Health Care and Behavioral Health Hub Grants through the WCTF. Through these regional partnerships, we have designed training programs that have prepared people for occupations like certified nursing assistants, medical assistants, behavioral health specialists, surgical technicians, and other high-demand health care roles.    
Since 2023, the administration has invested over $46.1 million in health care-related workforce development grants through the WCTF to train 4,550 individuals for careers in health care with 55 employers in regions across the state.  
The administration has also prioritized Registered Apprenticeship as a key strategy to develop talent, investing $13.5 million to expand programming while also expanding the Registered Apprenticeship Tax Credit. Since 2023, we have registered nearly 13,000 apprentices, leveraging this model to create jobs in construction, health care, life sciences, clean energy, early childhood education, and more.  
Investments to develop unemployed and underemployed jobseekers are critical strategies to prepare future workers and connect this untapped talent with industries and with employers eager for talent. 
Too many capable candidates are screened out because they do not hold a four-year degree, even when they possess the skills and experience needed to perform the job. In 2024, Gov.  Healey signed an executive order establishing skills-based hiring practices throughout the executive branch. 
To promote this practice across industries and expand our efforts, we launched the MassSkills Coalition. The coalition held several community learning sessions and its work has led to the Skills-First Hiring Toolkit, released in May to help private-sector employers make the same transition—from rewriting job descriptions and assessing candidates to strengthening onboarding and retention. Reducing unnecessary degree requirements expands opportunities for untapped talent. It is a practical response to employers who cannot afford to overlook qualified people. 
We know navigating all of this can be daunting, for jobseekers, workers, and employers. As much as we continue to invest in career training, we need to invest in the infrastructure that connects talent to opportunities. We are modernizing tools across the MassHire system, most especially enhancing that front door experience to unlock a true talent marketplace for jobseekers and employers to connect.  
Massachusetts’s greatest competitive asset has always been its people. Our task in government, in partnership with business, labor, academia, and all workforce partners, is to ensure that every resident can develop their talents, find a pathway into our economy, and build a future in Massachusetts. Our administration will continue to invest in our people, attract new talent, and strengthen our economic competitiveness. 
Lauren Jones is the secretary of labor and workforce development.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Drake College GOP, university officials disagree on response to Charlie Kirk posts
description: A Republican student group at Drake University is asking university administration to decry social media posts that it says celebrate the assassination of right-wing podcaster Charlie Kirk. The university states it cannot do so due to the anonymity of the posts. Drake College Republicans stated in a news release published Thursday that Drake University offic[...]
text:
Drake College Republicans are calling out the university for its lack of response to social media posts about Charlie Kirk's death. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)A Republican student group at Drake University is asking university administration to decry social media posts that it says celebrate the assassination of right-wing podcaster Charlie Kirk. The university states it cannot do so due to the anonymity of the posts.
Drake College Republicans stated in a news release published Thursday that Drake University officials are refusing to speak out against posts made on Yik Yak, an anonymous social media site based around college campuses, around the anniversary of Kirk’s shooting death at Utah Valley University.
“The wave of students celebrating this violence, as if it is a holiday, reflects the decline of civility on Drake’s campus and in our country, the very decline Charlie Kirk fought against and eventually cost him his life,” said Josie Thompson, chair of the Drake College Republicans, in the release.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Both the Drake College Republicans and Drake Strategic Communications Director John Krantz confirmed that Thompson met with officials early this week to discuss the posts. Thompson said in the release she was informed that the administration did not plan to publicly condemn the posts.
Krantz said in an emailed statement that “Drake has no ability to govern or offer recourse” regarding Yik Yak posts because it is an anonymous platform. He said Thompson refused the administration’s suggestion that it send out an email to the student body focused on university civility principles and encouraging responsible social media usage.
“Many of the statements on YikYak were inappropriate, in poor taste, and not in alignment with the values and principles of civility across differences upon which our university stands,” Krantz said in his email.
Some of the posts referenced Drake College Republicans, according to screenshots of posts sent to the Iowa Capital Dispatch by the student group, with one calling the group “corny.” Other posts used phrases like “kirkmas” and “kirkaversary.”
Drake officials also thought that putting out a statement specifically about the social media posts may “spur more posts at a time when the conversation had already ceased,” Krantz said, while a more general statement could be more meaningful for the overall issue.
Thompson said in the release it “says something” that Drake decided to remain silent on this issue compared to past topics the university has addressed publicly, and wondered how the university would react if these posts were in response to a liberal political figure’s killing or targeting a different student organization.
“The Drake Administration is choosing silence over civility,” continued Thompson. “It’s time for the University to stand up to this type of rhetoric and serve all of its students, including Republicans.”
When Kirk was killed on Sept. 10, 2025, Krantz said Drake College Republicans worked with the university’s office of student affairs to organize a vigil “which was held successfully, civilly, and without incident.”
This year, the organization is again working with Drake Democrats, another student organization, to gather signatures to make the university a midterm election polling place and on other voter registration initiatives.
“We will continue to foster this type of collaboration across political differences while offering support for any members of our community who feel attacked or unwelcome,” Krantz said in his email. “We are exceptionally proud of the vast majority of our students and campus community who are empathetic and thoughtful in their words and their work, and who are actively collaborating to build a political space where differences don’t mean division.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Bryan Avila avoids comment on claim Trump’s ‘gone too far’ on deportations
description: TAMPA — The Tampa Tiger Bay Club had hoped to hold a forum this month between the two major party candidates for governor, Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly. After the Donalds campaign cited a scheduling conflict, aides offered his running mate, former Miami-Dade County state Sen. Bryan Avila, to speak in his stead. […]
text:
Florida Republican Lt. Gov. nominee Bryan Avila speaking at the Tampa Tiger Bay Club on Sept. 18, 2025. (Photo by Don Kruse for the Florida Phoenix)TAMPA — The Tampa Tiger Bay Club had hoped to hold a forum this month between the two major party candidates for governor, Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly. After the Donalds campaign cited a scheduling conflict, aides offered his running mate, former Miami-Dade County state Sen. Bryan Avila, to speak in his stead.
That became a bit awkward on Friday when audience members asked Avila on several occasions whether he or Donalds disagreed at all with any of President Donald Trump’s policies, such as his mass deportations of undocumented immigrants that fellow Florida Republican U.S. Rep. Maria Salazar declared in a new campaign ad on Thursday had “gone too far.”
Speaking on behalf of Donalds, Avila seemed intent on not saying anything remotely controversial.
“We have to go back to the four years prior to the current administration,” he said when asked about Salazar’s ad by Alex Sink, elected chief financial officer in Florida 20 years ago but who narrowly lost a bid for governor sixteen years ago.
“We had around 10 million illegal immigrants come into the country, some of them through the Southwest border, some of them came through Canada,” Avila said
He continued his response for a few more minutes, but never answered Sink’s question, eliciting protests from a couple of members of the audience.
On two other occasions Avila drew the same question: Were there any Trump policies that he or Donalds disagreed with?
The first time Avila completely ignored the question, instead saying that the campaign was seeing “tremendous energy” and “momentum” and disputing any polls that showed anything otherwise. The second time he said, “We are definitely in disagreement with how the Fed has been handling our interest rates.”
Lost in that response, however, is that the Federal Reserve Board is structured as an independency government agency, and that Trump himself was angry this week after the central bank increased interest rates by a quarter point, from 3.75% to 4%, the first such interest rate hike in three years.
Donalds himself did appear to distance himself from the president earlier in the week when he said “he had concerns” regarding Trump’s proposed $5,000 dividend checks, announced during the midterm Republican Convention last week in Dallas. “I’m not sure how you’re going to be able to pay for that over the long term,” he said in a Fox News interview.
That response was much milder than the reaction from Gov. Ron DeSantis, who said last week, “If you are getting surplus revenue, you should cut people’s tax and return it to the people,” adding, “What I don’t think you want to do is borrow another trillion-and-a-half dollars and then try to flood that into the economy, because that will lead to more inflation.”
Trump endorsed Donalds for governor in February 2025, an endorsement the candidate has touted throughout his race to win the Republican primary election. Whether that Trump support will carry him to victory over Jolly in November is less certain.
The Jolly campaign on Friday again said that Donalds had “ducked” debating Jolly at the Tampa Tiger Bay Club in responding to a posting by Donalds on social media that he had accepted three gubernatorial debates to take place before the Nov. 3 election
“David Jolly has already accepted two debates, with Tampa Bay Tiger Bay and CBS Miami’s Jim DeFede,” said Mark Riddle, a senior adviser to the Jolly-Gwen Graham campaign. “Byron Donalds has ducked those two, plus countless debates with his fellow Republicans in the primary. It’s pretty clear he’s not acting in good faith. The two campaigns will work on a debate schedule that’s best for Floridians. We look forward to the debates.”
Donalds originally called for Jolly and himself to engage in three gubernatorial debates in July. Jolly responded at the time, “Get through your primary and we’ll talk.”
A member of the Tampa Tiger Bay Club told the Phoenix last week that in fact the Donalds campaign had originally agreed for Donalds to appear with Jolly, then called back to say they wanted him to appear separately.
That board member said the Donalds campaign called back a third time to say he would not be able to attend and was offering Avila to appear instead. A spokesperson close to the Donalds campaign denied that sequence of events, saying they had never scheduled Donalds to appear at the event.

title: Trump rapid third-country removal policy blocked at appeals court
text: WASHINGTON — A federal appeals court Friday struck down the Trump administration’s policy to quickly send noncitizens to countries they are not from, finding that immigrants must have an opportunity to challenge their removal if they fear for their safety.The decision largely upheld a Boston federal judge’s February ruling that found the Department of Homeland Security's policy unlawful. But the immigration officers can still conduct third-country removals if they follow the proper procedures, such as adequate notice and an opportunity for an immigrant to raise a fear-based claim to that country of removal.Third-country removals, deportations from the United States to a nation other than an immigrant’s home country, occur when the immigrant’s home country does not accept the person’s repatriation. Once rare, the procedure has spiked under the second Trump administration that has entered into partnerships with several countries, some with human rights concerns, to take third-country removals from the U.S.The three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit also raised doubts that a country that accepts a person that is not their own citizen could “credibly provide blanket assurances that all removed noncitizens will not be persecuted or tortured there unless it intends to provide them with some sort of affirmative protection against rogue agents and non-state actors.” The panel also upheld the lower court's finding that the notice to a third country was inadequate – about 24 hours – and that the policy was unlawful.It gives “no notice at all of an impending third-country removal when the country to which the noncitizen is to be removed has provided credible (in the State Department's judgment) diplomatic assurances that noncitizens removed there from the United States will not be persecuted or tortured,” the panel wrote.The panel included circuit judges Lara E. Montecalvo, Jeffrey R. Howard and Seth R. Aframe. Former President Joe Biden nominated Montecalvo and Aframe. Former President George W. Bush nominated Howard.The Trump administration in May 2025 made an emergency request to the Supreme Court after U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy blocked the policy. The Supreme Court in June 2025 temporarily allowed for the removals, before sending it back to the lower court. Murphy again in February issued an order that blocked the policy and required DHS to carry out the statutory obligations of proper notice of removal to a third country and to give a noncitizen enough time to raise any concerns for their safety to their removal to a third country. The Trump administration later appealed to the First Circuit, and could appeal again to the Supreme Court. DHS did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment Friday.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Wages, economic worries take center stage at NC AFL-CIO convention
description: Like a lot of people who’ve moved to North Carolina in recent years, Christa Jackson was looking for a lower cost of living. These days, she’s not finding it. “I moved here three years ago from Los Angeles. Never thought that my very fuel-efficient, 12-gallon car would cost me $46 to fill-up here,” said Jackson. […]
text:
Calandra Hackney, left, and Christa Jackson with the Actors Equity Association attended the North Carolina AFL-CIO’s annual convention in Cary, NC on September 17, 2026. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)Like a lot of people who’ve moved to North Carolina in recent years, Christa Jackson was looking for a lower cost of living. These days, she’s not finding it.
“I moved here three years ago from Los Angeles. Never thought that my very fuel-efficient, 12-gallon car would cost me $46 to fill-up here,” said Jackson. “It’s ridiculous.”
Jackson, a member of the Actors Equity Association, attended the North Carolina AFL-CIO’s annual convention in Cary to discuss policies that would improve the outlook for working families struggling in the current economy.
Gov. Josh Stein did not shy away from addressing one of the greatest economic disparities in the state as he addressed the convention Thursday.
A new report released over Labor Day weekend ranked North Carolina as the worst state in the country for workers. By contrast, in each of the last six years, North Carolina has been ranked number one or number two in the nation for business.
Labor Day 2026: North Carolina ranks best for business economy, dead last for workers

“The General Assembly has not raised the minimum wage in 17 years,” said Stein. “And the minimum wage for tipped workers is $2.13 an hour. You have to work an hour to fill up your gas tank with half a gallon.”
Republican state lawmakers have argued it’s unnecessary to raise the $7.25 minimum wage because many employers already pay more than that in the current labor market. But advocates say that isn’t always the case, especially in rural areas where unemployment is higher.
Stein also pointed out that North Carolina is the only state in the country with a complete ban on collective bargaining by public employees.
“Shame! Shame!” responded union members in the audience.
Governor Josh Stein poses for a photo with members of National Nurses United after addressing healthcare costs and wages at the NC AFL-CIO convention. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
Stein told the audience of 250 labor activists that it is possible to build an economy that supports both working people and businesses.
“Strengthen public education. Invest in workforce development, including apprentices. Lower the cost of living. And make sure that you all have a seat at the table,” said Stein.
Stein said his administration is working to rein in rapidly rising costs for healthcare and housing, two of the largest expenses for working families in North Carolina.
‘Harder to make ends meet’
Jackson lives in Angier, where housing costs are lower than in Raleigh or Holly Springs, but she’s still noticing that people are tightening their belts.
“I’m seeing the prices are higher. Restaurants are empty. Folks can’t afford to go out,” said Jackson.
Jackson said she’s been a union member for three decades and is now fighting for the next generation.
“I never went without health insurance. I have a pension from that work, which is so rare, I can retire, and I made a living wage,” said Jackson.
She said while some younger workers may be content with the gig economy, collective bargaining can help them get the job security and benefits they’ll need as they get older.
“I’m thinking they’re not going to be able to afford healthcare,” said Jackson. “They’re not going to have jobs that give them retirement. They’re just going to have to continue to work and work and work and work.”
Calandra Hackney, also with the Actors Equity Association, agreed with that assessment.
“I think it’s harder to make ends meet for everyone,” said Hackney.
Hackney said she was worried about some of her colleagues being able to afford transportation.
Braxton Winston, president of the North Carolina State AFL-CIO (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
“In order to get a job. you have to get to the interview,” said Hackney. “I went to the pump yesterday and paid $4.19 a gallon for gas in Durham. For regular gas. That’s insane.”
Marching orders
Dolly Parton’s iconic “9 to 5” – a workplace anthem for many – played over the convention center speakers just before Braxton Winston, president of the North Carolina State AFL-CIO, took the stage.
Winston told delegates that real progress happens when workers, unions, community organizations, and elected officials work together to win lasting change.
He said one of the best ways to improve the current economic landscape is to encourage working people and their families to register, vote, and stay involved in local, state and national politics.
Winston encouraged union members to stick around after the two-day convention to help knock on doors in Raleigh in support of pro-worker candidates. Representing over 125,000 union members, Winston said, the NC AFL-CIO has the power to shape the outcome of many races this fall. The group has been mobilizing voters since spring.
“As we know, if you don’t have a seat at the table…” Winston said.
“You’re on the menu!” responded the audience.
Pages from the new NC State AFL-CIO’s Making History: An American Labor Coloring Book were featured at the convention, showcasing the struggles and victories of the labor movement. Crystal Lee Sutton was a North Carolina union organizer and advocate who gained fame in 1979 film Norma Rae. The illustrations are the work of artist Henry Adamson. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Murphy wades into midterms, CT voter turnout: CT politics news
description: Plus: Connecticut's unemployment rate falls as private sector jobs grow, and Connecticut's education department puts focus on STEM equity.
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more Connecticut political news, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
Murphy wades into the midterms
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy is stepping up his involvement weeks out from the midterm elections.
Murphy, a prolific fundraiser, is donating more than $500,000 to various Democratic committees including ones that handle competitive House and Senate races, according to Politico.
He also met with Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s Senate race who visited D.C. this week. The progressive candidate who’s a critic of Israel won a turbulent primary that divided Democrats. Murphy initially endorsed one of El-Sayed’s primary opponents, but praised him as “more of a bridge builder here than folks think he will be.”
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
How can CT get more people to vote?
The Voter Participation Task Force got underway this week, authorized by legislation passed in response to lobbying by Miles Rapoport, the former secretary of the state. 
Voter turnout in Connecticut is above the national average, but trails other states. Rapoport, who is co-chairing the task force with Rep. Hilda Santiago, D-Meriden, says it will seek ways to improve turnout. Their recommendations to the General Assembly are due Feb. 1.
Turnout yo-yos from cycle to cycle, peaking in presidential years and falling in midterm and municipal elections. Connecticut’s turnout was 67% in the 2024 presidential election — 2.4 percentage points above the national average. In the 2022 midterm, it fell to 49%.
— Mark Pazniokas, Capitol Bureau Chief
Unemployment rate falls; private sector jobs hit high in August
The August jobs report from the Department of Labor once again highlights Connecticut’s complicated economic picture, with unemployment dipping slightly to 5.1% and payroll jobs falling by 300 while private sector job growth grew to 1,495,700 jobs.
The unemployment decrease, while small, is the first drop after months of increases. But the state also continues to see people exit the labor force; in August the labor force declined by 4,100.
The figures add to already mounting concerns about the state economy. A new Connecticut Business and Industry Association survey of the state’s businesses finds that businesses in the state are reporting hiring issues, with 25% of respondents saying that they are struggling to find skilled workers.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
CT education department puts focus on STEM equity
At this year’s back to school conference for Connecticut superintendents, the keynote speech was all about jobs — STEM jobs.
National Math and Science Initiative CEO Jeremy Anderson told school leaders the STEM-related workforce is projected to grow 3.5 times faster than any other by 2032.
Anderson also noted STEM access remains inequitable and encouraged schools to proactively cultivate a “STEM identity” in students from underrepresented demographics (e.g. nonwhite, female). He said NMSI has found students who see themselves as future scientists and engineers are far more likely to get a STEM degree in college.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
CT launches haunted history trail
The state’s latest tourism campaign is going in a spooky direction for fall, with officials announcing a new Haunted History Trail that calls attention to the lore, legends and history of Connecticut.
The trail includes more than 130 places from around the state, from haunted sites like hotels and cemeteries, to museums and theaters. The state is also calling attention to the history of the Connecticut Witch Trials, which spanned more than four decades and started before the more widely known trials in Salem, Mass.
The campaign comes as the state looks to build off of a big year for tourism, with visitors to the state generating some $20.1 billion in economic impact in 2025.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Providence whistleblower hotline leads to four investigations in first year
description: An anonymous tipster named “Gold Piano” was among the first to come forward with a lead for Providence’s new whistleblower hotline: A retired city police officer whose ex-wife’s health insurance was still being covered through the city. The complaint became one of four full investigations in the first year of SpeakUp!PVD, the city’s whistleblower hotline […]
text:
Providence City Hall is pictured in downtown Providence. The city received 19 anonymous tips during the first year of its new whistleblower hotline, four of which led to full investigations. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)An anonymous tipster named “Gold Piano” was among the first to come forward with a lead for Providence’s new whistleblower hotline: A retired city police officer whose ex-wife’s health insurance was still being covered through the city. 
The complaint became one of four full investigations in the first year of SpeakUp!PVD, the city’s whistleblower hotline introduced in January 2025 by the city’s internal auditor, Gina Costa.
Gold Piano’s allegation of improper health plan coverage was later substantiated, and calculated by Costa to have cost the city a modest $831.42 for the ex-spouse’s coverage. Now the auditor said she’s asked the city for broader verification of policies regarding retirees’ dependents. 
“They opted to do non-union employees,” Costa said in an interview Friday of the review the city ultimately conducted. “But retirees have not been addressed, as far as I know. I do think that retirees should be addressed as soon as possible.”
The case was among the 13 reports deemed substantive out of a total of 19 anonymous tips received through SpeakUp!PVD during its first year. Gold Piano and the other 18 tipsters were all assigned code names by Costa’s office to help identify their cases.
The other three tips Costa investigated in full had no financial impact on the city, while several submissions were ultimately deemed “commentary” by Costa’s office — complaints about a coworker or supervisor’s behavior, rather than actual misuse of city funds.
“There’s a lot of things where I would just call the administration and say, ‘You know, you may want to take a look at this,’” Costa said. “It’s not even for me to audit on. It just could be a behavioral thing.”
The first annual report of Providence’s new whistleblower hotline covering the 2025 calendar year was received by the City Council Thursday night without discussion at its first meeting back from recess.
Costa noted that City Hall has two other avenues for complaints that may fall outside her office’s purview: ethics and human resources.




Quotation







There’s a lot of things where I would just call the administration and say, ‘You know, you may want to take a look at this.’ It’s not even for me to audit on. It just could be a behavioral thing.


– Gina Costa, internal auditor for the city of Providence



But the case of the retired police officer whose ex-wife’s health insurance was still covered by the city despite the officer’s remarrying was something that Costa could look into. It required much collaboration with human resources, which had to access much of the information Costa needed. 
Costa’s investigation determined the allegation was accurate and that the retired officer was not required under the divorce’s terms to maintain coverage for the ex-wife. The officer’s current spouse was not also enrolled, Costa said Friday.
“That was a very long one,” Costa said of the investigation.
Costa said she learned from human resources that the former spouse had not expensed any medical treatments during the time she was no longer eligible for coverage. The city’s contribution was for the premiums only. 
Costa said she sought clarification on what city policy, if any, outlines retirees’ responsibilities to notify the city of life changes that would affect their dependents’ eligibility for benefits. But Costa said she did not receive final confirmation of the policy, which she was told was with the city’s law department. 
“I’ve asked for that policy four times,” Costa said. “I finally had to close that report and left it the way I did. Because they never showed me the policy.”
The report received by the City Council Thursday night phrases the outcome as “New policy being created to address this issue.”
Rhode Island Current asked Mayor Brett Smiley’s administration several questions about the audit, including whether the city ultimately completed a dependent eligibility review for retirees or whether the $831 was recovered. A spokesperson for the mayor acknowledged a request for comment Friday but did not have a response as of Friday afternoon.
Costa said she offered to help review retiree records, but she said that HR declined the assistance. So she can’t determine whether other ineligible dependents of city retirees may have their health insurance subsidized by the city.
The city was also supposed to ask the retiree to reimburse the expenses incurred, but Costa couldn’t confirm whether the money was recovered since it’s outside her department. 
“The whistleblower hotline is a tremendous asset,” Costa said. “I do hope that people do call if they see anything that’s wrong … because it really is a good asset for the city, especially for the auditor’s office.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: MBI’s investigation into fatal toddler shooting is now on attorney general’s desk, Senatobia police chief confirms
authors: Mukta Joshi and Joseph Cranney, Verite News
description: A supporter cries after a march for 1-year-old Kohen Wiley in Senatobia on Friday, June 26, 2026. The state Department of Public Safety says a police officer responding to a shoplifting call on Sunday, June 14, 2026, shot at a car that drove in the officer's direction, killing Kohen.
text:
Mukta Joshi is a reporter at Mississippi Today. She is spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellow. Joseph Cranney is a reporter at Verite News. Both report for the Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center in collaboration with The Times.
The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation has completed its review of the Senatobia Police Department’s fatal shooting of a Black toddler and sent its findings to Attorney General Lynn Fitch, the department’s interim police chief said this week.Angelica Maze, the chief, said Fitch will decide when to release more information about the shooting of the toddler, 1-year-old Kohen Wiley. Maze, appointed earlier this month after her predecessor was fired, released a statement on Thursday after months of uproar about law enforcement’s refusal to release body-worn camera and surveillance footage of the incident. 
A representative for Fitch said the office wouldn’t comment because the case remains active. If the attorney general decides to pursue a case against any officers involved, the findings would be presented to a Mississippi grand jury, which would decide if there is sufficient evidence to bring criminal charges. 
Patrick Lumumba, who founded the Senatobia Committee for Accountability and Transparency in the wake of the shooting, which occurred on June 14, said Maze’s statement doesn’t address any of the community’s concerns. 
“We still don’t have any video footage. We still don’t have any clarity as to what M.B.I. has determined,” Lumumba said. “We don’t know anything other than the files are on Lynn Fitch’s desk.”The Senatobia Board of Aldermen fired the department’s former chief, Harold Vanderford, after Mississippi Today, Verite News and The New York Times revealed he had routinely used racist slurs against Black people in private texts. 
Kohen was fatally shot in a Walmart parking lot after two women, including his mother, were accused of shoplifting diapers and baby clothes. At least five officers converged on them as the pair got into a car, with Kohen seated on the lap of his mother, Vellesiya Wiley, in the front passenger seat. 
The state Department of Public Safety says a police officer responding to a shoplifting call on Sunday, June 14, 2026, shot at a car that drove in the officer’s direction, killing 1-year-old Kohen Wiley.  Credit: Courtesy of Carlos Haynes and Veronica Roberson
Wiley said she had lifted her son up to show officers that there was a baby in the car. Then she heard three or four gunshots. Bullets struck the car, the driver and Kohen. 
Neither woman has been charged with shoplifting. 
In a statement the day of the shooting, MBI said the car had driven toward officers, “almost striking” one. The agency released documents “in error” that identified a Senatobia officer, Hunter Foster, as the subject of its investigation. The next day, the Board of Aldermen placed Foster on paid administrative leave. 
Since then, law enforcement has remained tight-lipped about the shooting and the progress of the state’s investigation. Sean Tindell, the commissioner of the Mississippi Department of Public Safety, which oversees M.B.I., said the investigative report and video footage would be made publicly available only if a prosecuting agency confirmed the case would not be prosecuted, or if a grand jury refused to indict.
Tindell announced his run for attorney general, and Fitch announced her run for governor in August. 
The only video footage that the public has seen was captured by an eyewitness, Desirae Smith. Her video shows three officers and one sheriff’s deputy running behind the car as it drove away. Smith said nobody in law enforcement had contacted her. The authorities haven’t reached out to Wiley either, said Veronica Roberson, her mother.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trump announces all 50 states joining Medicaid drug pricing model
description: President Donald Trump speaks as South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden, from left, Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves and Abe Sutton, director of the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation, listen[...]
text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump announced Friday that all 50 states will join in on a program set to provide Most Favored Nation pricing to some drugs within the Medicaid program, bringing the net price of selected drugs down to prices paid in certain other countries.
The Trump administration claims that Medicaid will save billions on prescription drug costs as a result of the plan, dubbed the Medicaid “GENEROUS” model. Experts say the savings are unclear since the content of the deals isn’t public.
“This one thing alone should win us the midterms,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office Friday, flanked by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz and others, including Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves.
Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves speaks during an event with President Donald Trump about healthcare, in the Oval Office of the White House, Friday Sept. 18, 2026, in Washington.  Credit: AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin
Friday’s announcement comes as cost-of-living issues are at the forefront of voters’ concerns ahead of the midterm elections in November. In a way to address affordability concerns, Trump has cut deals with pharmaceutical companies so that the cost of some drugs in the U.S. would not be dramatically higher than in other affluent nations. But critics say his administration has not presented a viable plan for broadly addressing rising health costs, especially after Republicans let expire Affordable Care Act subsidies earlier this year that sent plan costs soaring.
Last year, Trump signed an executive order instituting a “Most Favored Nations” policy, where the U.S. would commit to paying the same price for medications as the nation that pays the lowest price anywhere in the world.
The White House in May estimated that Trump’s deals with pharmaceutical companies to lower some of their U.S. prescription drug prices to levels charged in other countries could save $529 billion over the next 10 years.
Patients in Medicaid, the state and federally funded program for people with low incomes, already pay a nominal co-payment of a few dollars to fill their prescriptions, but lower prices could help state budgets that fund the programs.
Trump said “every state will have the ability to use those extra billions of dollars to invest in other healthcare improvements or something else.”
The true cost of the claimed savings is unclear since few details of the deals struck by the Trump administration and participating pharmaceutical companies have been made public, making it hard to independently verify the projected savings.
Kathy Hempstead, a senior policy adviser at the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, told The Associated Press that there is significant pressure on the administration to provide more granular data to justify its cost-savings claims, and that the lack of information creates a barrier to legislative action.
“He is saying Congress should codify all of his MFN arrangements,” Hempstead said. “But it’s kind of unreasonable because it’s not clear what Congress would actually do. No one knows what is in these deals.”
She added that there is concern about whether the current administration’s tenure will affect the longevity of these price cuts and whether prices will revert once the administration leaves.
Some want to see more people benefit from lower drug pricing.
JD Hayworth, a former Republican congressman and spokesperson for the Pharmaceutical Reform Alliance, said in a statement that Friday’s announcement reflects “meaningful progress, but that progress remains incomplete,” as millions of Americans not enrolled in government healthcare want lower drug prices.
Drug prices for patients in the U.S. can depend on a number of factors, including the competition a treatment faces and insurance coverage. Most people have coverage through work, the individual insurance market or government programs like Medicaid and Medicare, which shield them from much of the cost.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Former federal officials call foul on Trump’s endangered species action
description: A coalition of former federal officials have come out against continued Trump administration changes to the Endangered Species Act.
text:
A biologist retrieves red-cockaded woodpecker chicks from a nest for banding and data collection near Fort Polk, Louisiana, May 26, 2022.  (Ian Fischer/USFWS)A coalition of former federal officials have come out against continued Trump administration changes to the Endangered Species Act. 
Seven former officials from top leadership at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration released a joint statement Friday against White House efforts to exempt companies from accountability for incidental deaths of endangered species that occur in the course of economic activity. 
The bipartisan collection of former officials led the agencies in charge of executing the Endangered Species Act over the course of four presidential administrations. 
“We haven’t always seen eye to eye. But when you’ve spent your career watching species come back from the edge, you develop a clear sense of what keeps wildlife alive,” the coalition said in a statement. 
“Stripping habitat protections and eliminating accountability for death of endangered species will lead to the extinction of some of America’s most iconic wildlife,” the officials added.
Their statement comes after the New York Times reported on an internal memo sent to U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service field offices that redefines what it means to “take” an animal on the endangered species list. 
Similar attempts to exempt industry from accidental deaths of endangered species under previous administrations were found to be unlawful.
The same seven officials have previously raised concerns about the administration’s changes to how the Endangered Species Act is interpreted by federal agencies, saying habitat destruction would no longer count as harm to an endangered species. 
The group includes:

 Daniel Ashe, former U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service director under President Barack Obama administration
Jamie Rappaport Clark, former U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service director under President Bill Clinton 
Janet Coit, former NOAA assistant administrator for fisheries under President Joe Biden
H. Dale Hall, former U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service director under President George W. Bush
Eileen Sobeck, former NOAA assistant administrator for fisheries under the Obama administration,
 Martha Williams, former U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service director under the Biden administration
Steven Williams,  former U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service director under the Bush Administration

Louisiana has a variety of plant and animal species protected by the Endangered Species Act living in habitats around the state. This includes creatures like the Dusky Gopher frog, Fat Pocketbook mussel and Pallid Sturgeon.

name: National
title: Federal judge dismisses lawsuit over Title X grant funding for pregnancy prevention efforts
description: A federal judge in Pennsylvania on Thursday dismissed a lawsuit challenging changes to the way grants are awarded under a program that provides funding for services such as family planning and reproductive health wellness exams. The National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Association and the Family Health Council of Central Pennsylvania filed the la[...]
text:
A federal judge dismissed a lawsuit over the new language guiding the application process for grants under Title X, a program meant to serve lower income families who may not otherwise have access to family planning services, including contraception. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline)A federal judge in Pennsylvania on Thursday dismissed a lawsuit challenging changes to the way grants are awarded under a program that provides funding for services such as family planning and reproductive health wellness exams.
The National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Association and the Family Health Council of Central Pennsylvania filed the lawsuit in June, alleging that U.S. Health and Human Services was politicizing the Title X grant funding program and violating the intent of the law with its new process for evaluating applications.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer P. Wilson, an appointee of President Donald Trump, said the family planning organizations that filed the lawsuit did not present a “sufficiently concrete harm” in their case and dismissed it.
Trump changes pregnancy-prevention program to promote childbearing

“… What plaintiffs face is uncertainty over how to best apply for a federal grant, and that is not a sufficient hardship to create a justiciable controversy,” Wilson wrote in her ruling.
Stateline previously reported that according to the complaint, the case was initially assigned to U.S. District Judge Yvette Kane, an appointee of former President Bill Clinton, but the case was reassigned the same day to Wilson.
Congress established the Title X grant program in 1970 to serve low-income or uninsured people, including those who make too much to qualify for Medicaid, who may not otherwise have access to family planning and reproductive health services. Typical services at Title X-funded clinics include contraception, pregnancy tests, testing for sexually transmitted infections and wellness exams. Abortion services cannot be covered by Title X dollars.
The complaint argued that the federal agency’s 2027 funding round, which opened in April and closes in January, requires all applicants to meet an “alignment review” to determine their eligibility for funding. Applicants are required to align their work with the priorities laid out by HHS and associated federal agencies, which includes a commitment to ending diversity, equity and inclusion efforts and gender-affirming care. 
The complaint also said the agency requirements conflicted with the law, which states that factors such as how many patients would be served by an applicant must be considered as well.
According to a news release from the American Civil Liberties Union, which assisted in representing the organizations in the case, HHS removed the provision stating it could reject applicants for failing to meet the alignment review.  
Contraception services dropped after ‘defunding’ provision hit clinics

The Trump administration’s funding notice also shifts the focus of the Title X grants from expanding access to services such as contraception to achieving healthy pregnancies and strengthening family formation. It also directs clinics to promote natural methods of family planning, such as menstrual cycle tracking, which is less effective than contraception at preventing pregnancy, according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
Clare Coleman, president and CEO of the National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Association, told Stateline in June that the process was designed to favor new applicants who had never applied for funds before. That could include religious organizations such as crisis pregnancy centers and major Catholic health systems. 
“At a time when people across the country are struggling with high costs, this administration is trying to force health care providers to adhere to its political priorities to secure federal funding,” Coleman said in a statement on Friday. “While this federal court ruling is a significant setback, NFPRHA and its members will continue to prioritize nationally recognized clinical standards, evidence-based best practices, and patient experience in delivering Title X-funded care, over demands for ideological alignment.”  
Stateline has reached out to HHS for comment about the case.
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.

description: Voting in Wisconsin’s midterm elections has officially begun. Local clerks across the state were required to send absentee ballots to voters with valid requests already on file by Thursday, Sept. 17.  Data from the Wisconsin Elections Commission shows that 299,849 absentee ballots have already been requested and 4,309 have already been returned.  The first a[...]
text:
Voting booths set up at Madison, Wisconsin's Hawthorne Library on Election Day 2022. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Voting in Wisconsin’s midterm elections has officially begun. Local clerks across the state were required to send absentee ballots to voters with valid requests already on file by Thursday, Sept. 17. 
Data from the Wisconsin Elections Commission shows that 299,849 absentee ballots have already been requested and 4,309 have already been returned. 
The first absentee ballots were sent after months of wrangling by the administration of President Donald Trump to restrict ballots sent through the mail. While the court system thwarted that effort, concerns about the timely return of absentee ballots through the mail remain. 
Absentee ballots must be returned to a voter’s local election clerk by the time polls close on Election Day, Nov. 3. To give ballots enough time, election officials have recommended they be placed in the mail at least 10 days before Election Day. WEC Administrator Meagan Wolfe recently changed  that recommended deadline to 14 days before Election Day, or Oct. 20. 
Voters can also return their absentee ballots directly to their municipal clerk’s office, take it to their polling place on Election Day or, in communities that use them, drop their ballots in an official municipal absentee ballot drop box. 
Early in-person absentee voting will open Oct. 20. Hours and locations for early voting and returning mailed absentee ballots can be found on municipal clerk websites. 
The biggest race on the ballot in Wisconsin this year is the open race for governor between Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany. Wisconsin’s eight congressional seats, 99 state Assembly seats and 16 state Senate seats are also up for election. Control of the Legislature is up for grabs for the first time in more than 15 years. 
Voters will also decide statewide races for attorney general, treasurer and secretary of state and will vote on three proposed constitutional amendments. The constitutional amendments would prohibit state and local governments from instituting diversity, equity and inclusion policies, prevent government edicts closing places of worship during emergencies and limit the governor’s line-item veto authority. 
Voters can see the candidates and referendum questions on their ballots at MyVote.WI.gov.
