name: VTDigger
title: Proposal 4 would enshrine unequal rights, not equal ones
description:
Higher taxes, more bureaucracy, endless lawsuits — Proposal 4 promises all three.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Proposal 4 would enshrine unequal rights, not equal ones.
text:
This commentary is by Renee McGuinness, the spokesperson for No on Proposal 4 PAC and the policy analyst for the Vermont Family Alliance.
Think your taxes are high now? If a majority of Vermonters vote to adopt Proposal 4 on the Nov. 3 general election ballot, get ready for them to go even higher. 
Proposal 4 is being sold as an equal rights amendment. It is the opposite.
The impact of Proposal 4 would be to provide the legal framework to sustain Vermont’s existing discriminatory laws and bureaucracy and implement more discriminatory laws, all at taxpayer expense. Adoption could increase government spending by expanding bureaucracy to uphold rights for a closed list of specified groups. It would result in endless lawsuits by plaintiffs claiming their rights have been violated — either under Proposal 4 or under the 14th Amendment, which would also burden taxpayers.
The Senate and House Judiciary committees’ own expert witness, Peter Teachout, a professor at Vermont Law and Graduate School whose field is state and federal constitutional law, pointed out several problems with the language of Proposal 4, describing the three-sentence amendment as “flawed” and the purpose section — which does not appear on the ballot — as “ambiguous” for courts.
The second sentence of Proposal 4 presents a closed list of groups that would be protected. Teachout told the House Judiciary Committee on May 1, 2024, that, legally, “if you include certain classes in a closed list, you mean to exclude others.” 
“I would just rather go to the mat with a constitutional amendment that is clear about who’s entitled to the protections and whether all people in Vermont are entitled to the same level of protection or whether some groups are entitled to greater levels than others,” Teachout told the House Judiciary Committee. He added that he would vote “no” on Proposal 4 and wait another four years for the Legislature to get the language right. 
Big Hartman, the executive director and general counsel of the Vermont Human Rights Commission, told the House Judiciary Committee on May 1, 2024, “The last (third) sentence in Article 23 really is important guidance for the Vermont Supreme Court to ensure that this clause is not misinterpreted and used to strike down DEI (diversity, equity and inclusion) initiatives that the state already has in place and that it may implement in the future.”
Jay Greene, from the Office of Racial Equity, wrote in support of Proposal 4 in a letter to the House Judiciary Committee dated April 28, 2024, stating:
“The office further appreciates the addition of language (the third sentence of Proposal 4) intended to guide the Vermont Supreme Court to interpret the Article as follows: ‘Nothing in this Article shall be interpreted or applied to prevent the adoption or implementation of measures intended to provide equality of treatment and opportunity for members of groups that have historically been subject to discrimination.’ We are concerned that without this additional guidance (third sentence of Proposal 4), the Equal Rights Amendment could be misinterpreted to claim that socially dominant groups are harmed by the pursuit of equity, diversity, justice, and inclusion.”
Who are the members of “socially dominant groups” to which Greene refers? Do they not deserve equal protection under the law? Isn’t the original intent of our U.S. and Vermont constitutions to protect individual rights, not group rights?

READ MORE

Voting “no” on Proposal 4 will not end equal rights in Vermont. Voting “yes” would actually enshrine unequal rights into the Vermont Constitution. If Proposal 4 passes, it will worsen Vermont’s existing affordability issues through discriminatory laws and expanded bureaucracy to uphold those discriminatory laws. And lawsuits will be endless since Proposal 4 creates a hierarchy of rights rather than protecting equal rights.
Any chance of salvaging Vermont’s equal protection under the law and affordability would end if Proposal 4 is adopted.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma schools employ thousands of adjunct teachers as lawmakers consider appropriate use
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — More than 2,700 adjunct teachers are covering public school courses without a related certification, state data shows. However, a majority of those instructors are certified to teach a different grade level or subject area, said Jeff Smith, the program director for teacher certification at the Oklahoma State Department of Education.  Lawmaker[...]
text:
A classroom sits empty Aug. 7 at Skyline Middle School in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — More than 2,700 adjunct teachers are covering public school courses without a related certification, state data shows.
However, a majority of those instructors are certified to teach a different grade level or subject area, said Jeff Smith, the program director for teacher certification at the Oklahoma State Department of Education. 
Lawmakers hosted Smith and other speakers at the state Capitol on Thursday to discuss adjunct hires in public schools. Adjunct teachers are required to have “distinguished qualifications” in their career field, but state law doesn’t mandate that they hold a college degree or any form of teacher certification.
“The lion’s share of adjunct teachers are certified in some capacity,” Smith said. “So, the majority of adjunct teachers aren’t people that — you get the idea that they’re just bringing them in off the street.”
Adjunct numbers have grown each year, quickly reaching the thousands, after 2022 when the state Legislature removed a limit on the number of hours  these instructors could teach per semester. The change effectively allowed them to teach full time if a district permitted it. 
Educators who hold a teaching license also are considered to be “adjuncting” when they teach outside of their certification area, Smith said. More than 70% of the 2,768 adjunct teachers in Oklahoma public schools fit this description.
Another 821 of them hold no teaching certification but are meant to have relevant work experience, he said.
Four years after expanding adjuncts’ potential work hours, state legislators have begun restricting their use in schools.
House Bill 4427, which was signed into law this year, will prohibit adjunct instructors from teaching core subjects in elementary schools, including math, English language arts, science and social studies. 
The bill takes effect in the 2027-28 school year.
Any adjuncts already teaching these subjects could continue to do so if the Oklahoma State Board of Education grants their district a waiver and the teacher completes training in the science of reading, according to the law.
Schools will be forbidden from employing an adjunct teacher for more than five years unless similarly granted a waiver. If the state Board of Education gives permission, the school could continue employing the adjunct for another five years.
The state House originally passed even stricter language in the bill, but the Senate approved a version that more closely resembles what’s written in law today.
“We thought it was a pretty good bill, kind of making this thing what we needed (it) to be,” House Common Education Committee leader Rep. Dick Lowe, R-Amber, said during the interim study. “We didn’t get that through on the other side. We ended up taking a bill we weren’t real pleased with, but that’s OK. Life goes on, but we still think there’s some work to be done.”
Interim study examines approaches to teacher hiring
Lowe and other lawmakers, along with two members of the state Board of Education, heard from Moore and Oklahoma City school district leaders during the interim study Thursday.
Schools across the state should replicate what both districts are doing, Lowe said, particularly Moore’s New Teacher Induction Academy, which provides orientation, instructional coaching, mentorship and professional development to recent hires.
Rep. Dick Lowe, R-Amber, sits in the House chamber of the state Capitol in Oklahoma City on April 16, 2025. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Moore Public Schools has never permitted use of uncertified adjunct teachers, Superintendent Robert Romines said during the study Thursday. 
Brad Herzer, chief talent officer of Oklahoma City Public Schools, said his district has stopped hiring adjuncts who hold no teaching certification.
Instead, both districts are focused on adding support for early career educators and reducing their numbers of emergency certified teachers, they said.
To receive an emergency certification, a candidate must have a bachelor’s degree but isn’t required to have any classroom training when first hired. 
Oklahoma City schools set an individual plan with each emergency certified teacher to help them reach full certification, Herzer said. By doing so, the number of district teachers holding an emergency certification has fallen by almost half.
The district no longer employs an emergency certified teacher after five years if the individual still hasn’t passed a certification exam, Herzer said.
Educators can have success even without traditional credentials, particularly if they have prior classroom experience as a substitute or a teaching aide, said Justine Morina, a senior policy director at ExcelinEd, a national organization focused on education. 
Adjunct teaching is a “strong and important pathway” to recruit new educators from different industries, she said during the interim study, but candidates should be able to demonstrate content-area knowledge through a related college degree.
Morina pointed to policies in other states like Mississippi, which allows a performance-based teaching license, and Arkansas, where teachers can work one grade above or below their certification area. Arkansas also allows teaching candidates who narrowly failed a certification exam to enter the classroom, as long as they demonstrate three successful years of teaching and pass either performance assessments or a micro-credential.
“If they’re coming into the classroom for the first time, we need to make sure they have certain guardrails, yes,” Morina said. “That’s (knowing) content; that’s ideally some prior teaching experience. If they’re already in the classroom, how do we then rethink it so we can look at who’s doing really well and make sure we retain those teachers and put them on pathways for long-term certification.”

title: Washington state House candidate pleads not guilty to DUI charge
description: A Democratic candidate for the Washington state House of Representatives pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence Friday in her first court appearance after she was arrested last month.  Krista Perez, 40, of Tacoma is charged with a DUI with an enhancement for refusing a breath test.  Her Aug. 11 arrest took place days […]
text:
Krista Perez, a candidate for a Washington state House seat, sits next to defense attorney Scott McGinty during an arraignment hearing on Friday, Sept. 18, in Tacoma Municipal Court. Perez pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)A Democratic candidate for the Washington state House of Representatives pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence Friday in her first court appearance after she was arrested last month. 
Krista Perez, 40, of Tacoma is charged with a DUI with an enhancement for refusing a breath test. 
Her Aug. 11 arrest took place days after she beat incumbent Rep. Melanie Morgan, D-Parkland, in the primary election. Perez, is vying for Morgan’s seat in the 29th Legislative District in Pierce County. Morgan will also be on the ballot in November. 
Judge Steven Krupa released Perez on her own recognizance — she did not have to post bail. 
A pre-trial hearing is scheduled for the morning of Oct. 30. 
Perez is accused of driving her pickup truck into a parked car, causing a chain reaction that left four other cars damaged in Tacoma near Lincoln High School, according to a police report. Perez confirmed she was driving but said she didn’t know what happened, the report stated. 
Perez told police she had a glass of wine and rated her level of intoxication at a four out of 10, according to the police report. 
When asked to perform field sobriety tests, Perez told a Tacoma officer that she didn’t understand and eventually declined to participate, according to court documents. 
If convicted, her sentence could be more severe because she would not take a breath test. 
Perez’s criminal defense attorneys are frustrated with recent media reports regarding the case. 
“It’s a DUI. Why do people care?” Bryan G. Hershman, defense attorney, told the Standard. “Focus on the campaign.”
Krupa asked Scott McGinty, another defense attorney present during Friday’s arraignment, to comment on media requests to record and take photos of the hearing. McGinty deferred the decision to the court.
“Somehow the media has gotten all the body cam footage already before the defense … it’s a bit frustrating,” McGinty said. 
Perez works as a strategic partnerships manager for the state’s Department of Commerce. She ran for Tacoma City Council last year but lost the election.

name: VTDigger
title: Pre-dawn calf washes and tail fluffing: Scenes from opening day at Tunbridge World’s Fair
description:
More than 2,100 students visited the fairgrounds Thursday, where young exhibitors and veteran judges showed them what goes into raising, showing and judging animals.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Pre-dawn calf washes and tail fluffing: Scenes from opening day at Tunbridge World’s Fair .
text:
Adelyn Pike, 8, of Bradford, with her oxen team at the Tunbridge World’s Fair. Photo by Jeb Wallace-Brodeur for VTDigger
At the Tunbridge World’s Fair, the future of Vermont farming depends on the kids — and their massive animals — who are keeping the traditions alive.
“Not a lot of people get to interact with animals, especially big animals like this,” said Sylvia Johnson, 17, hanging out near her grand champion heifer, Gift. “So it’s kind of cool to educate people.”
That was the purpose of Agricultural Education Day, which brought more than 2,100 students to Thursday’s opening day of the Tunbridge World’s Fair, which ends Sunday. For fair organizers, the day is a chance to show children that the event is more than rides, games and food, and to pass along agricultural knowledge that depends on another generation learning it.
With the rides dormant to prevent distraction, students moved through barns and exhibits, watched young people show animals and completed scavenger hunts about agriculture and the fair’s history.
Johnson had been at the fairgrounds since 5 a.m., washing calves before the Guernsey show. Guernseys are a specific breed of dairy cattle known for producing golden-colored milk. Other breeds, like Holstein, Ayrshire and Jersey cows, also compete at the fair. By the early evening, Johnson was doing homework in the barn and watching the exhausted animals rest. She showed off her Gift’s curly tail, which she likes to fluff out to look “super frizzy, kind of like Dolly Parton’s hair.”
“This is like the most chill time,” she said. “I’m doing my homework, just watching the calves chill out. They’re all pretty tired.”

Mason Perron, of Walpole, N.H., relaxes with her cattle during the Tunbridge World’s Fair. Photo by Jeb Wallace-Brodeur for VTDigger

Johnson, who has participated in 4-H for nearly a decade, also helps younger members care for their calves.
The educational day is part of a much older tradition. Jen Thygesen, a member of the fair’s board of directors, comes from a family with a long history at the fair. Her father once served as its president, and she now leads a 4-H group that showed cows Thursday morning.
Some members’ classmates came to watch the show and support their participating friends, Thygesen said. One group of high school boys stopped to ask her about the fair’s history.
“You’re here with your friends, and you see people that you don’t see all year long,” Thygesen said. “The sense of community here is amazing.”
Vermont’s 13 agricultural fairs collectively record more than 314,000 visits annually, according to Abbey Willard, director of the Agricultural Development Division at the Vermont Agency of Agriculture, Food and Markets. 
The state distributes between $300,000 and $400,000 each year to help fairs improve infrastructure and support the administrative work required to run them.



Willard said fairs remain important gathering places for farmers who spend much of the summer working in the fields. But their future also depends on giving children direct experiences with animals and the people who raise them.
That transfer of knowledge continued Thursday afternoon, when Jared Felch judged the Junior Poultry Show. Felch has raised birds since he was 9 and has judged competitions for 14 years. He said his primary goal is to draw young people into agriculture and show them that poultry involves far more than chickens laying eggs.
During the poultry show, Felch gently examined each of the seven birds, holding their heads still with his thumb and spreading their wings to inspect individual feathers. As he eliminated birds, he called their young handlers over, crouched beside them and explained his decisions. 
Judging can come down to the color of a single feather, he said.

Poultry judge Jared Felch, of Berlin, examines a chicken during the Tunbridge World’s Fair. Photo by Jeb Wallace-Brodeur for VTDigger

The fair’s directors are extending that lesson beyond the fairgrounds with “The Fair Through My Eyes,” a contest for people 18 and younger. Participants may submit an essay, photograph, poem or visual artwork answering the question, “What did I learn at the fair?” Submissions are due Oct. 15, and awards will be announced later this fall.
“When I see a kid that says, ‘Hey, this is Buttercup,’ or ‘This is Julie,’ or whatever they have named their bird, and they get so excited about telling about their bird, it just makes it all rewarding at the end of the day,” Felch said. “That’s what it’s all about. It’s just to see that excitement in the kids.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: State lawmakers expected to face massive budget shortfall again next year
description: The Colorado Legislature will face a third straight year of intense budget woes when it convenes in January. State economists told lawmakers on Friday that there could be a nearly $1.6 billion budget deficit. “Medicaid alone is causing the vast majority of the issue,” Mark Ferrandino, the head of the Governor’s Office of State Planning […]
text:
Colorado state Rep. Kyle Brown, a Louisville Democrat, is pictured on the floor of the Colorado House of Representatives on the final day of the 2026 legislative session on May 13, 2026, at the Colorado Capitol in Denver. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)The Colorado Legislature will face a third straight year of intense budget woes when it convenes in January. State economists told lawmakers on Friday that there could be a nearly $1.6 billion budget deficit.
“Medicaid alone is causing the vast majority of the issue,” Mark Ferrandino, the head of the Governor’s Office of State Planning and Budgeting, told the Joint Budget Committee during a routine economic forecast.
It comes one day after Ferrandino and others told a legislative commission on Medicaid that the program, which provides health insurance for low-income Coloradans, ran nearly $158 million over budget in the last fiscal year and could go $443 million over budget by the end of the current fiscal year, which runs until next July.
Medicaid spending has long been the source of state budget issues, because it is increasing much faster than the state’s spending is allowed to grow under the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights. The volume and type of Medicaid health care services, rather than enrollment numbers, are generally driving up program costs.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
If lawmakers restricted Medicaid growth to the same level as TABOR spending limit increases, around 4%, they could save around $915 million, Ferrandino said. That could mean cuts to Medicaid services. Then, if they allowed a 13% level for the state’s reserve fund instead of 15%, as they did last session, the total budget hole would be closer to $330 million.
“I would characterize that as a typical, constrained Colorado budget that is manageable — not fun, but manageable — to where we sit today with the growth in Medicaid,” he said. “As we talked yesterday, in the administration’s opinion, (the issue) needs to be tackled within Medicaid and not impacted on the remainder of the budget.”
The Legislature had to close similar billion-dollar budget gaps during its last two sessions by making an array of one-time spending and program cuts. There is very little fat left to cut.
“Medicaid cost growth, largely driven by long-term care and prescription drugs, is higher than previously forecasted,” Rep. Kyle Brown, a Louisville Democrat, said in a statement. “Every state is dealing with rising Medicaid costs, and in Colorado we are working to reduce strain on our state budget by creating a more sustainable path for the program so that it doesn’t crowd out K-12 education or other core services funding. Medicaid spending must be reined in while protecting core services for the most vulnerable Coloradans.”
TABOR surpluses
Sen. Jeff Bridges, an Arapahoe County Democrat, brought up a model that some states employ, where a legislature allocates a certain amount to Medicaid with a hard cap.
“You just have Medicaid as a department choosing what they do and don’t provide, and how they manage that,” he said. “While I don’t like that the Legislature is removed from that, it does seem like that is a potential path forward on this.”
Legislative Council Staff, the Legislature’s nonpartisan research office, estimates that state revenue will be about $827 million over the TABOR spending cap in the current fiscal year and $580 the next fiscal year. The governor’s office predicts surpluses of around $607 million and $287 million. Surpluses need to be refunded to taxpayers, and those predicted levels will likely trigger a temporary income tax rate reduction.
Both sets of economists predict that the Family Affordability Tax Credit, a state tax credit for low-income families that’s available when revenues are high enough, will not be triggered in the 2027 tax year, but Council Staff thinks it may be partially available in the 2028 tax year.
Gov. Jared Polis will present his final budget proposal as governor in November. The six-member JBC will begin its work hearing from state agencies and making budget decisions in the coming months.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Report: Makudo faced complaints before he was CSCU chancellor
description: Evidence surfaced in 2022 that John Maduko may have behaved inappropriately toward women at two CT community colleges, a new report states.
text:
Grand River Solutions issued an excoriating report Thursday of the circumstances surrounding Interim Chancellor John Maduko’s abrupt departure from the Connecticut State Colleges and Universities system earlier this year.
Maduko resigned in late April in response to a sexual harassment complaint against him. It turns out this wasn’t the first sign of trouble: According to the report, evidence surfaced in October 2022 that Maduko may have behaved inappropriately toward women at two of the state’s community colleges. A series of systemic failures meant those concerns may not have reached the full Board of Regents and certainly failed to prevent Maduko’s appointment as interim chancellor in 2025, according to the report.
CSCU retained Grand River Solutions in June to conduct an independent review into its handling of Maduko’s case. The review found CSCU systematically failed to support impacted parties, lacked clear processes for addressing sexual harassment complaints and allowed private information to leak. 
One woman left CSCU in 2025 after alleged harassment from Maduko; another had her contract nonrenewed after a high-level administrator allegedly showed Maduko a complaint she had filed against him, according to the report. (The nonrenewal has since been reversed.)
“The Grand River Solutions review identifies serious issues involving accountability, reporting responsibilities, leadership decision-making, and institutional response. The Board of Regents and CSCU System Office accept these findings and are moving forward with a series of reforms to address them,” said Sam Norton, a CSCU spokesperson, in a written statement.
State legislators responded to the report shortly after its release.
“What we see in this report exemplifies gross misconduct and a severe lack of leadership at the CSCU Board level,” Sen. Gary Winfield, D-New Haven, wrote in a press release.
“Needless to say, the next legislature should weigh the possibility of changes to the state Board of Regents.”
The Democratic members of the Committee on Higher Education and Employment Advancement issued their own press release the same day.
“This is indicative of systemic failure to protect staff, and culpability extends past the former Chancellor. If, as indicated, the Board of Regents Chair and Vice Chair were aware of prior complaints and moved forward with his appointment, that is deeply troubling,” they wrote.
However, they expressed confidence that current interim chancellor Natalie Braswell and interim Board of Regents Chair Ari Santiago “take this seriously and are committed to making changes.” 
Both Braswell and Santiago assumed their roles as a direct result of the scandal involving Maduko.
The report also fills in details about the complaint that ultimately led to Maduko’s resignation. It states that in May 2024, Maduko began sending inappropriate sexual messages to a woman identified as Impacted Party 1. The woman allegedly told CSCU General Counsel Karen Buffkin in June 2025 the board should not appoint Maduko, but that information was not passed along.
Buffkin, who has been placed on paid administrative leave, told Grand River Solutions she did not recall Impacted Party 1’s comments.
On Apr. 13, 2026, Maduko sent several text messages soliciting Impacted Party 1 to “participate in or observe him engaging in a sexual act,” according to the report. This prompted her to approach Buffkin with evidence of Maduko’s conduct, setting an investigation in motion. Despite that, no measures were immediately put in place to protect or support Impacted Party 1. The next day, she had to speak with Maduko for an hour, during which, the report states, he continued making sexual comments.
Maduko submitted his resignation on April 24. On April 29, CSCU Title XI Coordinator Alphonso Atkins announced he was dismissing the complaint because Maduko’s resignation was “the highest-level sanction available” CSCU could have enacted. 
The report took issue with the dismissal. Dismissing Title XI complaints because someone leaves the system “prevents the institution from fully addressing its obligations under Title IX to prevent future harm resulting from the same or similar circumstances, and provide appropriate remedy to the complainant,” the report’s authors wrote.
The report also identified a degree of confusion, or at least poor communication, around who had the authority to investigate Maduko. Under state law, agency heads must be investigated by Connecticut’s Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities, not the agency itself; however, the Title XI coordinator never told this to the impacted parties or offered to assist them in that process, according to the report. 
Instead, the impacted parties “were left with the belief that the CSCU system dismissed or would dismiss their allegations against the Chancellor simply because the Chancellor was no longer employed by CSCU,” according to the report.
The report includes a series of in-depth recommendations for CSCU. These include remedies for the women impacted by Maduko’s alleged conduct, as well as changes to a wide range of specific CSCU policies and procedures.
Investigations relating to the report’s findings are ongoing.
“The report provides a clear roadmap for change. Our responsibility now is to implement those changes, hold ourselves accountable, and restore confidence in the systems that are intended to protect our students and employees,” Norton said in a statement.
Maduko could not be reached for comment.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: UPMC agrees to end gender-affirming care in settlement with Justice Department
description: UPMC is one of more than 20 hospitals that received subpoenas last year for the patient records of children receiving gender-affirming care, the overarching term used to describe a range of services provided to transgender people ranging from talk therapy to surgery.
text:
UPMC is one of more than 20 hospitals that received subpoenas last year for the patient records of children receiving gender-affirming care, the overarching term used to describe a range of services provided to transgender people ranging from talk therapy to surgery. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center will end gender-affirming care for minors under a settlement with the federal government.
The U.S. Department of Justice said Friday the move resolves its investigation into potential violations of federal law arising from the hospital’s treatment provided to transgender children. 
Under the agreement, UPMC will cease providing what the Justice Department characterized as “dangerous interventions to minors,” including administering puberty blockers, hormones and performing surgical procedures. The hospital will also pay a $950,000 fine, the DOJ said. 
UPMC is one of more than 20 hospitals that received subpoenas last year for the patient records of children receiving gender-affirming care, the overarching term used to describe a range of services provided to transgender people ranging from talk therapy to surgery. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The settlement was announced at the same time as the DOJ agreement with New York University Langone Hospitals to end gender affirming care and pay an $8.5 million fine.
Families of children treated at UPMC fought the demand, arguing that subpoenaing individual patient records exceeded the DOJ’s authority to investigate off-label use of prescription drugs and threatened to violate the families’ constitutional rights. 
A federal judge in March delivered a victory for the UPMC families, denying the DOJ’s demands after finding that the records could not be effectively stripped of identifying details, given the depth of the DOJ’s request. The agency challenged the decision but abandoned its appeal in August.
The Public Interest Law Center, along with the law firm Ballard Spahr, represented the UPMC families and those challenging similar demands of Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. The organization said Friday that UPMC had failed transgender children.
Transgender health advocates see long fight to keep children’s medical records private

“Gender-affirming care is legal in Pennsylvania, and gender-related discrimination is not,” Executive Director Mimi McKenzie said. “This type of care can be life-saving for trans youth. Our country’s shameful turn against vulnerable children will be made temporary. UPMC’s stain on its reputation, however, will last forever.”
The complete terms of the settlement were not made public Friday, the law center said. The DOJ did not immediately respond to an inquiry seeking a copy of the document.
UPMC said in a statement the settlement protects patient and family privacy and preserves the confidentiality of sensitive health information. It added that the agreement resolves what UPMC described as “a matter principally involving certain alleged gender-affirming care billing practices.”
It said it also contains privacy, confidentiality, and non-prosecution protections for patients, legal guardians, providers and employees. It also, “expressly includes no admission of wrongdoing, fault, or liability by anyone involved in providing or receiving gender-affirming care to minors at UPMC Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh or other UPMC-affiliated facilities. 
“UPMC chose to resolve the matter to avoid prolonged litigation, protect patients and families from unnecessary disclosure of sensitive personal and health information, protect employees, and remain focused on patient care and advancing its core mission,” the hospital said.
The Justice Department noted the settlement follows similar agreements with Mount Sinai Health System in New York, Texas Children’s Hospital, the Cleveland Clinic Foundation, and Connecticut Children’s Hospital.
It said UPMC and NYU took significant steps that entitled them to credit for cooperating with the DOJ, including ongoing cooperation with the department’s investigation of other entities providing gender-affirming care. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Brett Shumate, assistant attorney general for the DOJ’s civil division, said investigations into other providers are ongoing and, “those that have violated the law and not resolved their potential liability will be prosecuted to the fullest extent possible.”
The cases stem from President Donald Trump’s directive to prioritize investigations and enforcement actions involving federal law violations in the provision of gender affirming care. 
The investigations focus on potential violations of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the False Claims Act, and other federal health care laws, including fraudulent billing practices such as the use of false diagnosis codes to obtain payment from federal health care programs and private insurers.
“These schemes compound the harm inflicted on vulnerable children by fraudulently shifting the cost of potentially unlawful medical interventions to taxpayers and insurers,” the department said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: NMSU students in Las Cruces took part in National Voter Registration Day ahead of midterm elections
description: The League of Women Voters of Southern New Mexico partnered with the Doña Ana County Clerk’s Office to register potential voters on Sept. 15, 2026, National Voter Registration Day, on the New Mexico State University main campus in Las Cruces.
text:
The League of Women Voters of Southern New Mexico partnered with the Doña Ana County Clerk’s Office to register potential voters on Sept. 15, 2026, National Voter Registration Day, on the New Mexico State University main campus in Las Cruces. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)Several dozen people registered to vote on New Mexico State University’s main campus on Tuesday for National Voter Registration Day, with less than two months left until the midterm general elections.
The annual nonpartisan civic holiday is recognized each September as a coordinated push to register new voters and update registrants’ information ahead of the general election. The League of Women Voters of Southern New Mexico partnered with the Doña Ana County Clerk’s Office again this year to set up several locations across the NMSU campus to help people register and provide information about voting locations, ballot boxes and candidate details.
Britnie Robertson, an New Mexico State University freshman from Rio Rancho registered to vote in her first election on Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)
“I can tell anybody, New Mexico wants you to vote,” Rebecca Courtney, a member of the league and part of LWV’s voter registration effort, told Source NM. 
The League started its voter registration campaign on Sept. 4 at the Branigan Cultural Center in downtown Las Cruces and has registration and informational events scheduled through Oct. 17 at various public buildings and the Farmers and Crafts Market of Las Cruces. 
Volunteer registration agents are partnering with the local public high schools as well to register newly eligible voters who did not already complete their registration while applying for a driver’s license.
A majority of the university students who registered on Tuesday were freshman, Courtney told Source NM, some of whom filled out their registration for their hometowns in New Mexico outside of Las Cruces. Their completed forms are sent to their respective county clerk’s offices for processing.
Britnie Robertson, an NMSU freshman from Rio Rancho, told Source she registered to vote for the first time Tuesday and is excited to participate, though she is still learning about the candidates that will be on the ballot.
The League of Women Voters traditionally releases a voter guide with candidate information and answers to hot topic questions. Courtney told Source NM that the southern New Mexico guide is expected to be released in early October. The League refers people to Vote411.org to find a consolidated list of voter guides as well as information about registering to vote online, how to check your registration status and how to request an absentee ballot. The southern New Mexico chapter is also partnering with KRWG public media to host local candidate forums that will be recorded and broadcast several times ahead of the midterms.
“We only have two jobs to do—empower voters and defend democracy. That’s what we do,” Courtney told Source NM.
Early voting begins Oct. 6 and ends Oct. 31, while the last day to apply for an absentee ballot is Oct. 20.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ‘Cash flying out the door’: Audit reveals many financial, inventory missteps in WV arts department
description: The West Virginia Department of Tourism is correcting widespread financial mismanagement, including inappropriate cash-handling activities, that occurred within the Department of Arts, Culture and History.  A new audit from the West Virginia Office of the Legislative Auditor revealed a litany of past financial issues and inventory missteps within the Departm[...]
text:
Del. Marty Gearheart, R-Mercer, questions how the Department of Arts, Culture and History failed to properly remit sales tax for 10 years during a meeting of the Post Audits Subcommittee at the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia on Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)The West Virginia Department of Tourism is correcting widespread financial mismanagement, including inappropriate cash-handling activities, that occurred within the Department of Arts, Culture and History. 
A new audit from the West Virginia Office of the Legislative Auditor revealed a litany of past financial issues and inventory missteps within the Department of Arts, Culture and History. There were thousands of state artifacts held at the West Virginia State Museum missing from required inventory lists.
The Legislature moved the Department. of Arts, Culture of History under the Department of Tourism in 2025 at the direction of Gov. Patrick Morrisey. That’s when the laundry list of issues came to light.
Under the Justice administration, the arts department had two funds over-encumbered between $1.5 to $2 million, leading to a money shortfall. The Legislature last year made a $2 million supplemental appropriation to make sure all outstanding financial obligations within the department were covered.
The Legislative Auditor’s analysis also identified 72 grants totaling $900,000 that the arts department didn’t account for. 
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“Who dropped the ball in terms of oversight?” asked Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, as a group of lawmakers reviewed the audit on Sept. 14 at the state Capitol.
Adam Fridley, manager of the Legislative Auditor’s Office, presented audit findings to lawmakers.
“When you’re talking about a department of state government that has funds over-encumbered, I can’t tell you that in 13 years that I had seen that prior to this,” he said. “In a lot of ways, the buck stops with the administration of Arts, Culture and History at the time.”
Adam Fridley, manager of the West Virginia Legislative Auditor’s Office, speaks to the Post Audits Subcommittee at the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia on Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Former Secretary Randall Reid-Smith previously led the standalone Department of Arts, Culture and History until early 2025.
The audit also revealed that the arts department went 10 or 11 years without collecting sales tax on items, including on items sold at the gift shop.
“All of this sort of boggles my mind a little bit,” said Del. Marty Gearheart, R-Mercer. 
Gearheart, who serves on the House Finance Committee, estimated that half a million dollars was missed in collections due to failure to collect sales tax. He characterized the art department’s situation as “cash flying out the door.”
“If I’m a week late with my sales tax return, I get a notice,” Gearheart said. “It is beyond me to understand how 10 years of sales tax could be neglected. There’d have to be a room with notices that could fill a closet.”
The Legislative Auditor’s office couldn’t give a total summary of missing funds, saying that the lack of financial and cash-handling policies led to the situation. 
In October, a settlement was reached, covering a period from Jan 1, 2020, through Dec. 31, 2024, the department paid a total of $122,025 to cover the sales taxes not previously remitted, according to the audit. 
Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha, also questioned how the sales tax situation had gotten that far.
West Virginia Department of Tourism Secretary Kayla Kessinger. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“I think all of us in this room agree that it was egregious and it’s not going to happen again,” said Kayla Kessinger, newly-appointed secretary of the state’s Department of Tourism.
The Department of Arts, Culture, and History operated several collection points for cash receipts, including the Culture Center, the Coal Heritage Museum and more. 
“Cash was not properly stored at each collection point. While some collection points reported that cash was stored in appropriate safes or secure lock boxes, other collection points reported that cash was left in cash registers or unsecured folders on employees’ desks,” the audit said. 
“Some cash collection was held and used as petty cash  in violation of prohibitions under existing state law,” Fridley said. The Department of Tourism is working to reduce the number of cash collection points to prevent future issues, he added. 
Since 2020, the department hadn’t properly maintained asset inventories, leading to the discovery of more than 10,000 items outside of the official inventory record. 
The Legislative Auditor noted that the West Virginia State Museum did not have a singular inventory record that accurately tracked all of the museum’s assets. Museum staff have now reported over 34,000 artifacts.
The tourism department has taken several steps to rectify the financial and record-keeping situation, according to Fridley. There are new financial and cash-handling policies in place along with more staff focused on finances. The department continues to work on its artifact inventory system, saying it will take time for the staff to properly catalogue the inventory at the state museum. 
Kessinger said it was important to make sure state tax dollars are used efficiently. The financial issues under the arts department predate her appointment in August. 
“Thank you to the legislative auditors for working with the Department of Tourism so we could solve the problems that were created in years past and that we can continue to work toward continued development of strong policies that protect the state and our reputation with our citizens,” Kessinger told lawmakers.  
Young expressed concern about the possibility of similar financial problems in other agencies given how long it took for the arts department’s problems to come to light. 
“It seems like there’s no internal controls for these systems,” Young said.
In response, Fridley told lawmakers, “Are these issues present in other places in state government writ large? Unfortunately, I have no way of telling you that.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Shakespeare could have written this LSU-Ole Miss football plot
description: People walk through the Grove on the University of Mississippi campus as a crew sets up for ESPN "College GameDay" on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026.
text:
OXFORD — So I’ve heard this question several times this week: “Is this LSU-Ole Miss game the biggest college football game you have ever covered?”
Rick Cleveland
Well, no. It’s not even the biggest in the last 10 months. The Ole Miss-Georgia Sugar Bowl playoff game was bigger. The Miami-Ole Miss Fiesta Bowl was still bigger. Now then, this might be the most anticipated regular season game I’ve ever covered. No question, it would be in the first sentence of any conversation of that nature. 
This much is certain: This will be the strangest college football game I have ever covered. And by strange, I refer to all the bizarre surrounding circumstances – all the, for lack of a better term, football incest.
No. 7 LSU vs. No. 8 Ole Miss, two teams with star power and national championship hopes, make this the national game of the week. But you factor in Lane Kiffin returning to the scene of what Ole Miss fans consider his unforgivable betrayal, former Ole Miss stars now playing for LSU and so many other extenuating circumstances and you have a football tempest. Indeed, Shakespeare would have a ball with this scenario. Had football been a sport in the late 16th and early 17th centuries, Shakespeare might have written this play. This game has many of the elements of a Shakespeare masterpiece: betrayal, revenge, corruption, incest – you name it.
LSU head coach Lane Kiffin reacts during the second half of an NCAA college football game against Louisiana Tech in Baton Rouge, La., Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Matthew Hinton
Let’s put it this way: When I got into this business about a hundred or so years ago, I never imagined covering anything quite like this. How is this bizarre? Let us count the ways:
Mississippi head coach Pete Golding directs his players before the Fiesta Bowl NCAA college football playoff semifinal game against Miami, Thursday, Jan. 8, 2026, in Glendale, Ariz. (AP Photo/Ross D. Franklin) Credit: AP Photo/Ross D. Franklin

Just this Tuesday in Baton Rouge, LSU defensive end Princewill Umanmielen was served court papers pertaining to the $550,000 lawsuit Ole Miss filed against him for allegedly breaking the terms of his contract at Ole Miss. Umanmielen led Ole Miss in sacks with nine last season. He already has five for LSU.
Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry, who also seems LSU’s de facto athletic director, then posted about the Ole Miss athletic director on social media: “Keith Carter could have saved Ole Miss some money and waited until Saturday. He’ll be easy to find in the Ole Miss backfield often!”
Umanmielen is one of four former Rebels who helped Ole Miss to 13 victories last season. Others are linebackers T.J. Dottery, guard Devin Harper and wide receiver Winston Watkins. All are key players. LSU fans might term them opportunists. Ole Miss fans believe them traitors.
Of course, what Ole Miss fans resent most is that Kiffin tried his best to take Heisman candidates Trinidad Chambliss and Kewan Lacy and several other Rebels to Baton Rouge with him, as well. They still play for the Rebels.
Much has been made of the former Rebels – players and assistant coaches – now at LSU. But two former Tigers now play for Ole Miss: running back JT Lindsey and offensive lineman Carius Curne. Yes, the former Ole Miss coaches now at LSU know all about Ole Miss’s personnel, but one of Pete Golding’s key off-season hires was Frank Wilson, LSU’s star recruiter and the interim head coach after Brian Kelly’s dismissal last year. 
Head coaches Kiffin and Golding both coached under Nick Saban at Alabama, and then Kiffin hired Golding away from Saban at Ole Miss. They know each other’s tendencies inside and out. Here’s the crazy part: Golding now lives in Kiffin’s old house. You couldn’t make it up. And you can bet on this: For all the nice things Golding has said about Kiffin this week and in the past, he still burns inside because of the manner in which Kiffin tried to sabotage the Ole Miss program after he left.
Want more? Landry Kiffin, Lane’s daughter, remains a student at Ole Miss and has complained on social media this week about vulgar signs around Oxford and posts on social media about her and a former Ole Miss football player and a sexual relationship that didn’t happen. ”I opened my phone this morning to pictures of banners on houses around Oxford posted on different accounts saying really inappropriate things about me,” Landry Kiffin  said. “… I think that turning a girl into the punchline of a sexual joke because you’re upset at somebody she’s related to should not be okay.” Landry Kiffin dates Whit Weeks, an LSU linebacker.
With all the intrigue, a record crowd is descending upon Oxford, with or without game tickets. Oxford’s population is about 26,600. Estimates are 200,000 – and perhaps even 300,000 – will clog the roadways, the Oxford Square and the Ole Miss campus. By midafternoon Friday, traffic was insane and getting worse by the minute. Security has been beefed up with extra officers from the state Department of Public safety and police from Mobile and New Orleans for the Mardi Gras-like weekend. From above, Oxford must look like a stepped-on ant bed.
Back to Shakespeare: The bard’s plays, while heavy on incest, betrayal and corruption, also featured much hilarity. Ole Miss coaches found some humor this week when Kiffin listed $5 million transfer quarterback Sam Leavitt as “doubtful” because of an unspecified injury. “That’s Lane being Lane,” was the general reaction, along with laughter, in the Ole Miss camp. “We can’t complain much. He did that s— all the time when he was here,” an Ole Miss athletic official told me.

Kiffin was an Ole Miss hero in this town then. He is public enemy No. 1 now. In the minds of Ole Miss fans, Shakespeare’s Brutus had nothing on Lane Kiffin. Et tu, Lane?
A crew sets up for ESPN’s “College GameDay” in the Grove on the University of Mississippi campus on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Vance rallies Iowa Republicans, says Trump’s trade policies benefit farmers
description: COUNCIL BLUFFS — Vice President JD Vance told Iowans Friday that President Donald Trump’s trade and tax policies have helped farmers and working-class families, as he worked to rally support for gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn and other Iowa Republicans in the midterms. Trump’s tariff policies have been a point of concern for Iowa farmers over […]
text:
Vice President JD Vance spoke at a rally supporting Iowa Republicans including gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn at the Mid-American Center in Council Bluffs Sep. 18, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)COUNCIL BLUFFS — Vice President JD Vance told Iowans Friday that President Donald Trump’s trade and tax policies have helped farmers and working-class families, as he worked to rally support for gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn and other Iowa Republicans in the midterms.
Trump’s tariff policies have been a point of concern for Iowa farmers over the past year. Vance said the administration’s actions were necessary to reverse “bad trade policy, let’s be honest, from both Democrats and Republicans,” which he said “made it impossible for Iowa farmers to get their food to market.”
He spoke at a midday rally hosted by the Republican National Committee at the Mid-American Center in Council Bluffs.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We now have, thanks to Donald Trump’s hard work and fighting on behalf of Iowa farmers, 2 billion new consumers all over the world who are now open to American food instead of closed to American food,” Vance said. “Corn exports are up by 35%. Markets that were closed to our beef and dairy for decades are taking Iowa beef and dairy today, and China has committed to buying $17 billion (in agricultural products) from our farmers just this year.”
According to U.S. Department of Agriculture data, annual corn exports grew from $13.71 billion to $18.55 billion from 2024 to 2025, roughly returning export values to the levels seen in 2021 and 2022. Some farmers have expressed concern about Trump’s decision in August to suspend tariffs on imported ground beef to lower the cost of meat, which cattle producers said would have a negative impact on U.S. herds.
He also said the president had focused on prioritizing building domestic markets for American agricultural producers.
“What does it mean for the safety of our kids, of our grandkids, when we let foreign countries, many of which do not have our best interests at heart, when we let those foreign countries buy our food?” Vance said. “So what Donald J. Trump did when he came into office is he said, we are done with that. We are growing American food on American farms for American families. And I always tell you, ladies and gentlemen, whenever you hear me talk during this midterm campaign, I’ll say Rome was not built in a day. Because we know there’s a lot of work to do, but just two years in — not even two years in — President Trump has cut that deficit by 42%, and it’s fallen even faster this year.”
A critical component of supporting the Trump administration and Republicans’ goals on agriculture, Vance said, was electing Republicans in Iowa, including Lahn. Vance called Lahn, a businessman who owns a family farm in Belle Plaine, a “person who wakes up every single day and thinks about how we can defend the jobs, the prosperity, and the public safety of Iowans from every single walk of life.”
“Zach is going to be a fighter, ladies and gentlemen,” Vance said. “That’s what we need. We need somebody who’s willing to stand up, stand up and protect your families. Stand up and protect your farmers and your farmland. Stand up for every single Iowan who’s been told to sit down and take it, who’s been told that they’re backwards if they believe that Iowa farmland ought to belong to Iowans. Who’ve been told they’re racist for believing that Iowa schools ought to go to American citizens, and not to the foreign-born.”
Zach Lahn, the 2026 Republican candidate for Iowa governor, spoke with attendees at a rally with Vice President JD Vance at the Mid-American Center in Council Bluffs Sept. 18, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The vice president said Lahn “is going to be a great ally to those in Washington who are fighting for you as opposed to against you.”
Lahn spoke before Vance at the rally, where he told the crowd his campaign for governor was focused on preserving Iowa for the next generation. He said this means “defending the institutions that hold our culture together — the local communities, the church, the family, and ultimately, let me say this, ultimately, it’s the individual. This is what the West was ultimately built upon.”
“I want the next generation to grow up in the Iowa that we grew up with, the Iowa that we love,” Lahn said. “I want them to build a life here, build their families here, prosper here, and someday give something back to their children that was even better than what we gave them.”
Lahn said Vance got into politics and his current position “because he wanted to defend culture.”
“And I cannot wait to work with him, to work with Vice President JD Vance to defend the culture of Iowa and America,” Lahn said.
Vance’s Iowa event comes as the state’s elections are positioned to play a critical role in determining control of Congress. Iowa currently has an all-Republican federal delegation, but political forecasters say three of the four U.S. House seats will be highly competitive in the Nov. 3, 2026 midterms, in addition to the races for U.S. Senate and governor.
Republican incumbents in Iowa’s 1st and 3rd Districts were already projected to face tight races, but on Wednesday, Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the 2nd Congressional District race to a “toss-up,” writing, “Iowa seems like enough of a potential problem for Republicans that IA-2 merits being a Toss-up, too.”
Council Bluffs is located in the state’s one congressional district not expected to be competitive in 2026. The seat in Iowa’s 4th District, a longtime conservative stronghold, is open in 2026 as current U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra ran for Iowa governor — losing in the primary to Lahn. Political forecasters favor Republican nominee Chris McGowan to win against Democrat Dave Dawson in the general election. McGowan, who spoke to the crowd of roughly 400, told voters to “ignore the polls, let’s get out and vote.”
Republican voters in the region could play a large role in statewide elections, like the gubernatorial and U.S. Senate races. “What we’re gonna do, and especially in Iowa 4, we’re gonna turn out to make sure the rest of the state carries Zach Lahn to victory,” McGowan said.
Lahn faces Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand in the election.
Vance made critical comments about Sand in his speech, saying he was falsely presenting himself as a moderate candidate — a line of attack used by other Republicans on the campaign trail.
The vice president said Sand was “a man who is cut from the exact same cloth as Adam Hamilton and James Talarico,” referencing Democratic candidates running in Kansas and Texas. Vance said while Sand’s campaign advertisements highlight him “groaning about partisanship,” the Democratic candidate has “spent his entire life working for and donating to far-left Democrat causes.”
“Rob Sand has spent this whole campaign running away from the things he spent the rest of his career fighting for, and now he’s banking on voters being too dumb to see what’s happening,” Vance said.
On the campaign trail, Sand has said his time in the auditor’s office shows that he is willing to go against the Democratic Party, citing his decisions to have independent and Republican senior officials at the state auditor’s office, as well as his decision to reject a request from the Democratic National Committee on public records regarding the alleged “wrongdoing by (Gov.) Kim Reynolds.”
Vance also claimed Sand “is a billionaire who has repeatedly fought against tax cuts for middle-class Iowans.” Lahn released a campaign ad in August also calling Sand a billionaire. Sand’s only income is listed as his $103,000 salary as state auditor in campaign ethics disclosures. But the Lahn campaign told KCRG the comment references Sand’s wife, Christine Lauridsen, who owns the Lauridsen Group, a family-owned business with hundreds of millions in annual revenues — though the private company’s or the Lauridsen family’s net worth is not publicly available information.
Maddie Moher, press secretary for Sand’s campaign, said “after seven years as State Auditor and nearly 900 public town halls across Iowa, Iowans know Rob Sand as an independent watchdog who holds both parties accountable, protects taxpayer dollars, and fights to lower costs.”
“Zach Lahn has spent his entire campaign lying about Rob, and now he’s bringing in another D.C. insider to try to bail him out because he can’t answer for his frequent flights to Kansas or his decade-long career as a political operative,” Moher said. “The attacks Lahn has pushed have been repeatedly found false by independent fact-checkers and news outlets, and outsourcing his talking points to another Washington politician doesn’t make them true. Iowa voters know the leader who will actually show up and work for them is Rob Sand.”
Iowa Democrats said Vance’s event was a “desperate attempt to bail out Kansas carpetbagger and career political operative Zach Lahn.”
“Another insider D.C. politician is rushing in to prop up Zach Lahn because he has no answer for how he can be a full-time governor when he lives in Kansas,” IDP Chair Rita Hart said in a statement. “The truth is Lahn is a career political operative who wants to continue the worst of Kim Reynolds’ failed agenda for another four years, and his party bosses know he would be a reliable rubber stamp for the reckless tariffs and ongoing war in Iran that have sent the price of gas, utilities, and groceries skyrocketing. After years of underfunded public schools, farm bankruptcies, and record cancer growth rates, Iowans are ready for change, but Lahn is only offering more of the same.”
Vance last visited Iowa in May, when he spoke in support of U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, the Republican running for reelection in Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District.
Though his visits to Iowa have been focused on the midterms, trips to Iowa often signal interest in a future presidential bid. Vance has not announced a presidential run, but is considered likely to run as a GOP presidential candidate in 2028. A recent poll from YouGov/Bowling Green State University shows the vice president holding an early lead in the field compared to other potential candidates such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz.

name: VTDigger
title: Where there’s a will, there’s a way: Pop-up clinic to offer free estate planning services
description:
Legal professionals are volunteering to provide estate planning education and services Saturday to underserved Vermont communities.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Where there’s a will, there’s a way: Pop-up clinic to offer free estate planning services.
text:
A free pop-up clinic for estate planning will be held at Community National Bank in Barre on Saturday. Photo by Emma White/VTDigger
As Vermonters age, the lawyers who can help put their final wishes in writing are getting older — and scarcer — too.
With Vermont’s large aging population and shortage of lawyers, it can be tough to find legal counsel to help a person specify who inherits the assets and objects they leave behind. The issue is compounded by the rate of aging legal professionals in Vermont.
“On one hand, you have a shrinking legal community, in terms of number of lawyers, and certainly the number of lawyers serving remote areas, and then also you have an aging population,” said Don Hayes, the director of the South Royalton Legal Clinic and a professor at Vermont Law and Graduate School.
“So it’s almost a perfect storm. Things are kind of tugging in opposite directions.”
With that in mind, the Vermont Judiciary Commission on the Delivery of Legal Services is offering a free pop-up clinic for estate planning this Saturday. It’s open to anyone, but one goal is to empower low-income and underserved populations to gain control of their estates. Vermonters can register via email to attend the event.
The clinic, from 9:30 to 11:30 a.m. at the Community National Bank in Barre, is an opportunity for Vermonters to receive free legal counseling from volunteer attorneys and Vermont Law and Graduate School students. Everyone who attends will have the opportunity to speak to an attorney, and participants whose needs the clinic can accommodate will be able to walk away with a fully drafted and executed will, Hayes said.
The benefits of having one’s estate in order are numerous, Hayes said, particularly when designating a power of attorney — someone who can act in place of a person who becomes incapacitated — or establishing enhanced life estate deeds. These deeds can be an essential step toward building intergenerational wealth, Hayes added, by ensuring that real estate can pass directly to someone’s descendants without going through probate.
But especially in lower-income households, he said, estate planning can feel like less of a necessity.
“And even if that’s not true, if the perception is that it’s a really expensive endeavor, and I don’t even have money to pay for heat this winter, it’s going to be so deprioritized,” Hayes said. 
There’s also an education barrier to seeking estate planning services, Hayes said.
“Some people think that, you know, ‘I’m a lower-income household, I don’t have anything, what could I possibly use an estate plan for?’ But there’s so many things that, if you don’t have them in place, can really be punishing,” Hayes said. For example, a person might become incapacitated without having designated a power of attorney, Hayes said, leaving their loved ones unable to take over their estate.
Hayes said estate planning, such as the type this clinic offers, can help break down barriers and make legal services feel a bit more accessible.
“It’s a cool thing to be able to give legal services to people that feel that they can’t afford it or they don’t deserve it,” Hayes said.
The clinic is part of the mission of the Vermont Commission on the Delivery of Legal Services, which formed in 2025 to address the barriers Vermonters face when accessing legal services. According to Vermont Supreme Court Associate Justice Harold Eaton Jr., the average age of Vermont lawyers is one of the major factors playing into the overall shortage of legal services.
“We have an issue with the graying of the bar,” Eaton said. “By that I mean lawyers getting older, not being replaced by younger lawyers coming in. And in addition, we have a distribution problem in the sense that many lawyers are located in the more populated areas of the state, and that leaves some places without any legal services available or very little.”
This clinic was identified as a simple way of reaching underserved populations and alleviating some of the demand for legal services in a short time, according to State Court Administrator Therese Corsones.
“They were trying to look at something that could be focused and direct that could be accomplished in one day,” Corsones said.
A review of the clinic will be part of a larger report submitted in October evaluating the key findings of the commission during its past year of operation, Corsones said.
“One of the things we hope to gain from this clinic is to see what the need is,” Corsones said. “And if so, the plan would be to replicate the clinics around the state.” 
Hayes emphasized that even if writing a will does not have a huge impact on someone’s estate, it can still be a powerful thing to do.
“I’ve done wills for people in hospice where they know that they’re going to die, probably in the very near future,” Hayes said, “and their will is not changing anything that would happen at law otherwise. But it’s just the fact that they’re making that expression, they’re putting it down on paper. 
“There’s something very dignifying about being able to do that.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: As SC diesel prices rise, so do economic impact fears
description: The rising cost of diesel fuel is threatening the livelihood of South Carolina’s truckers and forcing operational changes at the Port of Charleston.
text:
A sign at a North Charleston gas station shows the price of diesel fuel at nearly $6.20 per gallon on Friday. (Photo by David Wren/SC Daily Gazette)The rising cost of diesel fuel is threatening the livelihood of South Carolina’s truckers, driving fears of inflation spikes and forcing operational changes at the Port of Charleston as the state’s economy confronts record pump prices that are expected to continue climbing.
“It’s painful everywhere,” said Rick Todd, president and CEO of the South Carolina Trucking Association. “Diesel fuel has been characterized as the workhorse fuel for the world. I mean, literally everything is driven by diesel.”
That includes the trucks that bring groceries and consumer goods to stores, industrial equipment used in factories and on farms, container ships that call on Charleston’s port and even the cranes that move containers through the terminal yards.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The statewide average for a gallon of diesel hit an all-time high of $6.17 this week, according to AAA, driven largely by the war in Iran and Middle East supply concerns. That’s a nearly 75% increase since the beginning of this year.
Prices aren’t expected to peak any time soon. Oil flow chokepoints in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait between Yemen and the Arabian peninsula — along with reduced refining capacity in the U.S. — have created the potential for diesel shortages, although incidents so far have been isolated.
Joey Von Nessen, a research economist at the University of South Carolina, said higher transportation costs will translate to more expensive groceries and other goods, potentially forcing consumers to pull back on spending that’s been resilient so far, even in the face of rising inflation.
“The bottom line is this represents another economic headwind as we head into the fall months,” he said. “It will definitely have an impact on demand if diesel prices stay elevated at their current levels.”
SC governor celebrates new law aimed at reducing insurance costs for restaurants, businesses

Todd said independent truckers and small trucking firms will feel the most pain, while large freight-hauling companies can blunt higher diesel prices by buying in bulk. Nearly two-thirds of South Carolina’s 24,000 registered motor carriers operate a single truck.
“For the average owner-operator or small fleet that doesn’t have buying power, they’re pretty much paying retail,” Todd said.
He predicts some truckers might simply park their rigs and look for other work until prices improve. Some might get out of the business altogether, as rising fuel costs and spiking liability insurance rates combine to make the occupation unprofitable.
“It’s not sustainable,” Todd said of current diesel costs. “This is uncharted territory in a lot of ways.”
Elevated fuel costs are also impacting the Port of Charleston, which relies on diesel to power most of its equipment and where trucks carry more than three-fourths of the cargo moving through container terminals.
There is a balancing act between reducing the use of diesel-guzzling machinery while, at the same time, not forcing truckers to burn more time and fuel than normal picking up or dropping off cargo, said Micah Mallace, president and CEO of the S.C. State Ports Authority.
The port reduced the number of cranes used to move containers earlier this year to cut costs. But as the year wore on and cargo volumes ticked up, so did the amount of time truckers spent idling within the terminals.
Less cargo has SC Ports Authority cutting its way toward growth

In response, the authority is scheduling more workers and crane operators during busier hours, while pulling back during less intensive times. The maritime agency also buys fuel at bulk contract prices, and as often as possible, operates its handful of hybrid cranes that require less fuel by running on a combination of electricity and diesel power.
“Weve seen inflation in our underlying costs because of diesel, but we’ve been able to mute that impact internally,” Mallace said. “But it’s a more dramatic impact for motor carriers and shipping lines, where their No. 1 or No. 2 operating cost is fuel. We’ve seen our partners really hurt by this and we are trying to think through ways to help offset their cost impact.”
The average cost to move a container from the port to a warehouse is between $395 and $595, according to BlackBridge Logistics. While that is among the lowest cost of any major U.S. port, fuel surcharges are increasing bills as much as 55%– costs that are generally passed on to consumers.
“Higher prices are the biggest short-term threat to the economic outlook,” Von Nessen, the research economist, said. “Another factor that we’ve seen emerge in the last several months is that prices are rising faster than wages, due primarily to this uptick in energy costs.”
SC Ports temporarily halts Leatherman operations in face of high costs, waning demand

When consumers lose purchasing power, it can cause an overall pullback in economic activity, he said.
It won’t take long to see if that threat comes to pass.
Historically, consumers start to reduce their discretionary spending, such as entertainment and dining out, within just a few weeks of fuel-related inflation. Fixed expenses, like housing and groceries, can start to show up as higher credit card balances or decreased savings.
“The longer we see prices rising faster than wages, the more likely we are going to see consumer spending cool,” Von Nessen said.

title: North Carolina Muslim groups push voter registration ahead of November election
description: At the Islamic Association of Raleigh’s mosque on Page Road in Durham, Nigel Edwards set up a table with voter registration information and a QR code directing people to election resources. It was part of a push Friday by Muslim organizations across North Carolina to encourage members of their community to register and vote in […]
text:
National Muslim Voter Registration Day table. (Photo: Sinthia Shabnam/MPower Change)At the Islamic Association of Raleigh’s mosque on Page Road in Durham, Nigel Edwards set up a table with voter registration information and a QR code directing people to election resources.
It was part of a push Friday by Muslim organizations across North Carolina to encourage members of their community to register and vote in the November election.
Nigel Edwards speaks with attendees at a voter registration table after Friday prayers, Sept. 18, 2026.(Photo:Ahmed Jallow/NC Newsline)
The response was mixed, said Edwards, president of the state’s Muslim American Public Affairs Council.
Some people were already registered. Others were not interested in voting. But Edwards said even registering one person who had never done so before would make the effort worthwhile.
“I had at least one brother who actually is going to register who’s never registered before,” Edwards said. “Even just one person is a success, in my opinion.”
Edwards said some people also did not know an election was coming.
“A lot of it is just simple awareness,” he said. 
National Muslim Voter Registration Day is a nonpartisan effort led by MPower Change. More than 80 Muslim organizations were participating in more than 15 states, including North Carolina, according to the organization. Events were planned in states including New York, New Jersey, Florida, Michigan, Georgia, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.
In North Carolina, about 12 to 15 locations were participating, said Sinthia Shabnam, who leads the group’s effort in the state.
Friday prayers are an important opportunity for organizers to reach older members of the community and others who may be less engaged in politics, Shabnam said. 
“It’s those aunties. It’s those uncles. It’s the elderly in the community. It’s the folks that don’t even know they could vote,” she said. “It’s actually the best time to reach that target audience.”
NC Board of Elections will no longer provide forms to voter registration drives

Abdul Allam, who attended Friday prayers at the Durham mosque, said voter registration efforts need to happen repeatedly to keep people engaged.
Some Muslims, he said, pay close attention to presidential elections but are less attentive to primaries and local elections.
“It has to be done multiple times, not once, because that keeps reminding people,” Allam said.
Allam said people also need help understanding how to register and participate.
“It’s not just voting for the president,” he said. “At every level it has an impact.”
The Charlotte Muslim Caucus also held registration and voter pledge events at about five locations in the Charlotte area. The group hoped to register about 50 people and get at least 500 people to pledge to vote, said Nasif Majeed, a co-founder of the caucus and the son of Charlotte state Rep. Nasif Majeed.

title: Podcast: Supporters of creating a state trust fund for unclaimed property explain Amendment K
description: South Dakota has collected over $1 billion in unclaimed property over the years, from sources including abandoned cash, stocks, bank accounts and even gold teeth. Much of that money has gone into the state budget, because not all of the rightful owners come forward to claim their property. Yet they could come forward at […]
text:
South Dakota State Treasurer Josh Haeder (left) and state Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, both support Amendment K, a ballot question that would create a state trust fund for unclaimed property. (Photos by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight; illustration by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight) 


Searchlight Report is a podcast from South Dakota Searchlight. Reporter and host Meghan O’Brien works with other Searchlight journalists to take listeners inside politics and policy in The Mount Rushmore State.			




 
South Dakota has collected over $1 billion in unclaimed property over the years, from sources including abandoned cash, stocks, bank accounts and even gold teeth. Much of that money has gone into the state budget, because not all of the rightful owners come forward to claim their property. Yet they could come forward at any time. That’s why lawmakers decided to start putting those assets into a cash-flow fund, and use only the interest to help fund the state’s budget.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
To put the money in a trust fund earning higher returns, lawmakers need the approval of South Dakota voters.
The ballot question is part of a legislative package that passed last year. One of the bills, which was signed into law, gradually transitions all unclaimed property money into a cash-flow fund that generates a small amount of interest for the state budget. Amendment K, which is on the Nov. 3 ballot, would put the money in a higher-earning trust fund managed by the state Investment Council, like other funds such as the retirement pool for public employees.
State Treasurer Josh Haeder and state Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, joined Searchlight Report to explain their support for the amendment. No organized opposition to the ballot measure has surfaced yet.
