name: Maine Morning Star
title: Is it time to rethink the Northeast’s cap-and-trade system?
description: Twenty years ago, a group of Northeastern states signed on to a plan to reduce the greenhouse gases spewing from power plants by making generators pay for the carbon they release. Since then, the region’s power sector emissions have dropped by half, and states have reaped more than $10 billion in revenue to invest in […]
text:
Granite Shore Power's Merrimack Generating Station in Bow, N.H., will be the last coal plant to close in New England when it shuts down in 2028. (Photo by Robert Zullo/ States Newsroom)
 
This story was originally published by Canary Media. 

	Twenty years ago, a group of Northeastern states signed on to a plan to reduce the greenhouse gases spewing from power plants by making generators pay for the carbon they release. Since then, the region’s power sector emissions have dropped by half, and states have reaped more than $10 billion in revenue to invest in energy programs.


By these numbers, the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, or RGGI, looks like a success. And plenty of clean energy advocates say the program has produced both direct and indirect benefits for the climate and residents’ utility bills.


Two decades in, however, the price power plants pay for each ton of carbon emissions is more than 12 times what it was at the beginning, clean energy development in the region faces daunting challenges, and emissions have started creeping back up. A growing chorus of voices is now questioning whether RGGI is still worth the investment at a time when soaring power prices are straining household budgets.


“I think it’s appropriate to look at RGGI and see to what degree it is amplifying its intended purpose, or if it needs to be pulled back,” said Dan Dolan, president of the New England Power Generators Association, a trade group representing most of the region’s generating capacity.


Globally, carbon cap-and-trade is a common strategy for lowering greenhouse gas emissions. The European Union, China, and South Korea all operate such systems. It’s been slower to catch on in the United States, however. RGGI is the first and only multistate carbon cap-and-trade program in the country; just California, Oregon, and Washington have state-level systems.


RGGI was designed to reduce climate pollution in two ways. First, there’s the cap-and-trade system. Large power generators in participating states are required to buy an allowance for every ton of carbon dioxide they produce, which creates a financial incentive to lower emissions. The cap on total emissions allowed in the region drops every year, generally pushing the price up over time. The price is set through quarterly auctions, though generators can buy and sell allowances on the secondary market, so the actual cost is often higher than that set by the auction. The expense is passed on to consumers.


Each state can then use the revenue collected through these payments to support its own programs for clean energy, energy efficiency, climate adaptation, and bill assistance, potentially leading to even greater reductions in power consumption and associated emissions.


RGGI ran its first auction in 2008 with 10 states: Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, and Vermont. The process yielded a price of $3.07 per ton of carbon dioxide.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.


Today, 11 states participate in the program. New Jersey dropped out in 2012 but rejoined in 2020, and Virginia participated in the auctions from 2021 to 2023, then restarted this year. The most recent auction, held last week, yielded a price of $37.65 per allowance.


During the first decade of RGGI auctions, carbon emissions in the nine consistently participating states fell sharply, from a peak of 117.5 million short tons in 2010 to a low of 61.9 million short tons in 2020. Much of this drop can be attributed to the retirement of coal-fired power plants across the region, particularly in New England and New York. In 2007, coal accounted for 15% of the electricity generation in those seven states; today, no coal plants operate in any of them.


RGGI’s carbon price likely helped drive that decrease, experts say. However, there were other contributing factors, including state climate regulations and the economics of trading coal generation for plants that use lower-priced, cleaner-burning natural gas.


“I don’t think you can realistically attribute it all to one mechanism,” said Paolo Moncada Tamayo, senior policy and data analyst for climate nonprofit Acadia Center and a strong supporter of RGGI.

Then, after 2020, emissions stopped falling and even started trending back up slightly, once the low-hanging fruit of the coal-to-gas transition was largely gone. Since that time, it’s been a lot harder for RGGI to have an impact, say supporters and critics alike.


“The earlier RGGI era was easier and cheaper,” Tamayo said. ​“We’re at a point where it’s not as easy and not as affordable to decarbonize.”
 



There is widespread agreement that the pace of renewable energy construction must pick up to kick-start further reductions as energy demand balloons. However, federal attacks have nearly stopped development of the offshore wind that much of the Northeast was banking on to help clean up the grid.


At the same time, congested transmission infrastructure and a patchwork of inconsistent local and county policies can make it hard for development to gain traction. Existing state-level renewable energy policies are generally not strong enough to get things going, said Noah Kaufman, a senior research scholar on clean energy at Columbia University. A much higher carbon price could have an effect, he said, but RGGI includes a mechanism to release more allowances as a way to lower costs if the price creeps up too high, and the participating states do not seem interested in changing that, he said.


“If they’re serious about those goals, they would need some pretty big policy shifts going forward,” he said. ​“If it were me and I didn’t have constraints or stakeholders, I probably would get rid of RGGI and think along the lines of some combination of clean electricity and clean heating standards.”


At the same time, some argue that RGGI is actively worsening emissions by encouraging utilities to buy dirtier power from adjacent states where generators don’t have to pay a carbon price. Critics say power plants in Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, and Virginia, in particular, are at a competitive disadvantage; those states are part of the grid run by PJMInterconnection, and generators in the grid region’s nine non-RGGI states don’t have to add the cost of RGGI onto their price tag.


“They can’t compete economically with dirtier coal or even gas plants from Ohio, from West Virginia,” said Ray Cantor, deputy chief government affairs officer for the New Jersey Business and Industry Association.


Cantor’s organization has launched a campaign to convince New Jersey leaders to again leave the program, and instead charge power plants $7 per ton of carbon emissions. The system would create about $135 million in annual revenue for New Jersey, according to an analysis commissioned by the business group, though Cantor acknowledges it would do little to curb pollution.


Others, however, say that the emissions and economic impacts made by investing RGGIrevenue are inarguable and invaluable. The investment of proceeds from 2024 alone are forecast to avoid 4.3 billion short tons of carbon emissions over their lifetime — roughly the amount of carbon released by burning 440 billion gallons of gasoline.


These investments also produce savings for consumers, largely through energy-efficiency measures, but also by supporting cost-cutting electrification and direct bill assistance, Tamayo said. In New England, the investment of RGGI revenue from 2025 should result in $1.3 billion in lifetime savings, according to her analysis.


“We can’t lose sight of that just because of a moment of high prices,” she said.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: SJC again upholds MBTA Communities housing law
description: As most cities and towns got into compliance with the housing law — eagerly or dragging their feet along the way — some holdouts were hoping that the state’s high court would rule that they did not have rezone. It was a longshot bid, after the SJC already upheld the law as enforceable by the attorney general’s office in early 2025.
text:
THE STATE’S HIGHEST court has swatted away a second challenge to the sweeping and controversial MBTA Communities housing law. In a brisk, unanimous, widely expected decision, the Supreme Judicial Court rejected the town of Marshfield’s bid to avoid compliance with the law on every argument it raised.  
Marshfield failed to show the 2021 law, which requires cities and towns near the MBTA system to zone for multifamily housing, cost the town anything beyond ordinary administrative work. And as it relates to the patchwork of local powers and other state regulations on housing, the court declared the act to be a “valid general law.”
In a 22-page decision upholding a lower court’s dismissal of Marshfield’s claims, Justice Serge Georges, Jr. wrote that the town’s complaint “does not plausibly allege” that the act or its regulations imposed an unfunded local mandate – the principal argument put forward by the town. Marshfield and its select board also lacked standing to bring a constitutional claim on behalf of town meeting voters, the court wrote. 
Lawmakers are not allowed to create mandates for cities and towns that would create substantial expenses without also providing a funding source for those expenses. But the court decided Marshfield did not offer specifics that would show that the MBTA zoning law imposed an impermissible “unfunded mandate.”  
As most cities and towns got into compliance with the housing law — eagerly or dragging their feet along the way — a few dozen holdouts were hoping that the state’s high court would rule that they did not have rezone. It was a longshot bid, after the SJC already upheld the law as enforceable by the attorney general’s office in early 2025. 
In a statement Friday afternoon, Attorney General Andrea Campbell applauded the ruling. 
“Massachusetts has a housing crisis, and it’s impacting everything from our ability to grow our workforce to the everyday cost of living,” she said. “Today’s decision by the SJC rejects Marshfield’s claim that the MBTA Communities Law is an unfunded mandate and reaffirms that the law is constitutional and compliance is mandatory.”
The law has been dogged by legal challenges since it emerged as part of a 2021 economic development bill signed by Republican Gov. Charlie Baker. His successor, Democratic Gov. Maura Healey, has embraced it as a showpiece policy to tackle the state’s dire housing crunch, while Republican gubernatorial hopeful Mike Minogue has castigated the policy as an offensive intrusion into local control that he plans to eliminate.
After Campbell took the town of Milton to court over its refusal to comply, and secured a ruling from the SJC backing the law last year, the path for resistance narrowed.
Methuen, Middleborough, and Wrentham asked the state auditor’s division of local mandates for an assessment on whether the law was an unfunded mandate. In February, the office sent letters concluding that it was, because it imposed more than incidental local administration expenses on municipalities. 
A group of municipalities, including Marshfield, took their case against the state and its housing office to Superior Court, arguing that implementing the law had created new costs and would lead to future cost burdens. Marshfield also claimed the law and its regulations infringed on town meeting voters’ constitutional rights, exceeded the Legislature’s authority under the Home Rule Amendment, and conflicted with the state’s Zoning Act.
A Superior Court judge dismissed the case in June, determining that the towns failed to show that the MBTA Communities law imposed an unfunded local mandate, nor did it unlawfully interfere with the town’s authority to develop and enforce zoning bylaws. 
The Supreme Judicial Court took the case up directly in late last year. 
Justices seemed skeptical during oral arguments in March, with Justice Dalila Wendlandt prodding the town’s attorney to concede Marshfield could have complied at essentially no cost by simply opening every zoning district to multifamily housing.
Though the town argued it had to bear costs from evaluating, preparing, and presenting proposed zoning amendments, the high court concluded that Marshfield did not offer proof that those costs were involuntary or anything more than “incidental local administration expenses.” 
As to arguments that the town would suffer future direct costs because of the housing law — either because of future rezoning efforts or possible infrastructure strain like increased students in need of local schools — the court said the claims were “too conclusory and speculative” to support that reading.  
The SJC gave little weight to the auditor’s office determination.  
It never identified any Marshfield-specific costs, and its conclusion doesn’t bind the court anyway, George’s wrote. The “ultimate legal question” on whether the town offers facts that establish an unfunded mandate “is one for the court,” he wrote. 
The town also argued that the law’s zoning requirement infringes on the constitutional voting rights of Town Meeting voters. But the high court concluded that because Marshfield is just a subdivision of the state, it cannot bring a constitutional challenge on behalf of town voters. 
As of August 31, 168 out of 177 MBTA Communities have submitted zoning plans to the state. Officials have determined 159 of them, including Marshfield, are fully or conditionally compliant, and say about 10,000 units are in the housing pipeline as a result of the transit-oriented housing law.
In an email after the ruling, Marshfield Select Board Vice Chair Eric Kelley said that he felt the town’s argument “was not effective on unfunded mandates.” 
The way the state has approached urging cities and towns into compliance was frustrating, he said. In his opinion, based on the way former Gov. Baker talked about zoning policy, the grants conditioned on the MBTA Communities law “were to be used as carrots for the community to accept and not as a stick to beat down the community to accept” and the law itself remains painfully “convoluted.”
Beyond Marshfield’s particular circumstances, the high court reaffirmed its position on the law’s legitimacy. 
Justices rejected the suit’s claim that the MBTA law deprived municipalities of meaningful authority to adopt or amend zoning bylaws, unless they adopted one that complies with MBTA Communities.
The state’s Home Rule Amendment does give municipal authority over local matters, Georges wrote, but “it does not prevent the Legislature, through a valid general law addressing a matter of statewide concern, from imposing substantive requirements that municipalities must implement through existing local procedures.”  
This law is aimed at addressing the state’s housing crisis, he wrote, a matter of serious public interest not tied to any one city or town that “falls squarely” within the Legislature’s authority.  
Nor does it violate procedure for local adoption or amendment of zoning laws, the court ruled. Marshfield had argued that the state zoning act sets out a system where the town amends its zoning through Town Meeting, but because the MBTA law requires compliant zoning it effectively forces the voters at Town Meeting to “vote yes” and approve the zoning. 
The SJC again rejected the argument. Town meeting voters retain the authority to debate, amend, approve, or reject any proposal placed before them,” Georges wrote. Rejecting one just means noncompliance. 
“That authority,” he wrote, “does not include the power to exempt the town from an obligation imposed by a valid state law.” 
This story is developing.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi’s Duff brothers again make Forbes list of richest people in the world
description: Thomas Duff, billionaire businessman and philanthropist, at KLLM Transport in Richland, Tuesday, June 17, 2025.
text:
Mississippi brothers James and Tommy Duff again made Forbes’ list of the top 400 richest Americans.
The billionaire brothers are the two wealthiest people in Mississippi, and they each saw their net worth rise from $4.1 billion last year to $4.5 billion, according to Forbes. They ranked 380 on the list.
Credit: Forbes
The Duff’s also made Forbes’ global billionaire ranking, with James coming in at 978 and Tommy at 982. 
The global list was topped by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX founder, with a current net worth of nearly $948 billion. Musk was the single largest overall political donor of the 2024 US election cycle, forking over hundreds of millions of dollars to support President Donald Trump. He later led Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, before leaving the administration in May of 2025.
Tommy Duff, 69, and Jim Duff, 65, built a multi-billion-dollar business empire that started as a small tire shop founded by their father. Southern Tire Mart, which is based in Columbia, now sells over 4 million new tires and 2.5 million truck tire retreads each year, Forbes said. The Duff brothers also cofounded and co-own Duff Capital Investors, a holding company with total revenue of $6 billion from more than 20 businesses.
Tommy Duff has been a political power broker in Mississippi and a philanthropist. He served an eight-year stint on the board of the state Institutions of Higher Learning, first appointed by then-Gov. Phil Bryant, and has been a major contributor to many Republican campaigns in Mississippi. 
He has said he is considering running for governor in 2027, but has not announced a decision.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado Springs leaders delay decision on Project Taurus data center
description: Members of the Colorado Springs City Council voted Thursday night to postpone a decision over a controversial data center project near Garden of the Gods. It came after a daylong hearing with hours of public comment and rebuttal from representatives of Raeden, the California-based company seeking to turn a former microchip factory into a large […]
text:
Raeden co-founder Jason Green speaks at a special hearing before the Colorado Springs City Council on Thursday. (Screenshot Colorado Springs City Council Facebook)Members of the Colorado Springs City Council voted Thursday night to postpone a decision over a controversial data center project near Garden of the Gods.
It came after a daylong hearing with hours of public comment and rebuttal from representatives of Raeden, the California-based company seeking to turn a former microchip factory into a large data center.
Colorado Springs police took three people into custody after a person claimed they were denied a chance to comment and the audience grew rowdy. There were shouts, boos and curses from the audience continually throughout the day.

A final decision on the project was delayed on a 7-2 vote until April.
“The one thing I’ve heard today, and it’s abundantly clear to me, is that we’re not ready,” Council member Roland Rainey said before motioning to postpone. “When it comes to accountability, rules and standards … that’s what I heard from a lot of the people who spoke today, that they want some type of standards, not just for this particular applicant, but for data centers in general.”
Majority of Coloradans dislike AI, new survey finds

Raeden wants to retrofit the former Intel chip factory near Garden of the Gods Road and Centennial Boulevard. The city’s planning department approved the proposal, dubbed Project Taurus, in June. After the planning commission upheld that approval, citizens appealed the decision to the City Council. That set the stage for Thursday, when the council was supposed to vote on whether the data center project is legal and meets code.
Council members instead want the time to seek answers about potential noise from the data center and how its energy use could impact everyday residential ratepayers. The developers have said the data center could draw up to 50 megawatts of power from Colorado Springs Utilities.
“This reminds of me of what happened with Ford Amphitheater, when we were promised whatever it took, and then we had no way to help the citizens, who even now years later are struggling to be able to sleep in their own beds (because of the noise),” Council member Dave Donelson said. “We wouldn’t be saying no to data centers. We’d be saying no to this data center at this location.”
Noise and electricity
Caitlin Quander, a land use lawyer representing Raeden, said the proposal is a simple adaptive reuse in a site that already allows data centers.
“We heard public comment and authentic emotion about hyperscale data centers, AI and the importance of the conservation of the environment. These are policy discussions happening nationally and at the state and local level. These are conversations that this city and its citizens can have at a broader level,” she said. “But this review and this project are different and specific. This is not a rezoning with broad criteria. This is not a referendum on data centers.”
Raeden co-founder Jason Green told members of the council that the project is not a hyperscale data center like those in Loudoun County, Virginia, which are the subject of intense community pushback over noise levels, including low frequency humming, and rising electricity demands. Houses sit about 400 feet from the site.
“We’ve answered every question that’s come our way and there have been demonstrable changes to the development plan at the behest of the community,” he said.
He said that includes having fully-enclosed generators and chillers placed as far away from houses as possible, and a 30-foot-tall wall on the perimeter of the property. The development plan also includes noise monitoring.
“We have no interest in there being a noisy data center. That’s not good for anybody,” he said.
Coloradans oppose data centers
But for those opposed, the vote over Project Taurus comes at a fraught political moment over big tech, data centers and the proliferation of artificial intelligence, which data centers support. A recent poll found that 75% of people oppose data centers in Colorado, and Coloradans overwhelmingly dislike tech giants like Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg.
“Large-load data centers like this one are the physical manifestation of the unchecked corporate power that reigns supreme in America, and the greed and recklessness of tech bro billionaires,” said Steph Vigil, a former Democratic state representative running for the Legislature again this year. “We are living in a second Gilded Age, and much like the first, rampant expansion of technology has come with empty promises to ordinary working people. We work harder, they get richer and the ecosystem is degraded just to serve their bottom line.”
On Sept. 9, Weld County Commission approved a plan from GlobalAI to develop what could be the largest data center in the state.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi River mayors call for water conservation protections amid growing data center demand
description: Melisa Logan, mayor of Blytheville, Ark., speaks at a press conference on the banks of the Mississippi River. Mayors representing more than 100 Mississippi River Basin communities met in Natchez, Miss., on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026, to announce a new framework and wish list for data center proposals.
text:
A group representing mayors from 10 states along the Mississippi River said they’re seeking regulation to help conserve water and “navigate the fast-growing AI data center economy.” 
The plan that the Mississippi River Cities & Towns Initiative announced Wednesday is to push in other states regulations modeled after legislation recently passed in Missouri, which bans the “mass exportation” of water. State lawmakers from Mississippi, Louisiana and Minnesota have committed to introducing similar bills, MRCTI said.
“As droughts persist and intense heat expands, the need to secure our water resources will only become more acute,” Sen. Derrick Simmons, a Democrat from Greenville, said at a press conference in Natchez during the group’s 15th annual meeting. “I am proud and eager to introduce a version of the Missouri bill that was enacted into law last year, and I hope to accomplish the same thing for Mississippi and get us closer to realizing a Mississippi River Compact.”
The group is modeling its Mississippi River Compact after the Great Lakes Compact, a 2008 agreement which Simmons said has kept the lakes’ water resources “secure and intact.” If enough states pass the export ban, the group can then push a federally recognized agreement through Congress, Minnesota state Sen. John Hoffman said at the news conference.
“With last year’s passage in Missouri and now three more states committing to move the legislation forward, we only need three more states to move us to the congressional level,” Hoffman said.
Missouri’s 2025 legislation requires anyone withdrawing water from the state and exporting it more than 30 miles outside the state to have a permit. The law does not apply to bottled water or packaged water intended for single use. 
MRCTI is a coalition, formed in 2012, made up of nearly 200 cities along the Mississippi River. Blytheville, Arkansas, Mayor Melisa Logan said Wednesday that 75% of the group’s member cities have been approached about hosting AI infrastructure. While usage amounts vary greatly, some research estimates that large data centers can use about 5 million gallons of water per day, largely for cooling, or the equivalent water use of a town of at least 10,000 people.

name: VTDigger
title: Federal government rejects winning bid for Montpelier’s former post office
description:
A local development corporation won the auction for 87 State St. in August, but the treasurer of the organization says the federal government wants more money for it. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Federal government rejects winning bid for Montpelier’s former post office.
text:
The building that houses the former Montpelier post office is up for auction, again. Seen on Thursday, June 11, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The federal government has rejected the winning bid for Montpelier’s former downtown post office building, throwing the future of the building into uncertainty. 
The 87 State Street Local Development Corporation, a nonprofit coalition of local organizations and developers, had made the winning bid of $540,000 in the auction that ended in August. On Friday, the group announced in a press release that the sale did not go through.
The treasurer of the corporation, Jon Copans, told VTDigger that he was surprised and frustrated by the decision to reject it. 
“Here we are again. It’s like Groundhog Day,” Copans said. 
The large marble-clad building at 87 State St. was significantly damaged by flooding in 2023, forcing the U.S. post office to relocate. The General Services Administration put the property on the market in 2025, and the Foundation for a Resilient Montpelier, a nonprofit flood recovery group, saw the possibility of turning it into a site for housing and businesses. 
But the two parties have been at odds since the beginning about the value of the property. The foundation walked away from a potential negotiated sale in early 2026, citing concerns about a report that showed widespread PCB contamination. Copans said at the time that the federal government was asking $2.4 million for the property. 
Instead, the foundation put together 11 local entities and secured state funding to bid on the property at open auction. However, Copans said federal government personnel told him this week that it was rejecting the bid because it was lower than the property’s value. 
“We believe there’s a fundamental misunderstanding of the market here in Vermont, the redevelopment realities of a property in a downtown with significant contamination, and significant questions about how serious that contamination is and how much it’s going to cost,” Copans said. 
The General Services Administration did not respond to a request for comment before publication time. 
Copans said the federal government indicated there would be another auction, but he’s not yet heard about the parameters, such as the timing. The sign advertising the initial auction still sits outside the building on State Street. 
An auction sign sits in front of the former Montpelier Post Office building on Friday, September 18, 2026. The building is up for auction again after the General Services Administration rejected a winning bid from a local developer. Photo by Tierney Flavin/VTDigger
He said the “fundamental reality” of the site’s importance to Montpelier hasn’t changed — the federal government has just added a few “perplexing” twists and turns to the process. 
“If you look out to the future, there is real opportunity in terms of the building and the property,” he said. “It’s just that we have to roll up our sleeves and work to get there.”
This story will be updated.

name: Delaware
title: Caesar Rodney Institute asks Delawareans to sign health care transparency petition
description: Policy group seeks support for legislation requiring medical professionals to clearly disclose their licenses and qualifications DOVER, Del. — The Caesar Rodney Institute is asking Delaware residents to sign an online petition supporting legislation that would require health care professionals to clearly identify their credentials before diagnosing or treati[...]
text:
Who is the physician assistant, the nurse, the nurse practitioner, and the doctor?   Image created by Delaware LIVE using AI on 9/18/26
Policy group seeks support for legislation requiring medical professionals to clearly disclose their licenses and qualifications
DOVER, Del. — The Caesar Rodney Institute is asking Delaware residents to sign an online petition supporting legislation that would require health care professionals to clearly identify their credentials before diagnosing or treating patients.
The petition calls on the General Assembly to revive and strengthen the Healthcare Professional Transparency Act, a 2024 proposal that did not advance to a vote.
CRI hopes signatures from patients, families and other community members will demonstrate public support for introducing the legislation again in 2027.
Michelle Parsons, M.D., director of CRI’s Center for Health Policy, said patients may not always understand whether the person providing their care is a physician, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or another licensed professional.
“Patients shouldn’t have to ask whether their doctor is actually a physician,” Parsons said. “They should already know.”
Petition calls for clearer identification
House Bill 447 would have required practitioners using the title “Doctor” to identify their educational degree and professional license. Most health care practitioners also would have been required to wear visible identification showing their license type.
The legislation also sought to require health care advertisements to accurately identify the professional licenses of the practitioners being promoted.
The bill was pulled before a committee vote in 2024 and was not brought back before the end of the legislative session.
Through its petition, CRI is asking Delaware lawmakers to bring the proposal back and strengthen its disclosure requirements. The institute wants patients to be told before receiving nonemergency care whether the person diagnosing or treating them is a physician, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or another licensed professional.
If a nonphysician uses the title “Doctor,” CRI wants that person’s profession disclosed at the same time.
“This isn’t about prohibiting earned academic titles or telling patients whom to choose,” Parsons said. “It’s about giving patients the information to make that choice for themselves.”
Expanded authority prompts questions
The petition follows Delaware’s expansion of the authority granted to several types of nonphysician health care professionals.
House Bill 141, enacted in 2021, eliminated the state’s previous collaborative-practice requirement for advanced practice registered nurses, including nurse practitioners. Nurse practitioners may independently evaluate patients, diagnose illnesses, order and interpret tests, prescribe medications and manage treatment.
Delaware has also expanded the role of pharmacists. Legislation approved in 2022 allowed pharmacists working under statewide protocols to test, screen and treat certain conditions. Additional legislation approved in 2026 broadened pharmacists’ authority to evaluate patients, identify certain health conditions, order laboratory tests and prescribe specified drugs and medical devices.
CRI said those changes make it more important for patients to understand the education, license and professional role of the person providing their care.
Some nurse practitioners earn a Doctor of Nursing Practice degree and may use the title “Doctor.” Parsons said that academic title is legitimate but does not mean the practitioner received the same education and clinical training as a physician.
An American Medical Association survey cited by CRI found that 39% of respondents identified someone with a Doctor of Nursing Practice degree as a physician. The survey also found that 19% believed a nurse practitioner was a physician and 17% believed a physician assistant was a physician.
CRI connects effort to AI protections
CRI is connecting its petition drive to House Bill 191, signed into law April 23. That law prohibits artificial intelligence and other nonhuman entities from being licensed as physicians, nurses, advanced practice registered nurses or physician assistants.
It also prohibits AI systems from using protected professional titles such as “Doctor” or “Dr.”
Parsons said the same principle — ensuring patients understand who or what is delivering their care — should apply to human health care professionals.
“If Delaware believes patients have a right to know when their ‘doctor’ is AI, surely they have a right to know when their ‘doctor’ isn’t a physician,” Parsons said.
Delaware law already requires a person using “Doctor” in connection with medicine or health care to specify the type of doctorate held. CRI contends, however, that existing law primarily regulates professional titles and does not require patients to be affirmatively told the license or professional classification of the person treating them.
CRI is asking Delawareans who agree with the proposal to add their names to the online petition and share it with friends, relatives and neighbors. The organization says broader community participation will strengthen its message to lawmakers ahead of the 2027 legislative session.
To Go Box

What: Caesar Rodney Institute Healthcare Professional Transparency Petition
What CRI is asking: Delawareans are encouraged to sign the petition urging lawmakers to revive and strengthen the Healthcare Professional Transparency Act.
Who may participate: Delaware patients, families, health care consumers and other supporters

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Secretary of State launches election-season ‘good questions’ campaign
description: The New Mexico Secretary of State on Sept. 18 launched a "good questions" campaign geared at answering voters questions for the Nov. 3 general election.
text:
The New Mexico Secretary of State's Office on Sept. 18, 2026, launched the "good questions" campaign intended to answer voters' questions heading into the Nov. 3 general election. (Screenshot)The New Mexico Secretary of State on Friday announced the launch of a new election-season campaign geared at answering voters’ questions.
The “good questions” campaign, according to a news release, was developed with Albuquerque-based Esparza Advertising and will appear as digital ads on a variety of sites, and on social media and radio. 
The state’s Sunshine Portal shows an approximate $64,600 contract with the agency by the SOS; Lindsey Bachman, the Secretary of State Office’s director of communications, legislative and executive affairs, said the campaign cost just under $60,000 before taxes.
The campaign, the Secretary of State’s office says, is intended to answer voters’ most common questions, all of which can be found on a dedicated webpage, and include queries such as: “Am I still registered?” and “Can I register on Election Day? 
Other questions delve into more political terrain, such as “Can noncitizens vote?” (the answer is no) and “Have changes with USPS or at the federal level changed my ability to vote by mail this year?” (the answer is also no).
US Supreme Court blocks Trump rule limiting mail voting, sides with Dem states

“With everything being said about the election this year, I have been really concerned about voters getting bad information about the process that keeps them from casting a ballot,” Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver said in a statement. “We know that New Mexicans have good questions about our elections, and the truth is that New Mexico runs some of the most accessible, secure and accurate elections in the country. We want to cut through the noise and provide voters with more information about what makes our process so great as well as the facts they need to safely vote and trust that their vote counted.”
The office’s news release notes the new campaign follows Toulouse Oliver’s previous efforts to combat rising election misinformation, including a Rumor versus Reality webpage and the 2024 “seeing is no longer believing” campaign focused on AI misinformation in elections.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Today’s politics make me feel like Dorothy in ‘The Wizard of Oz’
description: Dorothy knew song and dance are weapons that can strengthen resolve, remind us of our values, and focus us on the massive good out there.
text:
In the 1939 movie, “The Wizard of Oz,” our young heroine, Dorothy, is alone and terrified as a cyclone approaches. When I think about our national and international situation, I feel like Dorothy.
As the movie’s humongous, deafening storm moves in for the kill, a farm hand shouts, “It’s a twister!” Our world today feels like a twister–a horror movie-like chaotic cyclone of corruption, disruption, and turbo-charged hot air. 

Chris Amorosino

Unethical national leaders and their compliant underlings hurl out lies, falsehoods, and exaggerations that make me cringe. Their words and actions are more frightening than the lions and tigers and bears Dorothy fears meeting in the dark forest on her way to Oz. “Immigrants are stealing our jobs, oh my!” “Haitians are eating our pets, oh my!”  “Babies get 80 vaccines at once, oh my!”  We’ve got liars and tyrants, and fears, oh, my!
Even real news, factual reports, are so shocking they crash land in my mind like hurricanes of hyperbole. “CAIR, a Muslim Nonprofit, Gets a Terrorism Label in Florida and Texas,” screams a New York Times July 31 headline. A National Public Radio headline reads, “In Nebraska, Americans begin to lose Medicaid under [the current administration’s] work rules.” Slate.com adds to the gale with “[President’s] EPA Found a Sneaky New Way to Make Our Air More Polluted.”
But Dorothy’s example can save us. Remember the movie and ask yourself, “What would Dorothy do?” No matter what, she kept fighting to get home. Dorothy, naïve little Dorothy, never gave up even with a green wicked old witch screaming inches from her face the blood-curdling threat, “I’ll get you, my pretty, and your little dog too!”
In a foreign land Dorothy kept moving forward. She followed the wisdom of her senior advisor, Glinda, the Good Witch of the North: Follow the yellow brick road. Today Glinda would explain to a 2026 Dorothy that the yellow brick road is the rule of law, the U.S. Constitution, and our democratic norms. The road home is fighting our fears, maintaining our ethics, participating in our democracy, and upholding our values.
Granted, if I was Dorothy, I would not have picked a scarecrow, a tin man, and a cowardly lion to be my best buddies. But Dorothy was smart. She knew the worst thing would be to go it alone like the U.S. did in invading Venezuela and in killing at least 221 people on 67 alleged drug-trafficking vessels. Dorothy, a unifier, would not have pulled out of 66 international organizations, conventions, and treaties like the U.S. did in January 2026.
Today, when the most powerful person in the world announces he will use his power for a campaign of retribution against perceived enemies, a legitimate first response is for us to weep. Then learn. Then use our time and talents to act positively and peaceably. Write a letter. Lodge a protest. Fund a counter action. Spread the truth. Support a cause. Promote a candidate. That’s like clicking together the heels of Dorothy’s magical  ruby slippers. That’s how we use small but essential democratic tools to fight abuse, neglect, lies, lawlessness, and corruption. But taking positive, peaceful action isn’t the end.
We must dance and sing. In the movie, separated from family and having no idea how to get back to her Kansas home, Dorothy takes the time to sing. She skips arm in arm with her three best buds. Granted, she’s on a dangerous journey, but it’s no more dangerous than leaving the Paris Climate Agreement, ending USAID, rolling back EPA regulations, and starting a war in Iran for no reason.
Dorothy knew song and dance are weapons that can strengthen resolve, remind us of our values, and focus us on the massive good out there. Singing demonstrates unity as we unite with lyrics, chords, tempo, and rhythms. Singing binds us together in peace, goodwill, and beauty. When Oz’s Glinda sings, “Come Out, Come Out, Wherever You are” in Munchkinland can’t you envision that’s she’s talking about hope? Recent major decisions by our federal government make me envision a cabinet meeting where our leaders jump up and dance Gangnam Style as they belt out another song from the movie, “If I Only Had a Brain.”
Barbs, bombs, and bluster keep coming. We should keep coming, too. Keep talking. Unlike the cowardly lion in the movie, if I were king of the forest I’d remind us all of miraculous positive changes the nations of this world make happen. From 1945 to 1952 U.S. occupying forces turned the warmongering imperialist Japan into a democracy banned from using war to settle international disputes, giving women the right to vote, and breaking up giant farming monopolies. In 1945 Germany was in complete ruin. Twenty years later Germany was transformed into Europe’s economic powerhouse. And who foresaw the huge victory for freedom we witnessed in 1989 with the fall of the Berlin Wall? Great positive change comes not on our schedule but through our efforts when we stand up to aggressors with diplomacy, democracy, action, and policies that advance us all.
Early in the movie Dorothy wonders if there’s a place where we never get in trouble. No. Later she tells the cowardly lion that the wizard will fix everything. No. But somewhere over the ego, skies are blue and the dreams that we dare to dream really can come true.
Chris Amorosino lives in the Unionville section of Farmington.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: ICE agent Christian Castro released from Minnesota state custody, pleads not guilty in federal court
description: Christian Castro, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who shot a man through the door of a north Minneapolis home in January, was released Thursday evening on conditional bail from Hennepin County Jail, where he was held for state-level charges. At his first appearance at federal district court in St. Paul on Friday for […]
text:
Christian Castro, an ICE agent who prosecutors say shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in January and then lied about the circumstances surrounding the shooting, walks out of the courtroom after his first appearance at the U.S. District Court in Minnesota at the Warren E. Burger Federal Building in St. Paul, Minnesota Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Christian Castro, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who shot a man through the door of a north Minneapolis home in January, was released Thursday evening on conditional bail from Hennepin County Jail, where he was held for state-level charges.
At his first appearance at federal district court in St. Paul on Friday for a separate case, Castro pleaded not guilty to six charges of making false statements, stemming from six alleged lies he told FBI investigators after the shooting.
Castro had appeared in state court in downtown Minneapolis Thursday to face state charges of four counts of second-degree assault as well as one count of falsely reporting a crime.
ICE agent in Jan. 14 Minneapolis shooting makes first appearance in Minnesota state court

On Jan. 14, during the peak of Operation Metro Surge, Castro engaged in a car chase with Alfredo Aljorna, ending at Aljorna’s home in north Minneapolis. Castro and another ICE agent had mistaken Aljorna for another Latino man, according to an FBI affidavit. Aljorna exited his car and slipped as he tried to get inside his house, at which point Castro attempted to arrest Aljorna. Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, Aljorna’s roommate, tried to help Aljorna, leading to an 11-second scuffle between the three. After both men escaped and ran inside, Castro shot at them with the bullet passing through the front door and hitting Sosa-Celis in the leg before coming to a stop in the wall of a child’s bedroom, according to charging documents.
In an interview in the aftermath of the shooting, Castro told an FBI agent that Sosa-Celis and Aljorna had assaulted him with a broom and a snow shovel in a three-minute fight before Castro opened fire, leading to assault charges against the two men that were dropped after surveillance footage proved Castro’s statements false.
State prosecutors charged Castro in May, and a federal grand jury indicted him in early September. An assistant U.S. attorney in Minnesota had been pursuing hefty federal civil rights charges against Castro, but was instructed by Justice Department officials in Washington, D.C. to downgrade the charges. The attorney was then fired, CBS News reported, citing four unnamed sources familiar with the matter.
The state and federal cases are taking place simultaneously. Castro, who had refused to consent to extradition to Minnesota from a Texas jail for months, turned himself in to federal authorities in early September after a federal grand jury indicted him with the six charges. He was released on bond after appearing in federal court in McAllen, Texas, and ordered to appear in federal court in Minnesota for the Friday hearing. Castro drove up to Minnesota from Texas this week, where he was arrested Wednesday in downtown Minneapolis by the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension.
On Thursday, Hennepin County District Judge Paul R. Scoggin set bail at $200,000 if Castro agrees to not possess firearms, not contact witnesses, to be electronically monitored, to sign a waiver of extradition — an agreement to be extradited without a formal hearing in the future — and to surrender his passport to state authorities immediately if he gets it back from federal authorities.
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said that she expects Castro to file a motion to move the state case to federal court, which she said her office is prepared to litigate.
Castro was released on conditional bail from state custody at around 6 p.m. Thursday, according to the Hennepin County Sheriff’s jail roster. He wore a black suit and an ankle monitor to federal court Friday, a stark difference from the day prior, when he was still in state custody and appeared in state court in a glass-paneled box and an orange jail uniform.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Planned Parenthood endorses independent in Montana Senate race
description: Planned Parenthood’s political arm has endorsed the independent candidate in Montana’s U.S. Senate race, a rare departure by the organization that almost exclusively backs Democratic candidates.  Montana is uniquely positioned as a state that has all-Republican elected officials at the state and national level, but just two years ago voted to enshrine aborti[...]
text:
Planned Parenthood signage is seen in the Financial District neighborhood of Manhattan on April 16, 2021 in New York City. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)Planned Parenthood’s political arm has endorsed the independent candidate in Montana’s U.S. Senate race, a rare departure by the organization that almost exclusively backs Democratic candidates. 
Montana is uniquely positioned as a state that has all-Republican elected officials at the state and national level, but just two years ago voted to enshrine abortion rights in the state constitution by a 15-point margin. 
With the national GOP platform holding to an anti-abortion stance, groups focused on women’s reproductive healthcare have had two options in the Senate race for alternatives to Republican Kurt Alme — Democrat Alani Bankhead and independent Seth Bodnar. 
“Montana voters across the political spectrum overwhelmingly chose to protect reproductive freedom in their own constitution,”  said Alexis McGill Johnson, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Action Fund. “We know Seth Bodnar will meet this moment with the same clarity and represent the will of Montanans in the U.S. Senate.”
As of Friday, Bodnar is one of two candidates Planned Parenthood has endorsed who is not a registered Democratic candidate — Bill Hill, a nonpartisan in Alaska,  also received the endorsement. 
Planned Parenthood’s endorsement of Bodnar follows a recent poll by the Montana Free Press/Rutgers Eagleton showing him gaining ground in a three-way race, pulling 30% of the vote behind Alme’s 38%. Bankhead earned 16%.
Seth Bodnar during a 2025 military reunion event by alumni at the Canyon Club on the University of Montana on Friday, Sept. 12, 2025. (courtesy photo)
In the 2022 Dobbs decision, the U.S. Supreme Court overturned a longstanding precedent set in Roe v. Wade that said the constitution included the right to make a decision to have an abortion. The court had shifted to the right under President Trump’s first term, when he was able to appoint three justices to the bench. 
Non-GOP candidates see abortion as one way they can connect with voters in Montana. 
In a press statement, Bodnar used the endorsement to double down on his independent status and show his support for women’s decisions about their own bodies. 
“The government has no place in a Montanan’s doctor’s office, whether that government sits in Helena or Washington, D.C.,” Bodnar said in a statement. “Montanans already settled this at the ballot box, Republicans, Democrats, and Independents voted to protect it in our own constitution …That’s exactly the kind of decision I’ll always answer to Montanans on, not a party.”
Bankhead has also earned the support of national women’s rights groups. 
Earlier this week, her campaign announced an endorsement from the National Organization of Women Political Action Committee, which exclusively backs candidates with pro-choice policy positions. 
“NOW has been in this fight for 60 years, and they’ve never treated women’s rights as one issue,” Bankhead said in a statement to the Daily Montanan.  It’s reproductive freedom, it’s what you earn, it’s whether you can see a doctor, it’s whether you’re treated equally. That’s how I see it too.”
Kim Villanueva, chairperson for NOW PAC, said in a statement that this election “is personal” for women everywhere. 
“Our rights are being stripped away day by day, and the answer is simple — elect feminist candidates who won’t back down,” Villanueva said. 
Bodnar’s campaign used its endorsement to take additional shots at Bankhead, questioning her stance on reproductive rights and blasting associations she’s had with the conservative McLean Bible Church in Virginia and other conservative organizations in the past. 
“She belonged to a pro-MAGA megachurch whose pastor called abortion ‘a sin against God’ and who celebrated the overturning of Roe v. Wade,” said Kelly Webster, spokesperson for the Bodnar campaign. “While Bankhead may be comfortable with these far-right views, Montanans believe that a woman should have the right to make her own personal health care decisions without interference from politicians or anyone else.”
Bankhead’s policy stance as a candidate has always been pro-choice.
Alani Bankhead, a candidate for the United States Senate, speaks at the 2026 Montana Democratic Party Convention on June 20, 2026 at the Northern Hotel in Billings (Jenna Martin for the Daily Montanan)
In previous interviews with the Daily Montanan, she said everyone is allowed the freedom of religion, but that she does not believe in bringing religion  into politics. 
Bankhead said she attended McLean Bible Church while stationed in Washington D.C., until 2017.
Lon Solomon, who was the pastor at the time, has a sermon on his website titled “Abortion: the American holocaust,” but Bankhead said she never heard him preach any “anti-abortion rhetoric,” while attending the church. 
“I would never have gone to a church like that,” she told the Daily Montanan. “All I heard from him was to do the right thing.”
Bankhead said she is personally pro-choice, and her work with sex trafficking victims while in the military has given her a front row seat to the importance of allowing women to have agency over their bodies.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri train ride led to Kansas City-area measles case that’s exposed 250 people so far
description: It was the call Ray Dlugolecki had been dreading. And one he and other public health officials have been expecting. The assistant director at Jackson County Public Health learned on Sunday afternoon about a confirmed case of measles, not just in his agency’s jurisdiction, but in one of its own buildings. The previous week, an […]
text:
Jackson County health officials are still working to trace potential exposures to a single measles case reported Sept. 13. (photo submitted).It was the call Ray Dlugolecki had been dreading. And one he and other public health officials have been expecting.
The assistant director at Jackson County Public Health learned on Sunday afternoon about a confirmed case of measles, not just in his agency’s jurisdiction, but in one of its own buildings.
The previous week, an infected resident of eastern Jackson County had been inside the health department’s Lee’s Summit facility at 3651 N.E. Ralph Powell Road on two separate occasions.
Dlugolecki understood that the highly contagious virus, which has been spreading with increasing success in communities around the country, had finally reached his doorstep.
The welcome mat — a countywide vaccination rate too low for herd immunity — seemed to have made the scenario almost inevitable.
County officials said the person likely contracted the virus on an Amtrak train traveling from Sedalia to Chicago on Aug. 27.
And now, that single case has exposed more than 250 people in Jackson County to measles, a dangerous virus that had been all but eliminated in the United States only a few years ago. That number doesn’t include anyone across the state line in Johnson County who could have also been exposed.
“If we have pockets of individuals who are unvaccinated or can’t receive vaccines,” Dlugolecki said, “it gives the virus the opportunity to enter those communities and spread like wildfire.”
 A link to another case

Immediately after learning about the Lee’s Summit exposure, a team of six Jackson County Public Health employees came into the office to begin trying to trace the infected person’s movements and figure out where they could have been infected.
They worked into the night tracking down and notifying anyone who was in the room when the infected person was there or during a window after the person left. The measles virus can linger in the air as long as two hours.
So far, the health department has identified 251 people who had been exposed in Jackson County by this one case, including at least 10 who now have to quarantine for 21 days because they were not vaccinated or did not know their vaccination status.
And area health officials expect the number of people exposed to grow.
The team also traced the infected individual’s movements to public spaces in Overland Park, where the Johnson County Department of Health and Environment also opened an investigation.
Johnson County Health Director Charlie Hunt said no new cases had been identified by Sept. 16, but that could change, as symptoms can take seven to 14 days to show up.
Jackson County Public Health investigators said the local case is directly connected to another recent measles case of a Missouri resident who boarded Amtrak train 318, the Missouri River Runner, in Sedalia on Aug. 27 and rode to Chicago. Dlugolecki said evidence, including the timing of travel, symptom onset and epidemiologic information available, means the cases are likely linked.
According to state officials, two other measles cases have also stemmed from that person on the train — one in another person on board, and one in someone who lived in the same household — bringing the total cases related to the Amtrak exposure to four.
 A recipe for an outbreak 


To achieve herd immunity for measles, at least 95% of people must be vaccinated. But across the country growing distrust in public health and misinformation about vaccines has caused that number to fall below that threshold.
According to most recent data, in 2025 only 89.5% of Missouri kindergartners and 90.26% of Kansas kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps and rubella.
Recent data show a sharp rise in the number of parents seeking exemptions so their children can attend school without getting required shots. Missouri’s exemption rate jumped to 6.3% in the 2025-26 school year from 5.2% a year earlier, while Kansas’ jumped to 4.5% from 3.6%.
Growing fear stoked by misinformation about the safety of vaccines — including some coming from the White House — is likely partially to blame. And, since the COVID pandemic, public health guidance of almost any kind has been greeted with more skepticism overall.
But whatever the cause of declining vaccine coverage, the result is a population potentially ripe for an outbreak, KC-area public health officials said.
One infected person walking into a room with unvaccinated people could quickly spiral into a dangerous situation. In fact it is almost certain nine out of 10 unvaccinated people who are exposed will get sick.
“People have to realize there are constant sparks getting thrown,” said Nathan Koffarnus, an epidemiologist with the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services. “It’s just where they land, that’s the luck of the draw. … Now that there are more people walking around unprotected or underprotected, it’s a larger issue again.”
 How measles spreads

The measles virus spreads through the air when someone who is infected coughs, sneezes or talks. It can also be picked up from a contaminated surface like a countertop or table.
Two shots of the MMR vaccine, the recommended dose, are 97% effective, meaning if 100 vaccinated people are exposed, only three might develop the virus. That makes the MMR vaccine one of the most effective out there. For comparison, the influenza vaccine is typically only 30% to 50% effective, in large part because influenza, like the virus that causes COVID, mutates, creating a changing target that is more difficult for a vaccine to hit.
So far this year, of the 3,294 people known to have contracted measles in the United States, 95% were not vaccinated.
But rarely, people who get an MMR vaccine still get sick.
That was what happened in the recent Lee’s Summit measles case. Dlugolecki said the person at the center of the case had been vaccinated.
Catherine Satterwhite, executive director of the Center for Population Health and Equity at Kansas City University, said breakthrough cases happen with all vaccines. But in the case of measles, they are exceedingly rare.
“For somebody to have a breakthrough case, a lot of things have to happen,” she said.
Rarely, a person’s immune system doesn’t respond as expected to the vaccine, leading them to have less protection. It is also possible a vaccine could be somehow corrupted, possibly because it wasn’t stored at the proper temperature, causing it to provide less protection.
But even people who experience one of those extremely rare problems and get a breakthrough case of measles will still benefit from having been vaccinated, Satterwhite said. A breakthrough infection is usually less severe, comes with fewer serious side effects and is less easily passed on to others.
Satterwhite also said the Lee’s Summit breakthrough case provides a perfect illustration of why widespread vaccination is so important.
“We recommend vaccines on the population level to protect the people who either aren’t getting the (immune) response that we expect,” she said, “or who can’t get vaccinated.”
The few exceptions include infants. The first MMR dose isn’t recommended until a child turns 1, and the second is given around 5 years old. Some immunocompromised people also can’t receive the vaccine.
 The cost to health and taxpayers

Health officials hope that incidents like the recent exposure in Missouri cause more people to understand the risks of not getting the shots.
Just being exposed, even without symptoms, will require someone who is not vaccinated to quarantine for 21 days. And developing measles can cause serious illness, including pneumonia, encephalitis and, in rare cases, death. An ongoing outbreak in Pennsylvania is linked to four deaths so far.
The virus, which was responsible for 500 deaths every year before vaccines became available, was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000. But that status, achieved when there was no continuous spread for more than 12 months, is at risk.
Beyond the health costs of a measles outbreak, responding to infections costs tax money. The Washington Post reported that investigating a Colorado outbreak involving nine children and one adult earlier this year cost taxpayers half a million dollars.
Jackson County Public Health could not yet offer an exact price tag for their recent case, but  Dlugolecki said the agency has already dedicated more than 150 staff hours to the response. That includes epidemiology and communicable disease investigators, leadership, communications, nursing and staff temporarily reassigned from other areas of the health department to help identify and contact exposed individuals, verify immunity, provide quarantine guidance and coordinate follow-up, he said.
“That redistribution of staff also means other important public health work has had to pause or slow while the response is underway,” Dlugolecki said
Each exposed person may require multiple calls, vaccination record review, coordination with healthcare providers or employers, symptom monitoring and follow-up over the 21-day monitoring period.
“The larger point is that a measles response can become very resource-intensive very quickly, even when it starts with a single case,” Dlugolecki said. “Much of that burden comes from the number of people who may have been exposed and the amount of work required to make sure they are identified, informed and appropriately managed.”
 The vaccine worked too well?

Declining vaccination rates are the biggest reason the country is seeing more measles cases this year — the most in three decades. In some ways, said Koffarnus of the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, the vaccine may have been too effective.
“Cases have gone down so much over the past few decades that most people can’t remember ever knowing anyone that had it,” he said. “When you don’t see it and you don’t hear about it you think, ‘Well, that’s not something we have here in the United States.’ It’s tough for people to take that seriously and think, ‘Well, yeah, I probably should get the shot.’”
A popular meme often circulated among people who oppose the MMR vaccine involves “The Brady Bunch,” a 1960s sitcom. In a 1969 episode, the TV family happily navigates a measles outbreak, gleeful about time off school, appearing to experience very little distress.
People cite the show as an example of why measles isn’t much to worry about, an inaccurate view, health officials said.
But the truth is, the virus wasn’t much to worry about in recent years when vaccination rates reached 95% or higher. That wasn’t because the virus was no big deal — health experts are quick to point out —  but because the virus wasn’t spreading.
Clearly, that reality has changed, said Dlugolecki, something he didn’t expect when he began his public health career 13 years ago. He didn’t think waiting for the next report of a measles exposure would be part of his regular workload.
“I was shocked to see it come back as it has over the last couple of years,” he said. “I didn’t expect to see massive outbreaks in dozens of states with deaths being reported.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: More CT kids, youths accessing shelter services in 2026
description: The number of Connecticut youths accessing emergency shelters has increased by about 5% from 2025 to 2026, and resources are stretched.
text:
The number of Connecticut youths accessing emergency shelters has increased by about 5% from 2025 to 2026, and resources for that population are thin, homeless service providers said.
More than 970 children have accessed emergency shelter services in 2026, an increase from 928 in 2025 and 844 in 2024. Another 365 people aged 18 to 24 have accessed these services, according to data from the Connecticut Coalition to End Homelessness.
This comes at a time when the state has minimal shelter services for people under 18, said Stacey Violante Cote, of the Center for Children’s Advocacy. Late last year, the New Haven-based Youth Continuum shuttered under financial stress. This left only two youth shelters in the state — both in Fairfield County.
“It’s unsafe that we have minors that don’t have a place to go if they are kicked out of their house, or if they leave home,” Violante Cote said.
This has particularly posed problems for LGBTQ+ kids who might not be comfortable going into adult shelters, Violante Cote added.
Most children are accompanied by their parents, said Sarah Fox, chief executive of the Connecticut Coalition to End Homelessness. The increase is partly driven by rising costs of living and broader problems for families in making ends meet.
“All of these issues impacting our families have a direct impact on youth, and I do think that there’s a lot of areas that we need to focus on, including having resources ready for youth,” Fox said.
She added that the Connecticut Department of Education, which defines homelessness differently from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, likely has the more complete count.
In the education world, homeless students include those who are “doubled up” or sleeping on a friend or family member’s couch. The Department of Education also counts students who are living in hotels, where HUD typically does not.
This means that the state’s count of homeless students far outpaces numbers of youths accessing emergency services.
In the 2025-26 school year, state data shows that there were about 4,800 students experiencing homelessness. That made up about 1% of the total student population. That’s actually a slight decrease from 2024-25 when there were about 5,100 students experiencing homelessness.
Fox said that could be the result of an undercount. The students reported in the state’s data are those who come to the attention of the school district — they typically seek services and tell a school employee that they don’t have a stable place to sleep.
Violante Cote said for those students who are doubled up, sometimes it can be hard to get housing aid because many state services require that people be actually homeless — living on the streets or in shelters — before they can access the help. This can be a particular challenge for kids aging out of foster care, she said.
“We need to focus on housing and stability earlier and make sure that young people and families are connected to resources faster, so we can prevent housing instability,” Fox said.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware wins $16 million to strengthen charter schools
description: Five-year federal grant will support new and expanding programs while adding oversight and accountability measures DOVER, Del. — Delaware has secured a five-year, $16 million federal grant to expand access to public charter schools while strengthening the oversight, financial monitoring and support intended to ensure those schools deliver results for student[...]
text:
Photo: Classroom at the Sussex Academy, a charter school in Georgetown.
Five-year federal grant will support new and expanding programs while adding oversight and accountability measures
DOVER, Del. — Delaware has secured a five-year, $16 million federal grant to expand access to public charter schools while strengthening the oversight, financial monitoring and support intended to ensure those schools deliver results for students.
Grant could add about 1,900 seats
The Charter Schools Program grant begins Oct. 1. At least 90% of the money — approximately $14.4 million — will be distributed through competitive subgrants supporting the planning, opening, replication and expansion of charter schools.
Proposals will be evaluated based on educational quality, demonstrated community need, organizational readiness, financial sustainability and evidence of demand. If enough proposals meet those standards, the initiative has a five-year goal of increasing Delaware’s charter school enrollment capacity by approximately 10%.
About 19,000 students currently attend Delaware’s 23 charter schools. A 10% capacity increase could create room for approximately 1,900 additional students, although actual growth will depend on the proposals received and approved.
“Expanding opportunities for students cannot be about adding seats for the sake of adding seats,” Delaware Secretary of Education Cindy Marten said. “We have to start with what students and communities need and be equally focused on quality, strong implementation and accountability.”
Grant targets unmet educational needs
The Delaware Department of Education said the grant will target educational needs that are not being fully met by existing programs. Potential areas include alternative and therapeutic education, career and workforce pathways, rural education, dual-language instruction, literacy programs and flexible options for students who are older than their classmates or have not earned enough credits to graduate on schedule.
The initiative also seeks to improve charter school access for economically and educationally disadvantaged students, multilingual learners, students with disabilities and other groups that have faced barriers to educational opportunities.
“Charter schools are one part of Delaware’s public education system,” Marten said. “This investment gives us an opportunity to support strong educational models where there is documented need, learn from what is working, and use those lessons to expand opportunity across public education.”
Priority for underserved students and communities
Existing charter schools applying for replication or expansion funding will be judged partly on their academic performance and operational track records.
Proposals serving underserved communities, addressing transportation barriers or expanding opportunities for multilingual learners and students with disabilities may receive priority consideration. Programs offering workforce-connected education or replicating successful school models also may receive additional consideration.
State officials emphasized, however, that priority status will not allow an applicant to bypass the program’s quality, readiness or financial requirements.
Investment extends beyond individual schools
A portion of the federal award will be used to provide charter schools with technical assistance in governance, board development, fiscal management, regulatory compliance, leadership development and program implementation. The state also plans to establish peer-learning programs and professional communities where educators and school leaders can share successful practices.
The grant also calls for stronger charter-authorizing practices, including annual reviews of each participating school’s academic, financial and organizational performance.
“We are grateful for the partnership between the Delaware Department of Education and the Delaware Charter Schools Network,” said Kendall Massett, the network’s executive director. “We are equally grateful for this investment in our education system, and for what it makes possible for students across our state.”
Massett said the grant reflects “a shared vision for collaboration, flexibility, and support for the people and strategies best positioned to make a difference for students statewide.”
Schools will face continuing monitoring
Schools receiving subgrants will undergo continuing fiscal, program and performance monitoring. That process will include progress reports, budget reviews, site visits, performance evaluations and reviews of implementation milestones.
The Department of Education said it will use those findings to identify risks, direct additional assistance to struggling programs and take corrective action when necessary. An independent outside evaluator also will assess the initiative throughout the five-year grant period.
Lessons and successful practices identified through the program will be shared with both charter and traditional public schools through professional development, peer networks and other cross-sector programs.
First competition planned during opening year
The Community Funding Accelerator assisted Delaware with identifying the federal funding opportunity, determining the state’s eligibility and preparing the application.
During the grant’s first year, the Department of Education plans to establish its management and accountability systems, consult with education stakeholders and provide technical assistance to prospective applicants. It also will release the first competitive funding opportunity, train application reviewers and select the first group of grant recipients.
Details about eligibility, application requirements, available award amounts and deadlines will be announced as the first competition is developed.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: ‘I plant seeds’: Harrisburg teacher named South Dakota teacher of the year
description: A third-grade teacher for the Harrisburg School District was recognized as South Dakota’s 2027 teacher of the year at a banquet Wednesday in Fort Pierre. Christina Berger has taught at Liberty Elementary School for the last eight years, though she has more than 20 years of experience in elementary education. She started her career in […]
text:
Christina Berger teaches a class of third-graders at Liberty Elementary School in the Harrisburg School District. Berger was recognized as South Dakota's 2027 teacher of the year. (Courtesy of the South Dakota Department of Education)A third-grade teacher for the Harrisburg School District was recognized as South Dakota’s 2027 teacher of the year at a banquet Wednesday in Fort Pierre.
Christina Berger has taught at Liberty Elementary School for the last eight years, though she has more than 20 years of experience in elementary education. She started her career in North Dakota.
In a video recognizing Berger as a regional teacher of the year, Berger said she loves teaching “because who wouldn’t love organized chaos?”
Berger said helping children learn, especially in reading, and connecting with each of her students on a personal level brings joy to her career. That drive to create lasting relationships extends to parents and community members through her involvement in the district’s Parent-Teacher Organization and by hosting student teachers throughout her career.
“I plant seeds,” Berger said of her role as an educator, “and you get to see the result years and years later.”



 Christina Berger, South Dakota’s 2027 teacher of the year, is featured in a video when she was honored earlier as a regional teacher of the year. (Courtesy of South Dakota Department of Education)
Liberty Elementary Principal Aaron Weaver said in a news release that Berger’s influence reaches beyond the classroom.
“She leads with heart, integrity and an unwavering commitment to doing what’s best for kids,” Weaver said.
The teacher of the year recognition means she’ll serve as a representative for South Dakota public education across the state and country, including attending the National Teacher of the Year Program Orientation, Space Camp, Washington Week, and the Impact and Influence Virtual Conference.
South Dakota Secretary of Education Joe Graves said in the news release that Berger earned the award because she’s “crafted her own legacy in the Harrisburg School District.”
“Her colleagues, students, and parents positively compliment her and her teaching style with a common takeaway of every child feeling seen, valued, and supported,” Graves said.

The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
